Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write

# Write a test suite

> Write test cases, modules and elements by hand, in CSV or YAML.

Writing a suite by hand is the most direct way to create tests, and it's how most edits happen once a suite exists. You need a text editor or a spreadsheet app. This page covers the three files a suite is made of, in the order we recommend writing them.

## Set up a project

Create a project with `optics init`, then fill in its files:

```shell
$ optics init birch-tests
```

Pick **(Blank project)** when asked for a template. You get this layout:

```tree
birch-tests/
├── config.yaml                  # what to drive
├── test_cases/test_cases.csv    # which flows run
├── modules/modules.csv          # the steps
└── test_data/elements.csv       # names for things on screen
```

Optics finds each file by what's inside it, not by its name or folder. A CSV whose first row is `test_case,test_step` is a test-cases file wherever it sits. You can split a big suite across several files of each kind. If you haven't set up `config.yaml` yet, [Install Optics](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/install) and the [platform guides](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/) show what to put in it.

## Choose CSV or YAML

Both formats load into the same suite, and one project can hold both. Pick the one your team reads best:

- **CSV** opens in any spreadsheet. Each step is one row, so a diff shows exactly which step changed.
- **YAML** keeps a whole flow in one indented file, which reads well in a code editor.

The examples on this page show both. Choose a tab and the rest of the page follows. [Write tests in YAML](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/yaml) covers the YAML rules in detail.

## Name the things on screen

Start with **elements**: a name for each field, button or label your test touches, and how to find it.

**CSV**

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
email_field,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email']
password_field,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password']
sign_in,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']
sign_in,Sign in
search_bar,Search Birch
password,correct-horse
```
**YAML**

`birch.yaml`:

```yaml
Elements:
  email_field: "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email']"
  password_field: "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password']"
  sign_in: ["//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']", "Sign in"]
  search_bar: Search Birch
  password: correct-horse
```

The header is `Element_Name,Element_ID`, in any case. Repeat a name, or give a list in YAML, to add **fallbacks**: Optics tries the values in order until one works. Here `sign_in` is found by its id, or by its text if the id changes.

A value can be an XPath, visible text, or the file name of a picture of the element. [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define) explains each kind and when to use it.

**Tip:**
Elements can hold test data too, such as `email,ava@birch.shop`. Keeping data next to locators means one file holds everything that changes between environments.

## Write the steps as modules

A **module** is a named list of steps. Each step is one [keyword](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/) and its values.

**CSV**

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Launch Birch,Launch App
Sign In,Enter Text,${email_field},ava@birch.shop
Sign In,Enter Text,${password_field},${password}
Sign In,Press Element,${sign_in}
Sign In,Assert Presence,Picked for you
Add To Cart,Press Element,${search_bar}
Add To Cart,Enter Text Direct,trail runner
Add To Cart,Press Element,Trail Runner 2
Add To Cart,Press Element,Add to cart
Add To Cart,Assert Presence,Added to cart
```
**YAML**

`birch.yaml`:

```yaml
Modules:
  - Launch Birch:
      - Launch App
  - Sign In:
      - Enter Text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop
      - Enter Text ${password_field} ${password}
      - Press Element ${sign_in}
      - Assert Presence "Picked for you"
  - Add To Cart:
      - Press Element ${search_bar}
      - Enter Text Direct "trail runner"
      - Press Element "Trail Runner 2"
      - Press Element "Add to cart"
      - Assert Presence "Added to cart"
```

How a step is read:

- **Keyword names** are case-insensitive. `Press Element`, `press element` and `press_element` all work.
- **Values** fill the keyword's parameters in order. Add more `param_3`, `param_4` columns when a keyword needs them. Empty cells are skipped.
- **`${name}`** is replaced by the element or variable called `name`. A whole cell such as `${email_field}` tries each fallback in turn. Inside other text, such as `Hello ${first} ${last}`, Optics replaces each variable with its first value when the step runs. [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables) gives the full rules.
- **Named values** like `index=1` or `timeout_str=20` set one parameter by name, so you can skip the ones in between. They only work with the keyword's real parameter names, which the [keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/) lists. A first cell that starts with `text=`, `css=` or `xpath=` is a locator, not a named value: `Enter Text,text=Email,ava@birch.shop` types into the field that shows "Email".
- **`store_as=name`** keeps the value that the keyword returns, so later steps can use `${name}`. [Keep a value for later](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables#keep-a-value-for-later) shows how.
- **Plain text** such as `Add to cart` is used as-is. For `Press Element`, plain text means "the element showing this text".

**Values with commas in CSV:**
A comma ends a CSV cell. Wrap a value that contains commas in double quotes, and double any quotes inside it: `"{""script"": ""mobile: pressKey""}"`. Spreadsheet apps do this for you when they save as CSV.

### Wait for the screen before you act

Action keywords like `Press Element` and `Enter Text` act on the screen as it is at that moment. They don't wait for a page to finish loading. After a step that changes screens, add a check that waits, such as `Assert Presence` (waits up to 30 seconds by default). The `Sign In` module above does this with `Assert Presence,Picked for you`.

## Combine modules into test cases

A **test case** is a flow made of modules, run in order. List one row per module:

**CSV**

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
Suite Setup,Launch Birch
Shopper can buy running shoes,Sign In
Shopper can buy running shoes,Add To Cart
```
**YAML**

`birch.yaml`:

```yaml
Test Cases:
  - Suite Setup:
      - Launch Birch
  - Shopper can buy running shoes:
      - Sign In
      - Add To Cart
```

A test case named **Suite Setup** runs once before the others, and **Suite Teardown** runs once after them. [Organise a suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/organise) covers setup, teardown and sharing modules.

## Check the suite, then run it

Check that every keyword exists and every `${name}` is defined, without touching the device:

```shell
$ optics dry_run birch-tests
```

When the dry run passes, run the suite for real:

```shell
$ optics execute birch-tests
```

## See also

- [Keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/)
- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define)
- [Project files reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files)
- [Record a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) to build modules by doing the flow

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record

# Record a test

> Build a test by running steps one at a time against the live app, then save the ones that worked.

`optics live` opens an interactive session next to your device or browser. You type a step, Optics runs it straight away, and you see whether it worked. Every step that succeeds is recorded. When the flow is done, `/save` writes it into your suite as a module, ready for `optics execute`.

## Before you begin

You need a project with a working `config.yaml` that has **exactly one** driver enabled. Any project from `optics quickstart` or the [first test tutorial](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/first-test) works. For a phone, start the Appium server and your emulator first. See [Android](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android) or [iOS](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios).

## Start a session

```shell
$ optics live birch-tests
```

Leave out the folder to use the current one. Optics opens the app straight away (it runs `launch_app` for you), so the first line of the session is already a recorded step.

The screen has three parts:

```terminal
  ✓ launch_app
     1.21s
  ✓ enter_text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop
     0.48s  [XPath]
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
› press_element "Sign in"
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
appium:emulator-5554  ·  rec ●  ·  /help · /quit · Tab complete · Ctrl-K keywords · Ctrl-N AI mode
```

- **History**, at the top: each step with ✓ or ✗, how long it took, and how the element was found (`[XPath]`, `[Text]`, `[OCR]` or `[Image]`).
- **Input**, in the middle: where you type.
- **Status bar**, at the bottom: the device or browser you're connected to, and `rec ●` to show recording is on.

## Run steps

Type a keyword and its values, separated by spaces, and press Enter:

```terminal
› enter_text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop
› enter_text ${password_field} "correct horse"
› press_element "Sign in"
› assert_presence "Picked for you"
```

- Write keyword names in `snake_case` or in words: `press_element`, `Press Element` and `press element` all work.
- Put quotes around a value that contains spaces.
- Type `${` to pick from the elements already defined in your project.
- Put a name inside a longer value, such as `enter_text ${email_field} "ava+${tag}@birch.shop"`. Live uses the first value of `tag`. A name that is not defined fails the step.
- Type `name=value` to give a parameter by name. For example, `press_element "Add to cart" index=1` presses the second match. On Appium, `index=` also picks among native elements with the same text.
- Type `go_back` to go back one screen. Type `assert_text ${greeting} "Hi, Ava"` to fail the step when the element shows other text.
- Press Tab to complete a keyword name. The rest of its parameters appear in grey as a hint.
- Press Ctrl+K to browse every keyword.

If a step fails, it's shown with ✗ and the reason, and it isn't recorded. Try a different value and run it again. Only steps that work end up in your test.

## Save the recording

When the flow works, save it with a test case name and a module name:

```terminal
› /save Checkout Sign_In
  • Saved 4 step(s) → module 'Sign_In' in modules/modules.csv, test case 'Checkout' in test_cases/test_cases.csv
```

Optics then:

- appends the steps to `modules/modules.csv` as the module `Sign_In`,
- adds new elements to your elements CSV, or creates `elements/elements.csv` when the project has none,
- adds a `Checkout,Sign_In` row to `test_cases/test_cases.csv`,
- copies the session's screenshots to `execution_output/Sign_In/`,
- clears the recording, so the next steps you run become the next module.

Run more steps, then `/save Checkout Add_To_Cart` to add a second module to the same test case.

**Note:**
Names in `/save` can't contain spaces. Use underscores, or rename the module in `modules.csv` afterwards. If the module or test case already exists, Optics asks you to run the same `/save` again to confirm that you want to append to it.

`/save` writes the steps as you typed them. If you typed `press_element "Sign in"`, the module uses the text `Sign in`. To use a named element instead, type `${sign_in}`, or edit `modules.csv` afterwards and add the element to `elements.csv`. `/save` always writes CSV, even in a project that uses YAML.

`/save` does not write a value that you type into a secret field, such as a password. The step `enter_text ${password_field} "correct horse"` is saved as `Enter Text,${password_field},${password_field_value}`. The elements CSV gets the row `password_field_value,<redacted>`. Before you run the test, put the real value in that row, or read it with `Read Data`. See [Hide sensitive values](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables#hide-sensitive-values).

**Tip:**
When a password field is on screen, `/save` also hides a value that you type into a raw locator, such as `enter_text css=#user-name ava`. This makes sure that no password goes into your files. To keep the value, press the field first, or type into a named element, such as `${email_field}`.

## Commands and keys

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/save <test_case> <module>` | Save the recorded steps as a module in a test case. |
| `/elements` | Show every element defined in the project. |
| `/screenshot` | Save a screenshot to `screenshots/`. |
| `/device` | Pick a different connected phone or emulator (Appium only). `/device <id>` switches directly. |
| `/help` | Show help. |
| `/quit` | Leave. If you have unsaved steps, Optics warns you once; `/quit` again discards them. |

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| Enter | Run the step. |
| Tab / Shift+Tab | Complete a keyword or element name. |
| ↑ / ↓ | Recall earlier input. |
| Ctrl+K | Browse keywords. |
| Ctrl+N | Switch to plain-English mode. See [Describe a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe). |
| Ctrl+X | Stop a plain-English run. |
| Esc | Close a popup. |
| Ctrl+C or Ctrl+D | Quit. |

On Android, plugging in a new phone during a session switches to it automatically and opens the app.

## Where files go

| Path | What's in it |
|---|---|
| `modules/modules.csv`, `test_cases/test_cases.csv` | Saved modules and test cases |
| `screenshots/session_<time>/` | Screenshots from every step in the session |
| `logs/optics_live_<time>.log` | A full log of the session, useful when a step fails for unclear reasons |

## If it isn't working

- **"optics live needs a config.yaml…"**: run it from a project folder, or pass the folder: `optics live my_project`.
- **"optics live supports exactly one enabled driver"**: set `enabled: false` on every driver in `config.yaml` except one.
- **Every step fails with "run `launch_app` first"**: the app didn't open. Check that the Appium server is running and the device is connected (`optics doctor my_project`), then type `launch_app`.

## See also

- [Describe a test in plain English](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe)
- [Write a test suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write)
- [Keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe

# Describe a test in plain English

> Tell Optics what to do in a sentence, let an AI model drive the app, and keep the steps it took.

In plain-English mode, you type a goal like *add trail runners to the cart*. An AI model looks at the screen, picks one keyword at a time, and runs it on the real device until the goal is done. The steps it took are recorded like any other `optics live` steps, and `/save` writes them into your suite.

It works with Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, or a model you run yourself. It's the fastest way to draft a long flow, and the result is ordinary keywords you can read and edit.

## Before you begin

You need:

- A project that works in [`optics live`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record).
- An API key for an AI model, or a local model server such as Ollama.

### Install the AI engine

Pick the engine for the account you have:

| You have | Install |
|---|---|
| A Gemini API key, or Google Cloud Vertex AI | `gemini` |
| An OpenAI or OpenRouter key, Azure OpenAI, or a local model in Ollama, vLLM or LM Studio | `openai` |
| A Claude API key, or Claude on Amazon Bedrock or Vertex AI | `anthropic` |

Install that name, for example:

```shell
$ optics setup --install gemini
```

### Turn it on in config.yaml

Add an `llm_models` section to your project's `config.yaml`, using the same name:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
llm_models:
  - gemini:
      enabled: true
```

For a server such as OpenRouter or Ollama, add its `url`. Gemini uses `gemini-2.5-flash` unless you set a `model`. The other engines need one. Pick a model that accepts images, or set `vision: never` in [Agent settings](#agent-settings). See [llm_models](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#llm-models) for every setting.

### Give Optics your key

Set the engine's key in the terminal you run `optics live` from:

**macOS and Linux**

```shell
$ export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key"
```
**Windows**

```powershell
PS> $env:GEMINI_API_KEY = "your-key"
```

Use `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or the variable you named in `api_key_env`. A local server needs no key.

You can also give the key in `config.yaml`, under `capabilities.api_key`. Optics uses it before the environment variable.

**Tip:**
Write the key as a reference, such as `api_key: ${GEMINI_API_KEY}`. Optics reads the variable when it loads the file, so you can commit `config.yaml` with your tests and keep the key private.

## Describe a flow

Start `optics live`, then press Ctrl+N. The prompt changes from `›` to `ai ›`. Type what you want in plain English:

```terminal
ai › add trail runners to the cart
  ⋯ [ai] add trail runners to the cart
     thinking: open search and look for the shoes
    ✓ press_element '//*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/search"]'
       0.42s  [XPath]
    ✓ enter_text '//*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/search_input"]' 'trail runner'
       0.51s  [XPath]
     thinking: Trail Runner 2 is the first result
    ✓ press_element '//android.widget.TextView[@text="Trail Runner 2"]'
       0.88s  [XPath]
    ✓ press_element '//*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/add_to_cart"]'
       0.37s  [XPath]
  ✓ [ai] add trail runners to the cart
     done · 4 step(s) · 9.4s · recorded 4 (/save to keep)
```

Each turn, the model sees the screen as rows, such as `e7 button "Search Birch" [tap] #search`. It also sees the last 8 steps, your project's element names and the keyword list. The model picks one action on a ref, such as `e7`, and names the text that the next screen must show. Optics runs the action with a locator that matches only that element. Then it reads the screen again and judges the step as pass, fail or unknown.

The model's thoughts appear as `thinking:` lines. Every action is a normal keyword, and the history shows the locator it used.

Press Ctrl+X to stop a run, or Ctrl+N again to go back to typing keywords. You can mix both modes in one session.

## Keep the steps

The model ends a run with `done` and the text that proves the goal. Optics accepts `done` only when that text is on the screen. If the model gives no text, the run ends as `PASS (unverified)`. Check the app yourself before you keep those steps.

When the run ends with `done`, Optics asks the model to remove dead ends and detours. Only the steps that mattered stay.

Save the steps the same way as a manual recording:

```terminal
ai › /save Checkout Add_To_Cart
```

Optics records only runs that end with `done` or `PASS (unverified)`. If the model gives up, reaches its step limit, or you stop it, Optics records nothing from that run.

### Review what you saved

The agent turns each element it acts on into a named element, such as `${add_to_cart_button}`. Its values are the element's locators, then its label as the last fallback. If a project element has the same first locator, the agent uses that element. `/save` writes the steps to `modules/modules.csv` and the new elements to your elements CSV. Read both before you commit them. See [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define).

## Write goals the model can finish

- **Describe one outcome per instruction.** *Sign in as ava@birch.shop* works better than a whole checkout in one sentence. Run several instructions in a row instead.
- **Use the words on screen.** *Tap Add to cart* is clearer than *buy it*.
- **Give values explicitly.** *Search for "trail runner"*, not *search for shoes*.

A run stops when one of these occurs:

- It reaches `max_steps` steps (15 by default).
- 3 steps in a row fail.
- The model asks for a fourth blind action in a row, such as a scroll, a swipe, a key press or a coordinate tap.
- The screen does not change after 4 actions in a row.
- Optics rejects `done` two times, because the goal text is not on the screen.

Break long flows into smaller goals.

## Agent settings

Add an `nl_agent` section to `config.yaml` to change how the model works:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
nl_agent:
  vision: auto
  max_steps: 15
  escalation_model: ""
```

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `vision` | `auto` | When the model gets a screenshot. `auto`: on the first turn, after a step that did not pass, when the screen has fewer than 3 controls or a control without a label, and when Optics cannot read the rows. `always`: every turn. `never`: no screenshots, so a text-only model works. |
| `max_steps` | `15` | The most steps in one run. The minimum is 1. |
| `escalation_model` | `""` | A second model of the same engine for hard turns: a retry after a bad reply, a turn after 2 failures in a row, and a turn after a warning. Empty uses one model for all turns. |

## Limits

- Each step is a call to the model, so a run costs API usage and takes several seconds per step.
- The screen rows, and some screenshots unless `vision` is `never`, go to your model provider. Run the model locally for screens that show data you cannot send to a third party.
- AI self-heal is off during a plain-English run, so every step the model takes shows in the history.

## See also

- [Record a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record)
- [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal), which uses the same model to recover a failing step during a run
- [Let your AI agent build tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent

# Let your AI agent build tests

> Connect Optics to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client so your agent can drive a device and write the suite.

`optics mcp` is a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server. It gives an AI agent eyes and hands on a phone, TV or browser. The agent reads the screen as a list of rows, acts on a row by its reference, and sees what changed after each action. The agent explores your app, then writes an ordinary Optics suite that you review and run with `optics execute`.

The agent is yours. Optics doesn't call any AI service in this mode, so it works with whichever model your client uses.

## Before you begin

- An MCP client, such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or VS Code.
- A target to drive: a browser (Playwright needs nothing else), or a phone or emulator with an Appium server running. See [Platforms](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/).

### Install the MCP server

The installer includes the MCP server, so if you used it there is nothing to do. With pip, install the `mcp` extra in the same environment as Optics:

```shell
$ pip install "optics-framework[mcp]"
```

### Add Optics to your client

**Claude Code**

```shell
$ claude mcp add optics -- optics mcp
```
**Claude Desktop**

Add this to `claude_desktop_config.json` (**Settings → Developer → Edit config**), then restart Claude Desktop:

`claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "optics": { "command": "optics", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```
**Cursor**

Add this to `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project, or `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project:

`.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "optics": { "command": "optics", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```
**VS Code**

Add this to `.vscode/mcp.json`:

`.vscode/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "optics": { "type": "stdio", "command": "optics", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```

If your client can't find `optics`, use its full path, for example `~/.optics/bin/optics`.

### Ask for a test

Describe the flow and where the app runs. The agent starts a session, explores, and writes files:

```text
Use the optics tools to open https://www.saucedemo.com in Playwright.
Sign in as standard_user / secret_sauce, add the backpack to the cart,
and check that the cart badge shows 1. Then write it as an Optics suite
in ./checkout, run optics dry_run on it, and tell me how to run it.
```

For a phone app, include the Appium details: *start an appium session at http://127.0.0.1:4723 with platformName Android, deviceName emulator-5554, appPackage com.birch.shop*.

### Review and run the suite

The agent writes the same files you would: test cases, modules and elements, in CSV. Read them like a colleague's pull request, then run them:

```shell
$ optics execute checkout
```

## What the agent can do

The server gives the agent:

- **Session tools**: `start_session` (picks the driver, URL and device settings, and opens the app) and `terminate_session`.
- **Tools that act on the screen**: `tap`, `type_text`, `scroll`, `press_key`, `launch_app` and `check`. `observe` lists the screen and can add a screenshot. `run_keyword` runs any other keyword, such as `assert_text`.
- **Resources to read**: the steps the session ran as CSV rows, the current screen, the raw UI tree and the keyword catalogue. `optics://project-format` teaches the agent how to write suite files. `optics://browser-profiles` lists the Chrome and Edge profiles on your machine.

The screen comes back as rows such as `e4 input "Login" [tap] #login-button`. The agent taps `e4`, and Optics uses a locator that matches only that element. Each action returns the rows that changed. When the agent adds the text it expects, such as `expect_present: ["Products"]`, the reply also gives a `verified` verdict. Optics waits up to 5 seconds for that text, so a page that loads late can still pass.

A typical session goes: start a session, act on rows, check the result, read the steps and the project format, write the files, run `optics dry_run`, and end the session. The [MCP reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp) lists every tool and resource. For one tool per keyword, start the server with `--toolset full`.

## Keep the agent on track

- **The agent asks you before it signs in.** For a website that needs a sign-in, the agent reads `optics://browser-profiles`. It asks you which profile to use. If you choose none, it asks you for the credentials. Only a server that starts with the default `stdio` transport accepts a profile. See [Sign in with a browser profile](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp#sign-in-with-a-browser-profile).
- **Agents tap by reference, not by position.** The server hides coordinate taps by default, because those tests break on any other screen size. To allow them, set `OPTICS_MCP_ALLOW_COORDINATE_TAPS=1` before you start the server.
- **The steps resource is the start of the suite.** `optics://session/{id}/steps` gives the module and element rows for each step that passed. A typed password shows as `<redacted>`, so the agent must replace it. Ask the agent to run `optics dry_run` before it finishes.
- **Loops and conditions** (`Run Loop`, `Condition`, `Read Data` and the rest) aren't tools, because they only make sense inside suite files. The agent can still write them into modules.
- **Sessions are private to the server.** `optics serve` and `optics live` cannot see a session started over MCP. It ends when the server stops, or after 15 minutes without a call. When more than one session is open, the agent must pass `session_id`. The error lists the ids.

**Run the server over HTTP**
By default the server talks to one client over standard input and output. To share it on a network, or run it in a container, start it in HTTP mode:

```shell
$ optics mcp --transport http --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8090
```

Then point your client at `http://127.0.0.1:8090/mcp`:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "optics": { "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8090/mcp" } } }
```

The server has no authentication. Keep it on `127.0.0.1` or a trusted network.

**Let the agent recover failing steps with AI self-heal**
Self-heal uses an AI model to recover a step when every locator fails (see [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal)). Over MCP it's controlled by environment variables on the server, or by `ai_self_heal: true` in `start_session`:

```shell
$ export OPTICS_AI_SELF_HEAL=1
$ export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key"
$ optics mcp
```

For OpenAI, Claude or a local model, also set `OPTICS_LLM_PROVIDER`, `OPTICS_LLM_MODEL` and the engine's key. See [Environment variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp#environment-variables).

When a step is healed, the `result` of the reply includes `"healed": true` and the steps that worked, so the agent can update the suite.

## See also

- [MCP server reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp)
- [Describe a test in plain English](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe), the built-in AI mode
- [Run keywords over HTTP](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/http-api)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python

# Use Optics from Python

> Call Optics keywords from pytest or any Python script when a test needs real code.

Every keyword is also a method on the `Optics` class. Use it when a test needs logic the suite files can't express, or when your team already runs everything through pytest. You keep the same fallbacks, OCR and image matching as a CSV suite.

**Note:**
If CSV or YAML files can express your test, prefer them. Anyone on the team can read and review a suite file, and the runner gives you the step tree, screenshots and error detection for free. See [Choose how to create tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/).

## Write a test with pytest

This test signs in to the Sauce Labs demo store, adds a backpack to the cart, and checks the cart badge and the price in the cart. It runs as written with `pip install "optics-framework[playwright]" pytest`.

`test_checkout.py`:

```python
import pytest
from optics_framework import Optics

CONFIG = {
    "driver_sources": [{"playwright": {"enabled": True}}],
    "elements_sources": [
        {"playwright_find_element": {"enabled": True}},
        {"playwright_page_source": {"enabled": True}},
        {"playwright_screenshot": {"enabled": True}},
    ],
}

@pytest.fixture
def optics():
    with Optics(CONFIG) as session:  # quits the browser when the test ends
        yield session

def test_shopper_can_add_a_backpack(optics):
    optics.launch_app("https://www.saucedemo.com")
    optics.enter_text("//input[@id='user-name']", "standard_user")
    optics.enter_text("//input[@id='password']", "secret_sauce")
    optics.press_element(["//input[@id='login-button']", "Login"])  # fallbacks
    optics.assert_presence("Products", timeout="10")
    price = optics.get_text("//div[@data-test='inventory-item-price']")
    optics.press_element("//button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack']")
    optics.assert_text("//span[@data-test='shopping-cart-badge']", "1")
    optics.press_element("//a[@data-test='shopping-cart-link']")
    optics.assert_text("//div[@data-test='inventory-item-price']", price)
```

```shell
$ pytest test_checkout.py
```

## Configure the session

Pass the same lists you'd put in `config.yaml`, as a Python dict. `driver_sources` and `elements_sources` are required. The SDK reads these keys:

| Key | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `driver_sources`, `elements_sources` | What to drive and how to look at the screen. See the [config reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config). |
| `text_detection`, `image_detection` | OCR and image matching engines, if you use them. |
| `project_path` | A folder to search for image files and to resolve relative paths in `read_data`. Required for image elements. |
| `execution_output_path` | Where screenshots and results go. |

To reuse a project's `config.yaml`, load it yourself and pass the dict:

```python
import yaml
from optics_framework import Optics

with open("birch-tests/config.yaml") as f:
    config = yaml.safe_load(f)
config["project_path"] = "birch-tests"

with Optics(config) as optics:
    optics.launch_app()
```

Settings such as `ai_self_heal`, `llm_models` and `log_level` aren't read by the SDK.

## How calls differ from suite files

- **Method names are snake_case.** `Press Element` is `press_element`. Your editor's autocomplete lists them all.
- **Pass every value as a string.** `optics.press_by_coordinates("540", "1600")` works; numbers raise `TypeError`.
- **A list means "try these in order".** `press_element(["//button[@id='login']", "Login"])` tries the XPath, then the text. To check several elements at once, separate them with a pipe in one string: `assert_presence("Products|Your Cart")`.
- **`${name}` isn't looked up** in action methods. Pass the locator itself, or keep your own dict of locators.
- **There is no `store_as`.** Keep a return value in a Python variable, as `price` above.
- **Methods return values.** `get_text` returns the text, `capture_screenshot` returns a base64 PNG, and `assert_presence` returns `True`. A failed check raises an exception, which fails the pytest test.
- **`assert_text`, `is_element` and `go_back`.** `assert_text(element, expected)` fails on different text. `is_element(element, state, timeout)` accepts `visible`, `invisible`, `enabled`, `disabled`, `checked` and `unchecked`. `go_back()` goes back one screen.
- **Some defaults differ.** `assert_presence` and `assert_visibility` wait 60 seconds by default, and `detect_and_press` waits 10.

## Python-only methods

These have no CSV equivalent:

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `add_element(name, value)` | Add a value to a named element, for use in flow-control methods. |
| `get_element_value(name)` | Return the list of values for a named element. |
| `add_module(name, steps)` | Define a module as a list of `(keyword, [values])` pairs, for `run_loop` and `condition`. |
| `add_api(path_or_dict)` | Load API definitions for `invoke_api`. See [Call APIs in a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/api-calls). |
| `add_error_definitions(dict)` | Load on-screen error definitions. |
| `capture_and_detect()` | Check the current screen against those definitions and return the matches. |
| `quit()` | End the session. The `with` block calls it for you. |

```python
optics.add_element("term", "trail runner")
optics.add_module("Search", [("Enter Text", ["//input[@type='search']", "${term}"])])
optics.run_loop("Search", "${term}", "trail runner|pace knit")
```

## See also

- [Use Optics in Robot Framework](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot)
- [Generate pytest code from a suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/generate)
- [Keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/)

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot

# Use Optics in Robot Framework

> Import Optics as a Robot Framework library and use its keywords in .robot files.

Optics is also a [Robot Framework](https://robotframework.org) library. If your team already writes `.robot` suites, you can add Optics keywords to them and get its fallbacks, OCR and image matching without changing tools.

## Before you begin

Robot Framework isn't installed with Optics. Add it to the same environment:

```shell
$ pip install robotframework "optics-framework[appium]"
```

Swap `appium` for the engine you use. You also need a `config.yaml` with `driver_sources` and `elements_sources`. Any Optics project's config works.

## Write a suite

`checkout.robot`:

```robot
*** Settings ***
Library           OperatingSystem
Library           optics_framework.optics.Optics
Suite Setup       Open Optics
Suite Teardown    Quit

*** Variables ***
${EMAIL_FIELD}    //*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/email"]

*** Keywords ***
Open Optics
    ${config}=    Get File    ${CURDIR}/config.yaml
    Setup    config=${config}

*** Test Cases ***
Shopper Can Sign In
    Launch App
    Detect And Press    Allow    timeout=5
    Enter Text    ${EMAIL_FIELD}    ava@birch.shop
    ${sign_in}=    Create List    //*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/login"]    Sign in
    Press Element    ${sign_in}
    Assert Presence    Picked for you|Search Birch    timeout=20    rule=any
```

Run it like any Robot suite:

```shell
$ robot checkout.robot
```

## How Optics keywords behave in Robot

- **Setup takes the config's contents, not its path.** Read the file with `Get File` as shown above, then pass the text to `Setup`. If you use image elements, add `project_path: .` to the config so Optics can find the pictures.
- **Pass fallbacks as a list.** `Create List` builds the values to try in order. Writing several plain arguments fills the keyword's next parameters instead.
- **Separate several elements with a pipe** inside one argument: `Picked for you|Search Birch`.
- **Named arguments use the Python names**: `timeout=20`, `rule=any`, `index=1`.
- **There is no `store_as`.** Keep the return value in a Robot variable: `${price}=    Get Text    ${PRICE_LABEL}`, then `Assert Text    ${CART_TOTAL}    ${price}`. Assert Text fails on different text.
- **`Go Back`** goes back one screen, and **`Is Element`** accepts the states `checked` and `unchecked`.
- **Robot replaces `${…}` itself.** To pass an Optics variable to `Evaluate` or `Condition`, escape it: `\${total}`.
- **`Sleep` and `Evaluate` exist in Robot's BuiltIn library too.** Robot warns and uses the Optics version, which only accepts whole seconds. Write `BuiltIn.Sleep    2s` or `Optics.Sleep    2` to be explicit.

The [keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/) lists every keyword. The Python-only keywords in [Use Optics from Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python#python-only-methods), such as `Add Element` and `Add Module`, work in Robot too.

## Generate Robot code from a suite

If you already have a CSV or YAML suite, `optics generate` can write a starting `.robot` file from it. See [Generate pytest or Robot code](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/generate).

## See also

- [Use Optics from Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python)
- [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/organise

# Organise a suite

> Structure a growing suite with setup and teardown, shared modules, several files and run selection.

A handful of tests fits in three files. A suite that covers a whole app needs a little structure so changes stay small. This page covers the tools Optics gives you for that.

## Open and close the app once

Name a test case **Suite Setup** and it runs once, before every other test case. **Suite Teardown** runs once at the end. Use them to launch and close the app, so each test case can focus on its own flow:

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
Suite Setup,Launch Birch
Shopper can sign in,Sign In
Shopper can search,Sign In
Shopper can search,Search For Shoes
Suite Teardown,Close Birch
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1
Launch Birch,Launch App
Close Birch,Close And Terminate App
```

A name that ends with "Suite Setup" also works, such as `Birch Suite Setup`. Matching ignores case. Setup and teardown run even when you [select which tests run](#run-only-some-test-cases).

A test case whose name ends with **Setup** runs before each test case, and **Teardown** runs after each one. Use them to give each test a fresh start.

If Suite Setup fails, the test cases do not run, and the report shows them as skipped. Suite Teardown still runs. If the per-test setup fails, only its test case is skipped.

**Tip:**
Give each role to one test case only. Two test cases whose names end with "Setup" stop the run before it starts. A name such as *Setup wizard works* is an ordinary test case, because it does not end with "Setup".

## Reuse modules

A module can appear in as many test cases as you like. Keep each module small and focused on one screen or one task, such as *Sign In*, *Search For Shoes* or *Open Cart*. When that screen changes, you fix one module and every test that uses it follows.

To call one module from inside another, use `Execute Module`:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1
Buy Trail Runners,Execute Module,Search For Shoes
Buy Trail Runners,Press Element,Trail Runner 2
Buy Trail Runners,Press Element,Add to cart
```

Listing a module's name as a step on its own doesn't work; you need `Execute Module`. Steps inside a module called this way use only the first value of each element, so give important elements a value that's reliable on its own. [Conditions and loops](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions) explains the details.

## Split a suite across files

Optics reads every CSV and YAML file in the project folder and its subfolders, and recognises each by its first row (or top-level key in YAML). So you can split a large suite however suits your team:

```tree
birch-tests/
├── config.yaml
├── checkout/
│   ├── test_cases.csv
│   └── modules.csv
├── search/
│   ├── test_cases.csv
│   └── modules.csv
└── elements/
    ├── shared.csv
    └── checkout.csv
```

When two files define the same thing:

- **Elements** with the same name are merged, and every value becomes a fallback.
- **Modules** and **test cases** with the same name: the one read last wins, and Optics logs a warning. Keep names unique.

**Tip:**
Optics also reads files inside `execution_output/`. Keep stray CSV or YAML files, and copies of old suites, out of the project folder so they don't get picked up.

## Run only some test cases

Name the test cases to run, or to skip, on the command line. Wildcards `*` and `?` work, and case does not matter:

```shell
$ optics execute birch-tests --include "shopper can*" --exclude "Shopper can pay with a gift card"
```

For a fixed selection, list the names in `config.yaml` instead. A flag replaces these lists for that run:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
include:
  - Shopper can sign in
  - Shopper can search
exclude:
  - Shopper can pay with a gift card
```

Optics applies `include` first, then removes the `exclude` matches. Suite Setup and Suite Teardown always run. A name that matches no test case stops the run before it starts. [Pick test cases](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli#pick-test-cases) gives the full rules.

## Run the same suite on different devices

Keep one config file in a project. Optics uses the config it finds in the project folder, so two of them would compete. To run the same suite on several targets, keep one config per target outside the project and copy the one you need into place before the run:

```tree
birch/
├── configs/
│   ├── pixel-8.yaml
│   └── chrome.yaml
└── birch-tests/
    ├── config.yaml        # copied from configs/ before each run
    └── …
```

```shell
$ cp configs/pixel-8.yaml birch-tests/config.yaml
$ optics execute birch-tests
```

## Name things so failures explain themselves

The run's tree and the JUnit report use your names, so a good name saves a trip into the files:

- **Test cases** describe an outcome: *Shopper can add a backpack*, not *Test 3*.
- **Modules** describe a task: *Sign In*, *Apply Discount Code*.
- **Elements** describe what's on screen: `sign_in`, `cart_badge`, `promo_code_field`.

## See also

- [Write a test suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write)
- [Write tests in YAML](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/yaml)
- [Project files reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/yaml

# Write tests in YAML

> Keep a whole flow in one indented file, and learn the quoting rules that make YAML steps work.

YAML suites hold the same test cases, modules and elements as CSV, in one file you can read top to bottom. Optics loads both formats into the same suite, so a project can mix them.

## A complete suite in one file

`checkout.yaml`:

```yaml
Test Cases:
  - Suite Setup:
      - Launch Birch
  - Shopper can add trail runners:
      - Sign In
      - Add To Cart

Modules:
  - Launch Birch:
      - Launch App
  - Sign In:
      - Enter Text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop
      - Enter Text ${password_field} ${password}
      - Press Element ${sign_in}
      - Assert Presence "Picked for you"
  - Add To Cart:
      - Press Element "Trail Runner 2"
      - Press Element "Add to cart"
      - Assert Presence "Added to cart" timeout_str=10

Elements:
  email_field: "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email']"
  password_field: "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password']"
  sign_in:
    - "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']"
    - Sign in
  password: correct-horse
```

Keep `config.yaml` as its own file. You can split the suite into several YAML files, or keep elements in CSV and steps in YAML.

## The rules

### Section names are exact

Write the three top-level keys exactly as `Test Cases`, `Modules` and `Elements`, with that capitalization. Other spellings, such as `test_cases:`, are recognised as a suite file but load nothing, and the run then reports that there are no test cases.

### Each step is one line

A step is a single string: the keyword name, then its values separated by spaces. Optics matches the longest keyword name it knows at the start of the line, so `Press Element Sign in` is read as the keyword `Press Element` with the value `Sign`, then `in` as a second value. Quote any value that contains spaces:

```yaml
- Press Element "Sign in"
- Enter Text ${email_field} "Ava Birch"
```

A step that is exactly a module name runs that module.

### Named values

`name=value` sets one parameter by name, like `timeout_str=10` above. Quote the value if it contains spaces: `event_name="tap sign in"`. A first value that starts with `text=`, `css=` or `xpath=` is a locator, not a named value: `Enter Text text=Email ava@birch.shop`.

`store_as=name` keeps the value that the keyword returns: `Get Text ${price_label} store_as=price`. See [Keep a value for later](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables#keep-a-value-for-later).

### Expressions with = in them

Quote an expression that contains spaces, the same as any other value. Optics removes the quotes:

```yaml
- Condition "${status} == 'ready'" "Go Home" "Sign In"
```

### Module names as values

When a keyword takes a module name, such as `Run Loop` or `Execute Module`, quote names that contain spaces: `Run Loop "Search One" ${term} "trail runner|pace knit"`.

### Elements

An element is a single value or a list. A list gives fallbacks, tried in order:

```yaml
Elements:
  sign_in: ["//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']", "Sign in", sign_in.png]
```

Quote XPaths. They contain characters YAML treats specially, such as `[`, `@` and `:`.

## What stays in CSV

- **Error definitions** are CSV only. See [Catch error screens](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection).
- **`/save` in `optics live`** always writes CSV, even in a YAML project. Move the steps into your YAML file afterwards, or keep the CSV next to it.

## See also

- [Write a test suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write), with CSV and YAML side by side
- [Project files reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/

# How Optics finds elements

> Learn how Optics tries several ways to find each element, so one changed locator doesn't fail a test.

Most test tools give an element one locator, and the test fails the moment that locator changes. Optics assumes an element has several identities (its place in the UI tree, its text, what it looks like) and tries them in order before giving up. A redesign that breaks one identity falls through to the next.

## The order Optics tries things

When a step needs an element, Optics works through three layers of fallback.

### 1. Each value of the element, in order

An element can have several values in `elements.csv`. Optics tries them top to bottom and stops at the first that works:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
sign_in,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']
sign_in,Sign in
sign_in,sign_in.png
```

### 2. Each way to find that kind of value

Optics looks at a value and decides what kind it is, then tries the ways that fit, cheapest first:

| Value looks like | Optics tries | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| An XPath, such as `//*[@resource-id='login']` | The UI tree | A driver that exposes a UI tree |
| Text, such as `Sign in` | 1. The UI tree<br>2. OCR on a screenshot | OCR needs a [text detection engine](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) |
| An image file, such as `sign_in.png` | Image matching on a screenshot | An [image detection engine](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) |
| CSS, such as `css=#login` | The web page | Playwright, or a web page on Appium. See [Mobile web](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/mobile-web). |
| `text_only:Sign in` | OCR only, skipping the UI tree | A text detection engine |

Looking something up in the UI tree takes milliseconds. OCR and image matching read a screenshot, which takes longer, so Optics only uses them when the tree can't help. [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define) shows every kind of value.

### 3. Each element source, in config order

`config.yaml` lists **element sources**: the ways Optics may look at the screen, such as asking the app directly, reading its UI tree, or taking a screenshot. For an action, Optics tries them in the order of the list, with each way that fits in each source. Assertions always try the UI tree sources before OCR and image matching. If you enable more than one driver, each is tried in turn as well.

### Last resort: AI self-heal

If everything above fails and you've switched it on, an AI model looks at the screen and tries to finish the step, for example by spotting that *Sign in* is now *Log in*. It's off by default. See [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal).

## See which way worked

Optics records how it found each element, so you can tell when a test is passing on a fallback:

- `optics live` shows it after each step: `0.31s  [Text]`.
- When `save_captures` is `true`, screenshots in `execution_output/` show a box around the element Optics found, for drivers that report element positions. See [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results).

If a test keeps passing on its second or third value, the first one is probably out of date. Update it while you still know why.

## Make elements last

- **Put the most stable value first.** An id that developers don't change is better than text that marketing rewrites.
- **Add a text fallback** to important buttons. Text survives most layout changes.
- **Use images last.** Image matching is the slowest, and a restyled button stops matching. It's still the only option for icons with no text or id.
- **Narrow the search** when the same text appears twice on a screen. Use `index` to pick a match, or an [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest) to look in one part of the screen.

## See also

- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define)
- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images)
- [Search part of the screen](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest)
- [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define

# Define elements

> Name the things your tests touch, choose good values for them, and add fallbacks that survive redesigns.

An element is a name for something on screen, plus one or more values that tell Optics how to find it. Steps refer to elements by name (`${sign_in}`), so when the app changes, you update the element once and every test follows.

## Write elements

Elements live in any CSV whose header starts with `Element_Name,Element_ID`, in any case. The project template puts them in `test_data/elements.csv`.

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
sign_in,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']
sign_in,Sign in
cart_icon,cart_icon.png
search_bar,Search Birch
email,ava@birch.shop
```

To give an element several values, repeat its name on more rows. Optics tries them top to bottom. You can also add more columns whose names start with `Element_ID`, such as `Element_ID_text` or `Element_ID_image`, and fill them in on the same row:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID,Element_ID_text,Element_ID_image
sign_in,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login'],Sign in,sign_in.png
```

Both layouts mean the same thing. Use whichever is easier to read for your team. Empty cells are ignored.

## Choose the kind of value

Optics decides what a value is from how it looks:

| Write | Optics treats it as | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Starts with `/`, `//` or `(` | XPath, looked up in the UI tree | `//*[@resource-id='login']` |
| Plain words | Text: UI tree first, then OCR on a screenshot | `Sign in` |
| `text_only:` then words | Text, OCR only | `text_only:Sign in` |
| Ends in `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg` or `.bmp` | An image to match on a screenshot | `cart_icon.png` |
| `css=`, `#id`, `.class` or `tag[attr]` | A CSS selector. Playwright and web pages on Appium only | `#login-button` |
| Starts with `android.` or `XCUI` | A class name | `android.widget.Switch` |

On Playwright, you can also write these prefixes. A prefix can be in any case:

| Write | Finds |
|---|---|
| `id=login`, `data-testid=save`, `data-test=save`, `data-test-id=save` | An element by its id or test attribute |
| `testid=save` | The same as `data-testid=save` |
| `label=Email`, `placeholder=Search Birch` | A field by its label or placeholder |
| `alt=Birch logo`, `title=Open the cart` | An element by its alt text or title |
| `role=button[name="Save"]` | An element by its role and name |
| `text="Save"` | An element with exactly this text. `text=Save` also matches `Save changes`. |
| `loc=css:button.save`, `loc=role:button[name="Save"]`, `loc=href:/next` | The same as `css=`, `role=` and a link with this `href`. Agent browsers write locators in this form. |

See [Locators for web pages](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web#locators-for-web-pages).

### XPath

An XPath is a path through the app's UI tree. It's the fastest and most precise kind of value, and the best first choice when the app has stable ids:

- Android: `//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']`
- iOS: `//XCUIElementTypeButton[@name='Sign in']`
- Web: `//button[@id='login']`

To pick the second of several matches, wrap the XPath in parentheses and add an index: `(//android.widget.Button)[2]`.

### Text

Plain text matches an element showing that text, or with that accessibility label. It's the most readable kind of value, and it survives layout changes. If the text isn't in the UI tree, for example because it's drawn inside an image or a game canvas, Optics reads the screenshot with OCR, as long as a [text detection engine](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) is enabled.

Text matching in the UI tree tolerates small differences. To require exact matches, set `strict_element_match: true` in `config.yaml`.

**Text that looks like something else:**
A value is checked against the rules in the table above, top to bottom. Text that happens to start with `(` or `/`, or contains `[` and `]`, is read as an XPath or CSS selector: `(optional)`, `Price [USD]`, `.com`. On Appium and Playwright, put `text=` in front to force text: `text=(optional)`. On Playwright, a value that looks like CSS, such as `.com`, is also tried as visible text.

### Images

An image value is the file name of a cropped picture of the element. Put the picture anywhere in the project folder (the templates use `test_data/input_templates/`) and refer to it by file name only. Image matching is the slowest kind and needs an image detection engine. Use it for icons with no text or id. [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) shows how to capture a good picture.

### Values to avoid

`id:` values, such as `id:login`, aren't supported by any element source and always fail. Use an XPath on the id instead.

Assert Presence, Assert Visibility, Validate Element and Validate Screen skip class names. If every element in the check is a class name, the step passes without a check.

## Find the right locator

- **In `optics live`**, try a value with `press_element` or `assert_presence` before you write it down. The history line shows whether it worked and how it was found.
- **Android and iOS**: [Appium Inspector](https://github.com/appium/appium-inspector) shows each element's id, text and XPath.
- **Web**: right-click an element in Chrome and choose **Inspect**.
- **Any platform**: the `Get Interactive Elements` keyword lists the buttons, fields and text on the current screen. In `optics live`, run `get_interactive_elements` and open the JSON file it writes to the output folder.

## Pick one of several matches

When the same text appears more than once, `index` picks a match, counting from 0:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Add Second Product,Press Element,Add to cart,index=1
```

On Appium, `index` picks among the elements with the same text, in UI tree order. When a locator matches more than one element, the log shows how many matched and which one Optics used.

To look in one part of the screen instead, use an [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest).

## Keep data in elements too

Elements can hold any value a step needs, not only locators: an email address, a search term, a URL. Keeping them together means one file holds everything that changes between environments.

To keep a password out of log files, start its value with `@:`, for example `password,@:correct-horse`. Optics masks it as `****` in logs and types it without the prefix. `@:${password}` also works.

Optics also masks a value that `store_as` or Read Data writes to a secret name. A secret name contains a word such as `password`, `pin`, `otp`, `secret`, `token` or `key`, for example `api_token` or `myPassword`. The value must have 4 or more characters.

To put a line break or tab inside a value, write `\n` or `\t`. Write `\\` for a literal backslash.

## See also

- [How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/)
- [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables)
- [Project files reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files)

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images

# Find elements by text and image

> Use OCR and image matching to find elements the UI tree can't see, such as text inside images, canvases and video.

Some things on screen never appear in the app's UI tree: text drawn inside an image, a game or map canvas, a video player's controls, or anything on a device you can only watch through a camera. Optics can find these by looking at a screenshot, the way a person would. It reads text with **OCR** (optical character recognition) and finds icons with **image matching**.

Both are slower than the UI tree, so Optics only uses them after the faster ways fail. You turn them on in `config.yaml`.

## Turn on OCR

### Install an OCR engine

We recommend EasyOCR. It runs on your machine and needs no account.

```shell
$ optics setup --install easyocr
```

The first run downloads EasyOCR's models, which takes a minute.

### Enable it, and a screenshot source

OCR reads screenshots, so `elements_sources` must include a screenshot source for your driver (`appium_screenshot`, `playwright_screenshot`, `selenium_screenshot`, or `camera_screenshot`):

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
elements_sources:
  - appium_find_element:
      enabled: true
  - appium_page_source:
      enabled: true
  - appium_screenshot:
      enabled: true

text_detection:
  - easyocr:
      enabled: true
```

### Use text values

Nothing changes in your tests. Any text value, such as `Press Element,Trail Runner 2`, is tried in the UI tree first and with OCR second. To skip the UI tree and use OCR straight away, write `text_only:Trail Runner 2`.

Without an OCR engine, a text miss ends with "OCR was not tried: no text_detection engine is configured."

### OCR engines

| Engine | Name in config | Install | Good to know |
|---|---|---|---|
| EasyOCR | `easyocr` | `optics setup --install easyocr` | Local and accurate. Slower on the first call while models load. Reads English. |
| Tesseract | `pytesseract` | `optics setup --install pytesseract`, plus the [Tesseract program](https://tesseract-ocr.github.io/tessdoc/Installation.html) | Light and fast. Matches whole words exactly. |
| Google Cloud Vision | `google_vision` | `optics setup --install google-vision` | Cloud service. Set `capabilities.api_key` to a Vision API key or `capabilities.credentials_path` to a service account key file, or set `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`. Screenshots leave your machine. |
| Your own service | `remote_ocr` | Nothing | Sends screenshots to a URL you run. See the [engines reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines). |

List more than one engine and Optics tries them in order.

### Pictures from a camera

The `camera_screenshot` source gives OCR and image matching a picture. The picture comes from one of three places: a webcam (`camera_index`), an HTTP(S) URL (`url`, with an optional `token`) or a TCP frame server (`url: ip:port`). See [BLE and camera](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#ble-and-camera).

## Turn on image matching

Image matching finds a picture of an element, such as an icon, on the screen. It needs no extra install.

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
image_detection:
  - templatematch:
      enabled: true
```

Then use the picture's file name as an element value:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
cart_icon,//*[@content-desc='Cart']
cart_icon,cart_icon.png
```

### Capture a good template

The picture is called a **template**. How you crop it decides whether matching works:

1. Take a screenshot on the same kind of device you test on. Run the test once and use a `pre_…` screenshot from `execution_output/`, or run `/screenshot` in `optics live`.
2. Crop tightly around the element. Include its distinctive shape, and as little background as possible.
3. Don't resize the crop. Matching works best at the screen's own resolution, though it tolerates some scaling and rotation. Playwright screenshots are at CSS pixel scale, so crop Playwright templates from a Playwright run.
4. Save it as PNG anywhere in the project folder. The templates use `test_data/input_templates/`.
5. Refer to it by file name only: `cart_icon.png`, not a path. File names must be unique across the project.

Optics also picks up images inside `execution_output/`. Give templates distinctive names, so they never clash with a screenshot's name.

Before a tap, Optics changes the position of an OCR or image match from screenshot pixels to screen points, so that taps land correctly on iOS and on scaled screens.

## When to use which

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| The element has a stable id or text in the UI tree | XPath or text, no vision needed |
| Text drawn inside an image, canvas or video | OCR |
| An icon with no text or id | Image matching |
| A device with no UI tree, watched through a camera | OCR and image matching. See [Production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production) |
| The same word appears in several places | OCR with an [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest) or `index` |

## Speed things up

- **Keep the UI tree first.** List page source and element sources before screenshot sources, so vision only runs when it's needed. Assertions always check the UI tree first. They run OCR and image matching at most every 2 seconds, and only when the screen changed.
- **Search part of the screen.** An [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest) crops the screenshot before OCR or matching runs.
- **Turn off what you don't use.** An enabled OCR engine is loaded at the start of every run, even by `optics dry_run`.

## See also

- [How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/)
- [Search part of the screen](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest)
- [Engines and extras](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest

# Search part of the screen

> Limit where Optics looks for an element, so repeated text can't be matched in the wrong place and vision runs faster.

An **area of interest** (AOI) is a rectangle on the screen. Give one to a step and Optics only accepts an element inside it. Use it when the same text appears in several places, such as an *Add to cart* button that also appears in a product description, or to make OCR faster by reading less of the screen.

## Set an area

Four values describe the rectangle, each as a **percentage** of the screen, from 0 to 100:

| Parameter | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `aoi_x` | Left edge, from the left of the screen | `0` |
| `aoi_y` | Top edge, from the top of the screen | `0` |
| `aoi_width` | Width of the area | `100` |
| `aoi_height` | Height of the area | `100` |

The defaults cover the whole screen, which means "no area". Pass the values by name:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3
Add To Cart,Press Element,Add to cart,aoi_y=75,aoi_height=25
```

This looks for *Add to cart* only in the bottom quarter: it starts 75% of the way down and covers the remaining 25%.

Some common areas:

| Area | Values |
|---|---|
| Top half | `aoi_height=50` |
| Bottom half | `aoi_y=50,aoi_height=50` |
| Right third | `aoi_x=67,aoi_width=33` |
| Centre | `aoi_x=25,aoi_y=25,aoi_width=50,aoi_height=50` |

The edges must stay on the screen: `aoi_x` plus `aoi_width`, and `aoi_y` plus `aoi_height`, can be at most 100.

## How it works

- **OCR and image matching** crop the screenshot to the area before they search. They read less, so they're faster too.
- **The UI tree** can't be cropped. Optics finds the element as usual, then keeps it only if its centre is inside the area. This also applies to web pages on Appium. If the match is outside the area, Optics tries the next way, such as OCR.

When `save_captures` is `true`, each step that uses an area saves a screenshot with the rectangle on it: `…_with_aoi.jpg` in `execution_output/`. Use it to make sure that you chose the right part of the screen.

## Keywords that accept an area

`Press Element`, `Enter Text`, `Enter Number`, `Clear Element Text`, `Get Text`, `Swipe From Element` and `Scroll From Element`. Checks such as `Assert Presence` don't take an area.

In the Python library, only `press_element` accepts area parameters.

## Area or index?

Both pick one match out of several. Use `index` when you know which match you want by order (the second *Add to cart* button). Use an area when you know *where* it is, which keeps working when items are added or reordered.

You can combine them, but the order differs. For UI tree and web matches, `index` picks a match on the full screen first, and then the area is applied. OCR and image matching count `index` inside the area.

## See also

- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images)
- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define#pick-one-of-several-matches)
- [Action keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal

# Recover failing steps with AI self-heal

> Let an AI model look at the screen and finish a step when every way of finding its element has failed.

AI self-heal is the last line of defence. When a step cannot find its element with any value or any method, Optics sends a screenshot to an AI model. The model then tries to complete the step. If the button now says *Log in* instead of *Sign in*, the model can find it and press it, and the test continues. Self-heal is off by default.

## When to use it

Self-heal keeps long runs alive through small, expected changes to the UI. Examples are a scheduled check of a production app, or a nightly regression. There, a full report is better than a stop at the first renamed button.

Self-heal does not replace good elements. A healed step **passes**, so you must read the logs to see a real change in the app. Fix the element after the run, as [Find out what healed](#find-out-what-healed) shows.

## Turn it on

### Install the AI engine and set your key

Self-heal uses the same AI engine and key as [plain-English mode](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe#before-you-begin). Install the engine and set its key, for example:

```shell
$ optics setup --install gemini
$ export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key"
```

### Enable it in config.yaml

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
ai_self_heal: true

llm_models:
  - gemini:
      enabled: true
```

For OpenAI, Claude or your own model server, use the entry of that engine. See [Choose a model](#choose-a-model).

### Enable a screenshot source

The model works from a screenshot, so `elements_sources` must include a screenshot source, such as `appium_screenshot` or `playwright_screenshot`. Without one, self-heal does nothing.

If the AI engine is not installed or the key is missing, Optics logs a warning and runs without self-heal. A run never fails because self-heal is not available.

## Choose a model

Self-heal works with each engine under [llm_models](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#llm-models). Use a model that accepts images.

| Model | Engine | Key |
|---|---|---|
| Gemini | `gemini` | `GEMINI_API_KEY` |
| OpenAI, or a hosted service such as OpenRouter | `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY`, or `api_key` |
| Claude | `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |
| Your own server with an OpenAI-compatible API, such as vLLM, Ollama or LM Studio | `openai`, with the server in `url` | Only if the server asks for one |

### Use your own model server

The `openai` engine can call any server with an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. For example, a vLLM server can serve a small vision model on a machine in your network:

```shell
$ vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct --port 8000
```

Set the server address in `url` and the model name in `model`:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
ai_self_heal: true

llm_models:
  - openai:
      enabled: true
      url: http://gpu-box:8000/v1
      capabilities:
        model: Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct
```

If you start the server with an API key, give the key to Optics as `api_key: ${VLLM_API_KEY}` under `capabilities`. If the server rejects JSON-schema output, set `response_format: json_object`.

For a 2B model trained for self-heal, with measured results, read [Self-heal broken locators with a 2B model on your own GPU](https://optics-framework.org/blog/small-model-self-heal).

### Give the API key in config.yaml

Each engine reads its API key from `capabilities.api_key` first, then from its environment variable. Write the key as a reference, so that the file stays safe to commit:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
llm_models:
  - openai:
      enabled: true
      url: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
      capabilities:
        model: google/gemini-2.5-flash
        api_key: ${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}
```

Optics reads the variable when it loads the file. If the variable is not set, the run stops before it starts. Logs and reports show `****` in place of the key. The `openai` and `anthropic` engines also take `api_key_env`, the name of the variable to read.

## What it does

When a step that finds an element fails, Optics gives the model:

- The step that failed and the locator of its element.
- The name of the element in your suite, when the step uses `${name}`. For `Press Element,${stopwatch_tab}`, the model gets `stopwatch_tab`.
- A screenshot and a list of the elements on the screen, each with a reference such as `e7` that the model can name. Optics sends the UI tree only when that list is empty or does not show all the elements.
- Up to three rows of that list that are the closest match to the target, best first. See [How Optics points the model to the target](#how-optics-points-the-model-to-the-target).
- The steps that ran before the failure.

Optics tells the model to choose the row whose text or id matches the target. It also tells the model not to choose a row only because it is the main button on the screen.

The model can do up to five actions to complete the step. It can use only six keywords: Press Element, Enter Text, Scroll, Swipe By Percentage, Press Keycode and Press By Percentage. Optics finds the element of each action with its usual methods. If the step is complete within five actions, the step passes. If not, the step fails with the original error.

Self-heal covers the steps that find an element and do an action on it: Press Element, Enter Text, Enter Number, Clear Element Text, Get Text, Swipe From Element, Scroll From Element, and the keywords that use them (Detect And Press, Select Dropdown Option). Checks such as Assert Presence do not self-heal, so a missing element still fails a check.

### How Optics points the model to the target

Optics compares the target with each row on the screen and lists the closest rows in the prompt. It takes the words from the part of the locator that names the target:

- The resource id, if the locator has one. `//*[@resource-id='com.app:id/search_button']` gives `search` and `button`.
- Else the quoted values. Optics ignores XPath syntax such as `android.widget`.
- Else the full text of the locator.

Optics then makes more words from them:

- It divides words at each change of case and at each change between letters and digits. `loginButton` gives `login` and `button`. `timerPreset1` gives `timer`, `preset` and `1`.
- It joins each pair of adjacent words. "Stop watch" also gives `stopwatch`, so it matches a row that says "Stopwatch".
- It adds the words of the element name from your suite.

A row with the exact resource id comes first. The other rows are in order of the number of shared words. If two rows share the same number, a row that takes an action, such as a tap, comes before read-only text. Then the row with fewer other words comes first.

**Tip:**
Give your elements clear names in the elements file, such as `stopwatch_tab` or `timer_preset_1`. Optics sends the name to the model and uses its words to find the closest rows. A clear name helps a small model to find the correct row.

### When a heal ends

A heal of Press Element ends when the model presses the row that the locator names. The step passes, also when the model plans more actions. Optics compares the label and the id of the row with the value in the locator. It ignores case, separators, the words `tab`, `button`, `btn` and `icon`, and a plural "s". Thus `timerPreset1` matches `timer_preset_1`, and `tab_alarm` matches "Alarms".

A press on a different row can lead to the target, such as a press on a menu or a tab. Then the model tells Optics if the step is complete. The same applies to a locator with more than one quoted value, such as an XPath with two conditions.

## Find out what healed

With `optics execute` and `optics live`, a healed step shows as passed. To see what happened, turn on file logs:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
file_log: true
```

Then search `execution_output/internal_logs.log` for `AI self-heal`:

```text
AI self-heal: attempting recovery for 'press_element' on 'Sign in'
AI self-heal step 1/5 for 'press_element': action=keyword keyword=press_element params=['Log in'] reason=The button now reads 'Log in'
AI self-heal: recovered 'press_element' via keyword 'press_element'
```

Update the element with the value that the model used. In this example, add `sign_in,Log in` to `elements.csv`.

Over the [HTTP API](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/http-api) and [MCP](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent), the result of a healed step shows `"healed": true` and the steps that worked.

## Costs and limits

- Each healed step makes up to six calls to the model. Each call takes some seconds and uses your API quota.
- Self-heal sends screenshots to your model provider, unless the model runs on your own server. Use your own server for screens with data that you cannot share with a third party.
- The model never sees the text of a failed Enter Text step. It sees `<value>` and selects the field, and then Optics types the real text.
- The instructions to the model are for phones. Self-heal works in browsers too, but key presses use Android key codes.

## See also

- [How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/)
- [Describe a test in plain English](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe)
- [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/

# Run a suite

> Check a suite without a device, run it for real, and choose which test cases run.

Two commands cover almost every run. `optics dry_run` checks your files without touching a device. `optics execute` runs the suite on the device or browser in your `config.yaml` and writes the results to `execution_output/`.

## Check the suite first

```shell
$ optics dry_run birch-tests
```

A dry run reads every file and checks that:

- every test step names a module or keyword that exists,
- every keyword in every module exists, with a suggestion when you mistype one,
- every `${name}` is defined in an elements file or by an earlier step, such as `Evaluate`, `Read Data` or `store_as`. This includes a `${name}` inside a longer value.

It does not tap, type or open anything, so it is quick and safe to run before every commit. It still starts the engines in your `config.yaml`, so they must be installed and a driver must be enabled. `optics dry-run` is the same command.

A suite that uses only [flow control keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow), such as `Evaluate` and `Condition`, needs no driver. `optics execute` follows the same rule.

## Run it

```shell
$ optics execute birch-tests
```

Before the run, Optics checks that the target is reachable: for Appium, that the server answers and, for a local server on Android, that a device is connected; for Selenium, that the server answers. If not, it stops with a message saying what to start. Playwright needs no check.

Then it runs **Suite Setup**, each test case in order, and **Suite Teardown**, and prints a live tree:

```terminal
Test Suite
├── Suite Setup                                       |  1.21s |    PASS
│   └── Launch Birch                                  |  1.21s |    PASS
├── Shopper can sign in                               |  1.38s |    PASS
│   └── Sign In                                       |  1.38s |    PASS
└── Shopper can add trail runners                     |  4.02s |    FAIL
    ├── Sign In                                       |  1.31s |    PASS
    └── Add To Cart                                   |  2.71s |    FAIL
╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
```
