```terminal
│ Total Test Cases: 3 | Passed: 2 | Failed: 1          │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

### What happens when a step fails

- The rest of that test case is skipped, and its unrun steps show as `NOT_RUN`.
- The next test case runs as normal. One broken flow doesn't hide problems elsewhere.
- A **Failure details** box after the tree names each failed step and why it failed.

### Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | Every test case passed. |
| `1` | At least one test case failed, error detection found an on-screen error, or the run couldn't start (no driver enabled, server unreachable, missing files). |
| `2` | The command line is not valid, for example an unknown flag. |
| `3` | The test case selection is not valid. |
| `130` | You pressed Ctrl+C. |
| `143` | Optics received SIGTERM. |

CI systems use this to mark a build as passed or failed. Optics also writes the JUnit report when you stop a run with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. See [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results#what-each-outcome-writes).

## Choose which test cases run

Name the test cases to run with `--include`, or the ones to skip with `--exclude`:

```shell
$ optics execute birch-tests --include "shopper can*" --exclude "Shopper can check out"
```

- Matching ignores case. `*` and `?` are wildcards.
- You can use both flags. Optics applies `--include` first.
- Suite Setup and Suite Teardown always stay in the run.
- A name that matches no test case stops the run before it starts, with exit code `3`. The message suggests the correct name.

`optics dry_run` takes the same flags. To keep a selection for every run, put `include` and `exclude` in [config.yaml](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#include-and-exclude). The flags replace them for one run.

## Options

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--no-use-printer` | Print plain log output instead of the live tree. Useful when a CI log viewer garbles the tree. |
| `--include NAME ...` | Run only these test cases. |
| `--exclude NAME ...` | Skip these test cases. |
| `--runner pytest` | Run the suite through pytest instead of Optics' own runner. Most projects don't need this. |

To skip the reachability check, for example when the server is behind a proxy the check can't see, set `OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1`.

## How long steps wait

On Appium and Selenium, action keywords act on the screen as it is. They don't wait for it to change. On Playwright, an action waits up to 10 seconds for its element (`element_timeout_ms`). Checks wait:

| Keyword | Waits up to |
|---|---|
| `Assert Presence`, `Assert Visibility`, `Validate Screen` | 30 seconds |
| `Validate Element`, `Assert Text` | 10 seconds |
| `Detect And Press` | 30 seconds, then carries on without failing |

Pass a different time as the second value: `Assert Presence,Welcome,60`. For `Assert Text`, the time is the third value. Put a check after any step that loads a new screen, so the next action doesn't run too early.

## See also

- [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results)
- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci)
- [CLI reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results

# Read the results

> Find out what happened in a run from the JUnit report, the screenshots and the logs.

Every run writes its results to `execution_output/` inside the project folder. The terminal tree tells you *what* failed. The files tell you *why*.

## What a run writes

```tree
birch-tests/execution_output/
├── junit_output.xml                              # pass/fail for every test, for CI
├── 2026-10-09T14-02-11-…-pre_press_element.jpg  # the screen before each step
├── 2026-10-09T14-02-11-…-press_element_element_detection_result.jpg
├── 2026-10-09T14-02-14-…-failure_Shopper can sign in.jpg   # the screen of a failed test case
├── 2026-10-09T14-02-14-…-failure_Shopper can sign in.xml   # its UI tree
├── 2026-10-09T14-02-15-…-end_of_run.jpg         # the last screen
├── page_sources_log.xml                          # the UI tree, captured during the run
├── failed_steps_elements.json                    # the elements on screen when a step failed
├── internal_logs.log                             # with file_log: true
├── execution_logs.log                            # with file_log: true
└── logs.json                                     # with json_log: true
```

| File | When it's written | Use it to |
|---|---|---|
| `junit_output.xml` | Every run | Show results in CI. Standard JUnit XML that GitHub Actions, GitLab, Jenkins and others read. |
| `…pre_<keyword>.jpg` | Before each step that finds an element, with `save_captures: true` | See what was on screen when the step started. |
| `…_detection_result.jpg` | When Optics found an element by position, with `save_captures: true` | See exactly what Optics found, boxed in green. |
| `…_with_aoi.jpg` | When a step uses an [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest), with `save_captures: true` | Check the area covers the right part of the screen. It's drawn in blue. |
| `…failure_<test case>.jpg` and `.xml` | When a test case fails. Web pages write `.html`. | See the screen and the UI tree where the test case ended. |
| `…end_of_run.jpg` | At the end of the run, before Suite Teardown | See where the app was left. |
| `page_sources_log.xml` or `.html` | When the UI tree is read. Web pages go to `.html`. | Find the right XPath or text for an element. |
| `failed_steps_elements.json` | When a step fails, with `save_captures: true` | See each element on the screen of the failed step, with its label and bounds. |
| `internal_logs.log`, `execution_logs.log` | With `file_log: true` | Read every attempt Optics made, including which ways of finding an element failed. |
| `logs.json` | With `json_log: true` | Feed results into your own dashboards. |
| `detected_errors_<id>.json` | When an [error screen](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection) was found | See which error definition matched. |

## Investigate a failure

1. **Read the Failure details box** in the terminal. It names the test case, the step and the reason. `last error:` gives the error of the last fallback value, and `(cause: …)` gives the root cause.
2. **Open `failed_steps_elements.json`** to see the elements on the screen when the step failed. On a web page, each element has a `loc` locator that you can copy into your elements file.
3. **Open the `failure_<test case>` screenshot.** It shows where the test case ended. Then open the last `pre_…` screenshot before the failure. Is the screen what you expected? If it shows a loading spinner, the step ran too early: add an `Assert Presence` before it. If it shows a different screen, an earlier step went somewhere unexpected.
4. **Search the logs** for the element's value. With `file_log: true`, `execution_logs.log` has a line for every attempt, such as `Trying … on 'Sign in' ... FAIL`.
5. **Reproduce it in `optics live`.** Run the steps before the failure, then try the failing step with different values until one works. See [Record a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record).

## Turn on more logging

Add these to `config.yaml`:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
file_log: true      # write internal_logs.log and execution_logs.log
json_log: true      # write logs.json, a list of every run event
log_level: DEBUG    # more detail in the terminal and log files
```

`log_level` takes `DEBUG`, `INFO` (the default), `WARNING` or `ERROR`. Use `WARNING` to keep the terminal quiet so the tree stands out.

## Read the JUnit report

`junit_output.xml` has one `<testsuite>` and one `<testcase>` for each test case. Suite Setup and Suite Teardown also have one. The suite `name` and each `classname` are the name of the project folder, so name the folder after the suite. Each `<testcase>` has `kind`, `timestamp`, `time` and `status`. A failed test case also has a `<failure>`.

`kind` tells you the role of the test case: `suite_setup`, `setup`, `test`, `teardown` or `suite_teardown`. Use it to filter setup and teardown out of your test counts. A `<failure>` or `<error>` has a `code` attribute with the error code, such as `E0201`, when the failure has a code.

Inside each test case, every module and keyword is a `<kw>` with `status`, `starttime`, `endtime` and `elapsed`. CI tools that show nested steps display the same tree you saw in the terminal.

```xml
<testcase name="Shopper can find a missing link" classname="birch-tests" kind="test" time="3.79" ... status="FAIL">
  <kw name="Verify Missing Link" type="setup" status="FAIL" ... code="E0201">
    <kw name="Assert Presence" status="FAIL" ... code="E0201" elapsed="3.01">
    ...
    </kw>
    <kw name="Validate Element" status="NOT_RUN"/>
  </kw>
  <failure message="Keyword 'Assert Presence' failed after fallback attempts; ..." type="Failure" code="E0201">...</failure>
</testcase>
```

A status is one of these:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `PASS` | The test case, module or keyword passed. |
| `FAIL` | A check or an action failed. |
| `ERROR` | The run could not do its work, for example because the driver session was lost or the run stopped. |
| `NOT_RUN` | A failure or a stop kept it from running. |

After a failure, the steps that did not run are `NOT_RUN`. A test case that never started is `NOT_RUN` with a `<skipped>` element. A per-test setup or teardown has its own result, named `Setup (<test case>)` or `Teardown (<test case>)`. If a per-test setup fails, its test case does not run. The test case is `NOT_RUN`, and the `message` of its `<skipped>` starts with `Setup failed:`.

If error screens were detected, the report has an extra failing test case called `on-screen-error-detection`. See [Catch error screens](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection).

## What each outcome writes

Each outcome has an exit code and a result in `junit_output.xml`. A run that cannot start because of the project writes no report. Examples are a bad config and a test selection that is not valid.

| Outcome | Exit code | `junit_output.xml` |
|---|---|---|
| Every test case passed | `0` | Every test case is `PASS`. |
| A test case failed | `1` | That test case is `FAIL` with a `<failure>`. The steps after the failed step are `NOT_RUN`. |
| An error screen matched | `1` | An extra `on-screen-error-detection` test case has one `<failure>` for each match. |
| Suite Setup failed | `1` | Suite Setup is `FAIL`. Each other test case, except Suite Teardown, is `NOT_RUN` with a `<skipped>` whose `message` starts with `Suite setup failed:`. Suite Teardown runs. |
| A per-test setup failed | `1` | `Setup (<test case>)` is `FAIL`. Its test case is `NOT_RUN` with a `<skipped>` whose `message` starts with `Setup failed:`. Its teardown runs. |
| Config error, missing files or no driver enabled | `1` | Not written. |
| Test selection not valid | `3` | Not written. |
| The Appium or Selenium server cannot be reached, or no Android device is attached | `1` | Each test case is `ERROR` with an `<error>` that names the problem and has its code, such as `E0102`. Their steps are `NOT_RUN`. |
| The driver session is lost during the run | `1` | The test case in progress and each later one is `ERROR` with an `<error>` that has `E0106`. |
| You press Ctrl+C | `130` | Finished test cases keep their results. The one in progress is `ERROR` with `code="E0706"`. Later ones and Suite Teardown are `NOT_RUN` with `<skipped>`. |
| Optics receives SIGTERM | `143` | The same as Ctrl+C. |

A session is lost when the Appium server or the Selenium server stops, or drops the session, during a run. The terminal summary shows the affected test cases as failed.

If two sessions in one process share an output folder, such as with the Python SDK or `optics serve`, the second report is `junit_output_<session_id>.xml`. `optics execute` and `optics dry_run` always write `junit_output.xml`.

## Keep the folder tidy

Screenshots from every run accumulate in `execution_output/`. Clear the folder before runs where you need clean results, such as in CI:

```shell
$ rm -rf birch-tests/execution_output
$ optics execute birch-tests
```

To write results somewhere else, set `execution_output_path` in `config.yaml`. A relative path is relative to the folder you run `optics` from, and the folder must exist.

## See also

- [Catch error screens](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection)
- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci)
- [Troubleshooting](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/troubleshooting)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection

# Catch error screens

> Fail a run in CI when the app ends on a crash dialog, a "Session expired" message or any other error you define.

Some failures do not break a step. The app shows *Session expired*, or Android shows *Birch has stopped*, and the test still passes because no step looked for that message. Error detection catches these. You list the messages that mean something went wrong, and Optics checks the final screen for them in every run.

### List the error messages

Create a CSV anywhere in the project. The template uses `test_data/error_definitions.csv`:

`test_data/error_definitions.csv`:

```csv
error_code,match_string,description,severity
ERR_CRASH,has stopped,The app crashed with a system dialog,critical
ERR_NOT_RESPONDING,isn't responding,Android shows an ANR dialog,critical
ERR_SESSION,Session expired,The user was signed out,high
ERR_NETWORK,No internet connection,The app lost its connection,medium
ERR_SERVER,Something went wrong,The server returned an error page,high
```

| Column | Required | What it's for |
|---|---|---|
| `error_code` | Yes | A short name for the error. It appears in the report. |
| `match_string` | Yes | Text that means this error is on screen. |
| `description` | No | What the error means, for whoever reads the report. |
| `severity` | No | Any label you like, such as `critical` or `low`. |

### Run the suite as usual

```shell
$ optics execute birch-tests
```

There's nothing to switch on. If the project has an error definitions file, Optics uses it.

## What happens at the end of a run

Optics captures the screen once, reads all the text in the app's UI tree, and looks for each `match_string`. It does this before Suite Teardown when the suite has one, because a teardown often closes the app. Otherwise it does this after the last test case. Matching ignores case and finds the text anywhere: `session expired` matches *Your session expired. Please sign in again.*

For each match, Optics:

- logs a warning, which you can read in `execution_logs.log` when `file_log: true` is set: `ON-SCREEN ERROR DETECTED — code: ERR_SESSION | matched_on: match_string | match_string: 'Session expired' | severity: high | The user was signed out`,
- adds a failing test case named `on-screen-error-detection` to `junit_output.xml`, after the other test cases, with one failure per match,
- writes the details to `execution_output/detected_errors_<id>.json`.

The terminal tree shows `on-screen-error-detection` as `FAIL` and counts it in the summary:

```terminal
└── on-screen-error-detection                            |      0.00s |    FAIL
╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Total Test Cases: 4 | Passed: 3 | Failed: 1                                  │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

**A detected error fails the run:**
A detected error counts as a failed test case, so `optics execute` exits with code `1`. CI tools that read the exit code or the JUnit report show the run as failed, even when every step passed. See [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci#decide-pass-or-fail).

## Write good match strings

- **Use a phrase only an error would show.** `has stopped` is good. `Error` matches too much, such as a help page about error messages.
- **Copy the exact words** from a screenshot of the error, and keep them short. Matching is plain text, not a pattern, so `*` or `.*` are matched literally.
- **Avoid text that appears in your own tests.** A match anywhere on the last screen counts.

## Limits

- The check runs once, on the last screen. If the app recovers before the run ends, the error isn't seen. Add an explicit check in your test for errors that can appear and disappear mid-flow, such as `Assert Presence` on the screen you expect next.
- It needs the app's UI tree. On [production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production) driven through a camera, there's no tree to read.
- Optics skips the check if the app is already closed when it reads the final screen. This happens when the last test case ran `Close And Terminate App` and the suite has no Suite Teardown. Close the app in Suite Teardown instead.
- Definitions are CSV only. `optics dry_run`, `optics live`, the HTTP API and MCP don't run the check.

## See also

- [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results)
- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci)
- [Project files reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci

# Run tests in CI

> Run the same suite on every pull request and read the results in your CI system.

A suite earns its keep when it runs on every change. In CI, Optics needs the same three things as on your machine: Optics itself, the engines in your `config.yaml`, and something to drive. It reports through its exit code and a JUnit file, which every major CI system understands.

## Run a web suite

Web suites are the easiest to run in CI, because the browser runs on the CI machine itself.

**GitHub Actions**

`.github/workflows/optics.yml`:

```yaml
name: Optics

on: [push, pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read
  checks: write   # lets the report step post a check

jobs:
  web:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install Optics and the browser
        run: |
          pip install "optics-framework[playwright]==1.11.3"
          python -m playwright install --with-deps chromium

      - name: Run the suite
        run: optics execute birch-tests --no-use-printer

      - name: Publish results
        if: always()
        uses: mikepenz/action-junit-report@v6
        with:
          report_paths: birch-tests/execution_output/junit_output.xml

      - name: Keep the run output
        if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: optics-output
          path: birch-tests/execution_output/
```
**GitLab CI**

`.gitlab-ci.yml`:

```yaml
optics-web:
  image: python:3.12-bookworm
  script:
    - pip install "optics-framework[playwright]==1.11.3"
    - python -m playwright install --with-deps chromium
    - optics execute birch-tests --no-use-printer
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - birch-tests/execution_output/
    reports:
      junit: birch-tests/execution_output/junit_output.xml
```

CI machines have no display, so set `headless: true` under the Playwright `capabilities` in `config.yaml`:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - playwright:
      enabled: true
      capabilities:
        browser: chromium
        headless: true
```

To use a browser grid instead of a local browser, set the Playwright `url` and keep the token in a CI secret. Then you do not need `playwright install`. See [Use a remote browser](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web#use-a-remote-browser).

The `permissions` block lets the report step post its check. Without it, the step logs `Resource not accessible by integration` and no check appears. Pull requests from forks always get a read-only token, so on those the results are in the job log only.

## Run an Android suite

Android suites need an emulator and an Appium server on the CI machine. Linux runners with hardware acceleration, such as GitHub's `ubuntu-latest`, can run the Android emulator.

`.github/workflows/optics-android.yml`:

```yaml
name: Optics Android

on: [pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read
  checks: write

jobs:
  android:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Enable KVM
        run: |
          echo 'KERNEL=="kvm", GROUP="kvm", MODE="0666", OPTIONS+="static_node=kvm"' | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-kvm4all.rules
          sudo udevadm control --reload-rules
          sudo udevadm trigger --name-match=kvm

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 22

      - name: Install Optics and Appium
        run: |
          pip install "optics-framework[appium]==1.11.3"
          npm install -g appium
          appium driver install uiautomator2

      - name: Run the suite on an emulator
        uses: reactivecircus/android-emulator-runner@v2
        with:
          api-level: 34
          arch: x86_64
          script: |
            adb install app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
            appium > appium.log 2>&1 &
            sleep 5
            optics execute birch-tests --no-use-printer

      - name: Publish results
        if: always()
        uses: mikepenz/action-junit-report@v6
        with:
          report_paths: birch-tests/execution_output/junit_output.xml
```

Make sure `deviceName` in `config.yaml` matches the emulator (`emulator-5554` for the first one), and that `appPackage` and `appActivity` match the app you install.

## Decide pass or fail

`optics execute` exits with a non-zero code when a run does not pass, so the run step fails the job by itself:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | Every test case passed. |
| `1` | A test case failed, or an [error screen](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection) was found. The run also exits with `1` when it cannot start, for example when the server is not reachable. |
| `2` | The command line is not valid. |
| `3` | A name in `--include`, `--exclude` or the config `include` and `exclude` matches no test case. |
| `130` or `143` | A person or the CI system stopped the run with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. |

Optics also writes `junit_output.xml` when it stops with `130` or `143`. A run that cannot start because of the project, such as a bad config, writes no report. See [What each outcome writes](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results#what-each-outcome-writes).

An error screen adds a failing `on-screen-error-detection` test case to the report and changes the exit code to `1`. You do not need extra settings to fail the build on it.

## Make CI runs reliable

- **Pin the Optics version** (`optics-framework==1.11.3`), so a new release doesn't change behavior in the middle of a sprint. Upgrade on purpose, in its own pull request.
- **Run `optics dry_run` first** in a fast job. It catches typos in seconds, before you pay for an emulator.
- **Split a long suite** into parallel jobs with `--include` and `--exclude`, for example `optics execute birch-tests --include "checkout*"` in one job. See [Pick test cases](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli#pick-test-cases).
- **Start from a clean output folder.** CI checkouts usually are. On reused machines, delete `execution_output/` before the run.
- **Keep the artifacts.** Upload `execution_output/` when a run fails (see the web example). Its logs and screenshots usually explain the failure faster than the CI log.
- **Keep secrets out of the suite.** Pass model API keys such as `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as CI secrets, in environment variables. Optics writes `****` in place of a secret in the console, the logs and the JUnit report. See [Hide sensitive values](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables#hide-sensitive-values).
- **Wait for screens to load.** Runners are often slower than your laptop. Put `Assert Presence` before actions that follow a screen change, rather than adding `Sleep` steps.

## See also

- [Readiness checklist](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/checklist)
- [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results)
- [Android](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android) and [Web](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web) setup

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/checklist

# Readiness checklist

> Use this checklist before you rely on a suite in CI or for production monitoring.

A suite that passes on your laptop can still be flaky, slow or hard to debug in CI. Work through these items before the team starts trusting its results. Your ticks are saved in this browser, so you can come back to the list.

## The suite

- [ ] **Every test case has a clear outcome in its name.** *Shopper can add a backpack* tells whoever reads a failure what broke. *Test 3* doesn't.
- [ ] **Every screen change is followed by a check.** On Appium and Selenium, action keywords do not wait. Put `Assert Presence` or `Validate Element` after any step that loads a new screen, instead of `Sleep`. See [Run a suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/#how-long-steps-wait).
- [ ] **Important elements have a fallback.** Give key buttons and fields a second value, usually their visible text, so one renamed id doesn't fail the run. See [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define).
- [ ] **No test relies on another.** Each test case should be able to run on its own, with Suite Setup handling shared setup. Check with `optics execute <folder> --include "<test case>"`.
- [ ] **`optics dry_run` passes.** Run it before every commit, and as the first CI step.

## The configuration

- [ ] **The Optics version is pinned** in CI (`optics-framework==1.11.3`). Upgrade on purpose, in its own change.
- [ ] **Only the engines you use are enabled.** Every enabled OCR or image engine loads at the start of each run, even when no step needs it.
- [ ] **No secrets are in `config.yaml` or the suite files.** Keep API keys in environment variables, and refer to them as `api_key: ${GEMINI_API_KEY}`. Keep passwords in CI secrets.
- [ ] **The project folder holds one config file** and no stray copies of old suites. Optics reads every CSV and YAML in the folder.

## The run

- [ ] **Error screens are defined.** Add the crash, timeout and "something went wrong" messages your app can show to an [error definitions file](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection).
- [ ] **CI reads the exit code and the JUnit report.** An error screen gives exit code `1` and adds a failing test case to the report. See [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci#decide-pass-or-fail).
- [ ] **Screenshots are kept when a run fails.** Upload `execution_output/` as a CI artifact.
- [ ] **File logs are on for CI runs.** `file_log: true` gives you every locator attempt when a failure is hard to explain.
- [ ] **Someone owns the failures.** Decide who looks at a red run, and how fast. A suite people learn to ignore is worse than no suite.

## If you use AI features

- [ ] **Healed steps are reviewed.** With [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal) on, a healed step passes. Search the logs for `AI self-heal` after each run and update the elements.
- [ ] **Screens sent to the AI model are safe to share.** Plain-English mode and self-heal send screenshots to your LLM provider.

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/

# Supported platforms

> Learn which platforms Optics drives, what each one needs, and which keywords behave differently.

Optics runs the same tests on phones, TVs, browsers and locked production devices. A **driver** controls the device, and **element sources** are the ways Optics looks at the screen. You pick both in `config.yaml`.

## Support matrix

| Platform | Driver | Element sources | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android | `appium` (UiAutomator2) | `appium_find_element`, `appium_page_source`, `appium_web`, `appium_screenshot` | Needs the Appium server, adb, and a phone or emulator. |
| iOS | `appium` (XCUITest) | `appium_find_element`, `appium_page_source`, `appium_web`, `appium_screenshot` | Needs a Mac with Xcode, and a simulator or a signed real device. |
| Mobile web (Chrome, Safari, WebViews) | `appium` | `appium_web` with the Android or iOS sources | Same setup as Android or iOS. Finds `css=` and DOM XPath locators in the page. |
| Android TV | `appium` (UiAutomator2) | `appium_find_element`, `appium_page_source`, `appium_screenshot` | Same setup as Android. Move around with D-pad key numbers. |
| Samsung Tizen | `appium` (`platformName: TizenTV`) | `appium_find_element`, `camera_screenshot` | Element keywords move the remote focus. Touch keywords fail with E0105. |
| LG webOS | `appium` (`platformName: LGTV`) | `appium_find_element`, plus OCR | Element keywords move the remote focus. Touch keywords fail with E0105. |
| Web (Playwright) | `playwright` | `playwright_find_element`, `playwright_page_source`, `playwright_screenshot` | No server. Opens Chromium, Firefox or WebKit on your machine, or connects to a remote browser. Can emulate a phone. |
| Web (Selenium) | `selenium` | `selenium_find_element`, `selenium_page_source`, `selenium_screenshot` | Needs a WebDriver server or Grid. Chrome or Firefox. |
| Production devices (BLE + camera) | `ble` | `camera_screenshot`, plus OCR or image matching | Taps through a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, and sees the screen through a camera. |

Enable one driver and the element sources whose names start with that driver's name. The [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config) lists every key, and the [engines reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines) lists what each engine installs.

## Choose a driver for web

We recommend **Playwright** for most people. It needs no server, `optics setup` installs its browser for you, and it runs on your own machine.

Use **Selenium** when you already run a Selenium Grid, or need Firefox or a real Chrome on remote machines. It needs a WebDriver server running before each run. [Test websites](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web) covers both.

## What changes between platforms

Between phones and browsers, only `config.yaml` changes. Your test cases, modules and keywords stay the same. To run a suite on another platform, copy the project and swap the driver and element sources.

TVs on Samsung Tizen and LG webOS are the exception. They have no touch screen, so the element keywords press remote keys to move the focus. Touch keywords such as Swipe and Scroll fail with E0105 there. Use Press Keycode for single remote keys. [Test TV apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv) shows the locators and key names.

Element values usually do change, because each platform names things differently. Give an element one row per platform, and Optics tries each value in turn:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
sign_in,//android.widget.Button[@text='Sign in']
sign_in,//XCUIElementTypeButton[@name='Sign in']
sign_in,Sign in
```

The last row is plain text, which works on any platform with a UI tree, and with OCR on any platform that takes screenshots. [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define) explains fallback values.

## What doesn't work everywhere

Most keywords work on every platform. These are the exceptions:

| Keyword | Where it differs |
|---|---|
| Swipe, Scroll and other touch keywords | Fail with E0105 on Samsung Tizen and LG webOS. Press Element and Enter Text move the remote focus instead. |
| Press Keycode | Takes Android key numbers on Android and Android TV, remote key names on Tizen and webOS, and key names such as `Enter` on Playwright. Not supported on Selenium or iOS. |
| Swipe | Not supported on Selenium. On Playwright it scrolls the page up or down. |
| Launch App | Opens a package, a bundle id or a URL on Appium, and a URL on Playwright. On Selenium it opens `browserURL`. Not supported on production devices. |
| Go Back | Goes back one page in a browser, and presses Back on Android. On iOS it taps the navigation bar's back button. Fails with E0105 on TVs and production devices. |
| XPath and UI-tree text | Not available on production devices, which only have camera pictures. Use OCR and images. |
| [Error detection](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection) | Needs the page source, so it doesn't run on production devices. |

The [keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/) lists each keyword's behavior per driver.

## Platform guides

- [Android](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android): Set up Appium and adb, then run on a phone or emulator.
- [iOS](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios): Run on a simulator or a signed device with XCUITest.
- [Web](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web): Test websites with Playwright or Selenium. (Recommended)
- [Mobile web](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/mobile-web): Test Chrome, Safari and WebViews on a real phone.
- [TV](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv): Drive Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS with remote keys.
- [Production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production): Test locked devices through Bluetooth and a camera. (Advanced)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android

# Test Android apps

> Set up Appium and adb, then run your tests on an Android phone or emulator.

Optics drives Android apps through **Appium**, an open-source server that taps, types and reads the screen on a device. You run the Appium server on your machine, Optics talks to it, and Appium talks to the phone or emulator over **adb** (Android Debug Bridge, the SDK's device tool).

This page uses Birch, a sample shoe store app with the package name `com.birch.shop`. Replace it with your own app.

## Before you begin

You need:

- Optics installed. See [Install Optics](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/install).
- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) 20 or newer, to run the Appium server.
- The Android SDK. We recommend getting it with [Android Studio](https://developer.android.com/studio), which also creates emulators.
- An emulator, or an Android phone and a USB cable.

## Set up

### Install the Appium engine

```shell
$ optics setup --install appium
```

This adds the Python client that Optics uses to talk to Appium. It doesn't install the server.

### Install the Appium server and its Android driver

```shell
$ npm install -g appium
$ appium driver install uiautomator2
```

UiAutomator2 is the Appium driver for Android. It needs the `ANDROID_HOME` environment variable set to your SDK folder, and Java installed. Run `appium driver doctor uiautomator2` to check both.

### Make adb available

adb ships in the SDK's `platform-tools` folder. Add that folder to your PATH, then check it:

```shell
$ adb version
```

On macOS the SDK is usually in `~/Library/Android/sdk`, on Linux in `~/Android/Sdk`, and on Windows in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Android\Sdk`.

### Start an emulator or connect a phone

For an emulator, open Android Studio's **Device Manager** and start a virtual device.

For a phone, turn on **Developer options** (tap **Build number** seven times in **Settings > About phone**), then turn on **USB debugging**. Connect the cable and accept the "Allow USB debugging?" prompt on the phone.

Check that adb sees it:

```shell
$ adb devices
List of devices attached
emulator-5554	device
```

The first column is the device's serial. `device` in the second column means it's ready. `unauthorized` means you still need to accept the prompt on the phone.

### Find the app's package and activity

Optics needs the app's **package** (its id, such as `com.birch.shop`) and its **activity** (the screen it opens on). Open the app on the device, then ask adb what has focus:

```shell
$ adb shell dumpsys window | grep -E 'mCurrentFocus'
  mCurrentFocus=Window{4f2a1c u0 com.birch.shop/com.birch.shop.MainActivity}
```

The part before the `/` is the package, and the part after it is the activity. If you know the package, you can also ask Android for its launch activity:

```shell
$ adb shell cmd package resolve-activity --brief com.birch.shop
priority=0 preferredOrder=0 match=0x108000 specificIndex=-1 isDefault=true
com.birch.shop/.MainActivity
```

An activity that starts with a dot is short for the package plus that name: `.MainActivity` means `com.birch.shop.MainActivity`.

### Write config.yaml

Create a project with `optics init birch-android`, then replace its `config.yaml`:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - appium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://127.0.0.1:4723"          # where the Appium server listens
      capabilities:                          # must not be empty
        platformName: Android                # required; picks the Android setup
        automationName: UiAutomator2
        deviceName: emulator-5554
        udid: emulator-5554                  # optional; pins one device
        appPackage: com.birch.shop           # app opened by "Launch App" with no value
        appActivity: com.birch.shop.MainActivity
        # appium:settings: {allowInvisibleElements: true}  # optional; include off-screen elements
elements_sources:
  - appium_find_element: {enabled: true}     # asks Appium for XPaths, ids and text
  - appium_page_source:  {enabled: true}     # searches the app's UI tree
  - appium_web:          {enabled: true}     # finds css= and DOM XPath in web pages
  - appium_screenshot:   {enabled: true}     # screenshots for OCR and image matching
text_detection:
  - easyocr: {enabled: true}                 # needs: optics setup --install easyocr
image_detection:
  - templatematch: {enabled: true}           # finds .png templates anywhere in the project
log_level: INFO
file_log: true
json_log: true
```

Always set `url`. Optics can't connect if it's missing or empty. If you don't need OCR yet, delete the `text_detection` block, because an enabled OCR engine must be installed for every run.

### Check the setup

```shell
$ optics doctor birch-android
```

```terminal
Mobile
  ✅ adb                               found at /Users/you/Library/Android/sdk/platform-tools/adb
  ✅ adb devices                       1 connected: emulator-5554
  ⚠️ appium server                     not reachable at 127.0.0.1:4723
      → Start it in another terminal with the `appium` command.

Project
  ✅ config: driver                    appium enabled
  ✅ config: appium element source     enabled: appium_find_element, appium_page_source, appium_screenshot, appium_web
  ✅ config: appium settings           required settings present
```

Fix every ❌ row. A ⚠️ on `adb devices` or `appium server` blocks the first run too, and the doctor lists them under "Before your first real run". A ⚠️ for `deviceName`, `appPackage` or `appActivity` means the key is missing from `capabilities`.

### Start Appium

Open a second terminal and leave this running:

```shell
$ appium
```

It listens on port 4723, which matches `url` in the config.

### Run the tests

```shell
$ optics execute birch-android
```

The app opens on the device and the terminal shows each step as it runs.

## Write steps for Android

Tests for Android look like any other Optics test. Elements can be XPaths into the Android UI tree, visible text, or images:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
email_field,//android.widget.EditText[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email']
password_field,//android.widget.EditText[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password']
sign_in,Sign in
password,@:trailrunner
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Birch,Launch App
Open Birch,Assert Presence,Sign in,20
Sign in,Enter Text,${email_field},ava@birch.shop
Sign in,Enter Text,${password_field},${password}
Sign in,Press Element,${sign_in}
Sign in,Assert Presence,Trail Runner 2,15
```

`Launch App` with no value opens `appPackage` from the config. Pass a package to open a different app: `Launch App,com.android.settings`. The `@:` prefix marks `password` as secret, so it's typed without the prefix and masked in log files. To find XPaths and ids, open the app in [`optics live`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) or [Appium Inspector](https://github.com/appium/appium-inspector).

## What `optics execute` checks first

Before a run starts, `optics execute` runs a **preflight**. For Android it checks that:

1. The Appium server answers at `url`.
2. `adb` is on your PATH.
3. adb reports at least one device in the `device` state.

If a check fails, Optics stops and prints what to do:

```terminal
Cannot start

No Appium server reachable at http://127.0.0.1:4723.

Start one in another terminal:  appium
Then re-run:  optics execute birch-android
```

The adb checks run only when the plain `platformName` key is `Android`, in any capitalization, and `url` points to this machine (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1` or `0.0.0.0`). For a remote device farm, Optics checks only that the server answers. To skip the preflight completely, set `OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT`:

```shell
$ OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1 optics execute birch-android
```

`optics dry_run` has no preflight, so it works without a device.

## Press keys

Press Keycode sends an Android key by its number:

| Key | Number |
|---|---|
| Back | `4` |
| Home | `3` |
| Enter | `66` |
| Backspace | `67` |
| Tab | `61` |
| Volume up / down | `24` / `25` |
| Recent apps | `187` |

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1
Open home,Press Keycode,3
```

To press Back, use the Go Back keyword.

Android's [KeyEvent list](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/view/KeyEvent) has every number. To press Enter after typing, you can also write `Enter Text Using Keyboard,<enter>`. See [Press Keycode](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#press-keycode) for details.

## Tips

- **Steps do not wait for an idle screen.** UiAutomator2 waits up to 10 seconds for the app to stop changing before each command. Optics sets this limit to 1 second. To change it, set `waitForIdleTimeout` in milliseconds under `appium:settings`. `0` turns the wait off.
- **App data is kept between runs.** Optics starts each session with `noReset: true`, so Appium doesn't clear the app's data and a signed-in user stays signed in. Add `noReset: false` to `capabilities` to start every run from a fresh app.
- **Pick a device with `udid`.** When several devices are connected, set `udid` to the serial from `adb devices`. `deviceName` is only a label.
- **Include off-screen elements.** Android leaves elements that are scrolled out of view out of the UI tree. Add `appium:settings: {allowInvisibleElements: true}` under `capabilities` to include them.
- **Switch devices in `optics live`.** When you plug in another Android device during `optics live`, Optics notices and switches the session to it.
- **Android TV uses the same setup.** See [Test TV apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv) for remote-control keys.

## If it isn't working

- **"No Appium server reachable".** Start `appium` in another terminal. If it runs on another port or machine, make `url` match.
- **"No Android device/emulator attached".** Run `adb devices`. If the phone shows `unauthorized`, accept the prompt on it. If it shows `offline`, reconnect the cable or run `adb kill-server`, then `adb devices` again.
- **`E0104` "Appium capabilities not found in config".** `capabilities` is empty or missing. Add at least `platformName`.
- **`E0104` "Unsupported platform".** Check the spelling of `platformName`. Use `Android`.
- **Appium can't find the UiAutomator2 driver, or complains about `ANDROID_HOME`.** Run `appium driver install uiautomator2`, set `ANDROID_HOME`, and check with `appium driver doctor uiautomator2`.
- **The app opens on the wrong screen.** Check `appActivity`. If the app remembers an old state, set `noReset: false`.
- **A swipe or scroll passes but nothing moves.** Appium gesture errors are logged, not raised. Check the screenshots in `execution_output/`.
- **An element isn't found.** Actions don't wait, so put `Assert Presence` before them. [Troubleshooting](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/troubleshooting) covers more cases.

## See also

- [Test mobile websites](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/mobile-web)
- [Test TV apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv)
- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define)
- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci)
- [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config)
- [CLI reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios

# Test iOS apps

> Set up Appium with the XCUITest driver, then run your tests on an iOS simulator or device.

Optics drives iOS apps through **Appium** and its **XCUITest** driver, which uses Apple's own UI testing tools. You run the Appium server on a Mac, and Optics talks to it. iOS testing needs macOS, because Xcode only runs there.

This page uses Birch, a sample shoe store app with the bundle id `com.birch.shop`. Replace it with your own app.

## Before you begin

You need:

- A Mac with [Xcode](https://developer.apple.com/xcode/) installed from the App Store. Open it once to accept the license and install its components, then run `xcode-select --install` for the command-line tools.
- Optics installed. See [Install Optics](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/install).
- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) 20 or newer, to run the Appium server.
- A build of your app: a `.app` for the simulator, or a signed build for a real device.

## Set up

### Install the Appium engine

```shell
$ optics setup --install appium
```

### Install the Appium server and the XCUITest driver

```shell
$ npm install -g appium
$ appium driver install xcuitest
```

### Start a simulator

List the simulators Xcode provides:

```shell
$ xcrun simctl list devices
== Devices ==
-- iOS 17.5 --
    iPhone 15 (5D1C2A60-8F0E-4B7A-9C41-2E6F0C3B9A17) (Shutdown)
    iPhone 15 Pro (A3E9F7B2-1C44-4D2B-8E0A-7B5D9C6E2F01) (Shutdown)
```

Boot one by name and open the Simulator app to watch it:

```shell
$ xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 15"
$ open -a Simulator
```

### Install the app and find its bundle id

Install your simulator build, then read its **bundle id**, the app's unique name:

```shell
$ xcrun simctl install booted Birch.app
$ plutil -extract CFBundleIdentifier raw Birch.app/Info.plist
com.birch.shop
```

### Write config.yaml

Create a project with `optics init birch-ios`, then replace its `config.yaml`:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - appium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://127.0.0.1:4723"
      capabilities:
        platformName: iOS                    # picks the iOS setup
        automationName: XCUITest
        deviceName: "iPhone 15"              # the simulator's name
        bundleId: com.birch.shop             # required: the app Launch App opens
        # udid: <device udid>                # real devices
elements_sources:
  - appium_find_element: {enabled: true}
  - appium_page_source:  {enabled: true}
  - appium_web:          {enabled: true}     # finds css= and DOM XPath in web pages
  - appium_screenshot:   {enabled: true}
```

If you have several iOS versions installed, add `platformVersion: "17.5"` so Appium picks the right simulator.

### Check the setup

```shell
$ optics doctor birch-ios
```

Without `bundleId`, the doctor shows a failure, because XCUITest has nothing to launch:

```terminal
Project
  ✅ config: driver                    appium enabled
  ✅ config: appium element source     enabled: appium_find_element, appium_page_source, appium_screenshot, appium_web
  ❌ config: appium settings           bundleId missing in capabilities
      → Edit config.yaml in this project folder.
```

The `adb` rows in the Mobile section are for Android. Ignore them on iOS, even when the doctor lists the adb hint under "Before your first real run".

### Start Appium and run

Start the server in a second terminal and leave it running:

```shell
$ appium
```

Then run the tests:

```shell
$ optics execute birch-ios
```

Before the run, Optics checks that the Appium server answers at `url`. Set `OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1` to skip that check. The first session on a new simulator takes a few minutes, because Appium builds its helper app, WebDriverAgent, and installs it.

## Test on a real device

A real iPhone or iPad needs a few more steps:

1. Connect the device, trust the Mac, and turn on **Developer Mode** in **Settings > Privacy & Security**.
2. Find its id with `xcrun xctrace list devices` and set it as `udid` under `capabilities`.
3. Sign WebDriverAgent with your Apple developer team, so it can be installed on the device.

Signing is the step that most often goes wrong. Follow the [Appium XCUITest driver docs](https://appium.github.io/appium-xcuitest-driver/latest/) for real-device setup.

## Write steps for iOS

iOS elements have types such as `XCUIElementTypeButton` and attributes such as `name`, `label` and `value`. Use them in XPaths:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
email_field,//XCUIElementTypeTextField[@name='Email']
password_field,//XCUIElementTypeSecureTextField[@name='Password']
sign_in,//XCUIElementTypeButton[@name='Sign in']
sign_in,Sign in
back_button,//XCUIElementTypeButton[@name='Back']
```

Plain text such as `Sign in` is matched against the accessibility id and the `name`, `label` and `value` attributes. A value that starts with `XCUIElementType`, such as `XCUIElementTypeSwitch`, finds elements by type; add `index` to pick one of several.

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Birch,Launch App
Open Birch,Assert Presence,Sign in,20
Sign in,Enter Text,${email_field},ava@birch.shop
Sign in,Press Element,${sign_in}
Sign in,Assert Presence,Trail Runner 2,15
```

To see the real names in your app, open it in [`optics live`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) or [Appium Inspector](https://github.com/appium/appium-inspector).

## Keys on iOS

iOS has no Back key and no Android key numbers, so Press Keycode does not work on iOS. Instead:

- **Go back.** Use Go Back. It taps the back button in the navigation bar. If the screen has no such button, the step fails with E0401. Then tap the app's own button, such as `${back_button}` above.
- **Press Home.** Run XCUITest's `mobile: pressButton` command with Execute Script. Its buttons are `home`, `volumeup` and `volumedown`:

  `modules/modules.csv`:

  ```csv
  module_name,module_step,param_1
  Go home,Execute Script,"{""script"": ""mobile: pressButton"", ""args"": {""name"": ""home""}}"
  ```

- **Type and submit.** Type with Enter Text on a field, then tap the keyboard's own submit key by its label. Enter Text Direct and Enter Text Using Keyboard type into the field that has focus, so tap the field first. They accept `<enter>`, `<tab>`, `<backspace>` and `<space>`. Other keys fail with E0401.

## If it isn't working

- **The doctor shows ❌ for `bundleId`.** Add `bundleId` under `capabilities`. Only the plain key name counts for this check.
- **"No Appium server reachable".** Start `appium` in another terminal, and make `url` match its port.
- **Appium can't find the XCUITest driver.** Run `appium driver install xcuitest`, then restart `appium`.
- **Appium can't find the simulator.** Make `deviceName` match a name from `xcrun simctl list devices`, and add `platformVersion` if several iOS versions are installed.
- **WebDriverAgent fails to build or install on a device.** This is a signing problem. See the [XCUITest driver docs](https://appium.github.io/appium-xcuitest-driver/latest/).
- **`E0104` "Unsupported platform".** Check the spelling of `platformName`. Use `iOS`.
- **Each step takes about 10 seconds.** The app never stops changing, for example a timer. Optics limits XCUITest's idle wait to 1 second. To turn it off, set `appium:settings: {waitForIdleTimeout: 0}`.
- **An element isn't found.** Actions don't wait, so put `Assert Presence` before them. [Troubleshooting](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/troubleshooting) covers more cases.

## See also

- [Test mobile websites](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/mobile-web)
- [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android)
- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define)
- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci)
- [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web

# Test websites

> Set up Playwright or Selenium, then run your tests in a browser.

Optics tests websites with one of two drivers. **Playwright** starts a browser on your machine and needs no server. **Selenium** sends commands to a WebDriver server, such as a Selenium Grid, which runs the browser.

We recommend Playwright unless you already run a Selenium Grid, or need Firefox or a real Chrome on remote machines. The examples use the [Sauce Labs demo store](https://www.saucedemo.com), which you can sign in to with `standard_user` / `secret_sauce`.

## Set up

**Playwright**

Install the engine. Optics also downloads the Chromium browser that Playwright uses:

```shell
$ optics setup --install playwright
```

Then enable the driver and its three element sources:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - playwright:
      enabled: true                          # no url and no server needed
      capabilities:
        browser: chromium                    # or firefox, webkit
        headless: false                      # true: no window
        # viewport: {width: 1280, height: 800}
elements_sources:
  - playwright_find_element: {enabled: true}
  - playwright_page_source:  {enabled: true}
  - playwright_screenshot:   {enabled: true}
```

`optics setup` downloads only Chromium. For Firefox or WebKit, run `python -m playwright install firefox` or `webkit` in the Optics environment.

There's no server to start, so `optics execute` skips its preflight check for Playwright.

Chromium starts without the automation flags, so `navigator.webdriver` is `false`, as in a browser that a person opens. Selenium Chrome starts in the same way.

**Selenium**

Install the engine:

```shell
$ optics setup --install selenium
```

Selenium needs a WebDriver server. The quickest is Selenium's Docker image, which runs Chrome inside a container:

```shell
$ docker run -d -p 4444:4444 selenium/standalone-chrome
```

For Firefox, use `selenium/standalone-firefox`. If you already run a Selenium Grid, point `url` at it instead.

Then enable the driver and its element sources:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - selenium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://localhost:4444/wd/hub"   # your Grid or standalone server
      capabilities:                          # must not be empty
        browserName: chrome                  # required: chrome or firefox
        browserURL: "https://www.saucedemo.com"  # page opened when the browser starts
elements_sources:
  - selenium_find_element: {enabled: true}
  - selenium_page_source:  {enabled: true}
  - selenium_screenshot:   {enabled: true}
```

`capabilities` must include `browserName`, and only `chrome` and `firefox` work. `optics configure` writes `capabilities: {}` for Selenium, which can't start, so add these keys by hand. Other keys under `capabilities` are passed to the browser as WebDriver capabilities.

Before each run, `optics execute` checks that the server answers at `url`. If it doesn't, Optics stops with a "Cannot start" panel. Set `OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1` to skip the check.

Then check the setup and run your tests:

```shell
$ optics doctor my-web-tests
$ optics execute my-web-tests
```

## Open the site

Launch App starts the browser. How it picks the page depends on the driver:

| Step | Playwright | Selenium |
|---|---|---|
| `Launch App,https://www.saucedemo.com` | Opens the browser at that URL. | Opens the browser at that URL the first time. |
| `Launch App` with no URL | Opens a blank page. | Opens `browserURL`, or a blank page if it isn't set. |
| `Launch Other App,https://www.saucedemo.com/cart.html` | Opens the URL in a new tab. | Goes to the URL in the current tab. |

We recommend putting the URL in the Launch App step. Then the same module works with both drivers.

## Write steps for the web

Here is a full sign-in test for the Sauce Labs demo store. It works with both drivers:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
username_field,//input[@id='user-name']
password_field,//input[@id='password']
login_button,//input[@id='login-button']
backpack_add_button,//button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack']
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open the store,Launch App,https://www.saucedemo.com
Open the store,Assert Presence,Swag Labs,15
Sign in,Enter Text,${username_field},standard_user
Sign in,Enter Text,${password_field},secret_sauce
Sign in,Press Element,${login_button}
Sign in,Assert Presence,Products,10
Add the backpack,Press Element,${backpack_add_button}
Add the backpack,Assert Presence,Remove,5
```

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
Shopper can add a backpack,Open the store
Shopper can add a backpack,Sign in
Shopper can add a backpack,Add the backpack
```

### Locators for web pages

| Kind | Example | Playwright | Selenium |
|---|---|---|---|
| XPath | `//input[@id='user-name']` | Yes, also with `xpath=` | Yes. Leave out `xpath=`. |
| Visible text | `Products`, `text=Add to cart` | Yes | Yes |
| Bare id or name | `user-name` | No. Write `id=user-name`. | Yes. Tried as an id, name, class or link text when no text matches. |
| CSS selector | `#user-name`, `.inventory_item_name`, `css=button[data-test='login-button']` | Yes | No |
| Attribute prefix | `id=user-name`, `data-test=login-button`, `label=Username`, `placeholder=Username`, `role=button` | Yes | No |
| Alt text and title | `alt=Birch logo`, `title=Open the cart` | Yes | No |
| Test id | `testid=save-btn`, `data-testid=save-btn` | Yes | No |
| Exact text | `text="Save"` | Yes. It does not match `Save changes`. | No |
| Locators from other agent browsers | `loc=css:button.save`, `loc=role:button[name="Save changes"]`, `loc=href:/next` | Yes | No |
| Image | `cart_icon.png` | With image matching on | With image matching on |

We recommend XPath for web elements. It's the one kind of value that works the same way with both drivers, so you can switch drivers without editing elements.

A prefix can be in any case. `Get Interactive Elements` lists an element with a pointer cursor as tappable, even when it has no role, link or click attribute.

On Playwright, actions wait up to 10 seconds for the element to show. When a locator matches several elements, the log names the count and the one Optics used. Add `index=` or a more specific locator to pick another.

To see an element's id or attributes, right-click it in Chrome and choose **Inspect**. [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define) explains each kind of value.

## Press keys

| Driver | How to press Enter | Other keys |
|---|---|---|
| Playwright | `Press Keycode,Enter` or `Enter Text Using Keyboard,<enter>` | `Tab`, `Escape`, `Backspace`, `Delete`, `Space`, `ArrowUp`, `ArrowDown`, `ArrowLeft`, `ArrowRight`, and other [Playwright key names](https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-keyboard#keyboard-press) |
| Selenium | `Enter Text Using Keyboard,<enter>` | `<tab>`, `<backspace>`, `<space>`, `<escape>` |

Press Keycode isn't supported on Selenium. The keys go to whichever field has focus, so press the field first.

On Playwright, Press Keycode accepts a key name in any case. `ESC`, `arrowdown` and `KEYCODE_ENTER` work in the same way as `Escape`, `ArrowDown` and `Enter`. A name that Optics does not know fails with [E0403](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/errors#e04-keywords-and-parameters) and lists the valid names.

## Emulate a phone

Set `device` to a [Playwright device name](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json). The page gets that phone's screen size, user agent and touch input:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - playwright:
      enabled: true
      capabilities:
        browser: chromium     # webkit for an iPhone, to get Safari's engine
        device: "iPhone 15"
```

An emulated phone is still a desktop browser. To test the real Chrome or Safari on a phone, see [Test mobile websites](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/mobile-web).

## Start signed in from a saved file

Sign in once, save the browser state to a file, and every run starts signed in. Sign in by hand in the window that opens, then close it:

```shell
$ python -m playwright open --save-storage=auth.json https://www.saucedemo.com
```

Then point `storage_state` at the file. The path is relative to the project folder:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - playwright:
      enabled: true
      capabilities:
        storage_state: auth.json
```

**Warning:**
The file holds live session cookies. Do not commit it to version control.

## Start signed in with a browser profile

Use a browser profile when you are signed in to the site in Chrome or Edge on the same computer. Optics copies the sign-ins of that profile, so you do not sign in again. Each of the three options keeps sign-ins in a different place:

| Option | Use it when | Sign-ins come from |
|---|---|---|
| `storage_state` | The run must work on any computer, in CI, with `device` or in a remote browser. | A file that Playwright saved. See [Start signed in from a saved file](#start-signed-in-from-a-saved-file). |
| `profile` | You are signed in to Chrome or Edge on this computer. | A temporary copy of that profile. Optics deletes the copy at the end of the session. |
| `user_data_dir` | You want to sign in once in the Optics browser and keep the sign-in for later runs. | A folder that stays between runs. |

Set `profile` to the directory of the profile (`Default`, `Profile 1`), its name or its account email:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - playwright:
      enabled: true
      capabilities:
        profile: me@example.com
        channel: chrome
```

Optics copies the cookies, local storage and preferences of the profile into a temporary folder. It starts the browser with the copy. The real profile does not change. `channel` is `chrome`, `chrome-beta` or `msedge`. Without it, Optics uses the browser that owns the profile.

Most site sign-ins carry over. Google accounts are signed out in a copy. If the value matches no profile, or more than one, the run stops with [E0501](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/errors#e05-files-and-config) and lists the profiles that Optics found:

```terminal
No browser profile 'nobody@example.com'. Profiles: chrome 'Default' (Person 1, not signed in); chrome 'Profile 1' (Birch tester, tester@birch.example)
```

To keep the sign-in between runs, set `user_data_dir` to a folder, for example `~/optics-browser`. Sign in once in the window that opens. A path that starts with `./` is relative to the project folder and must exist.

`profile` and `user_data_dir` apply to a browser that Optics starts. Each of these stops the run with E0501:

- `profile` or `user_data_dir` with a remote `url`.
- `profile` with `user_data_dir`.
- `profile` or `user_data_dir` with `storage_state`.

`optics serve` refuses `profile`. `optics mcp --transport http` refuses it too, and no session API accepts `user_data_dir`. A local `optics mcp` on stdio lists the profiles in the `optics://browser-profiles` resource. See [MCP server reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp).

## Use a remote browser

Set `url` to a browser's endpoint, and Optics connects to that browser instead of starting one. You do not need to download a browser.

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - playwright:
      enabled: true
      url: "wss://grid.example.com/session"
      capabilities:
        protocol: cdp                 # or playwright
        headers:
          Authorization: Bearer ${GRID_TOKEN}
```

| `protocol` | Connects to |
|---|---|
| `cdp` (default) | A Chrome DevTools Protocol endpoint, such as Browserless or Chrome started with `--remote-debugging-port=9222` (`url: "http://127.0.0.1:9222"`). Chromium only. |
| `playwright` | A Playwright server, such as `npx playwright run-server`, BrowserStack or LambdaTest. The server's Playwright version must match. |

`${NAME}` in `url` or in a header is read from that environment variable when the browser starts, so your credentials stay out of the suite. If the variable is not set, the run stops and names it.

Optics opens a new context in the remote browser. To use the browser's own context and open tab instead, for example to use a profile that is signed in, set `context: existing`.

## Timeouts

All values are in milliseconds, under `capabilities`:

| Capability | Default | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| `element_timeout_ms` | `10000` | The wait for an element before an action |
| `navigation_timeout_ms` | `60000` | Page loads from Launch App and Go Back |
| `settle_timeout_ms` | `3000` | The wait for the page to stop changes before Optics reads it. `0` turns it off. |
| `connect_timeout_ms` | `90000` | The connection to a remote browser |
| `action_timeout_ms` | `15000` | Each other browser call, such as a key press or a screenshot |

`navigation_wait_until` sets the load event that a page load waits for: `domcontentloaded` (default), `load`, `networkidle` or `commit`.

## Run in CI without a screen

With Playwright, set `headless: true`. With Selenium in Docker, the browser runs inside the container, so the CI machine needs no display. To run Chrome headless on a Grid, pass Chrome's own arguments in `goog:chromeOptions`. Optics adds them to its own. In a Linux container or in CI, add `--no-sandbox` and `--disable-dev-shm-usage`:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - selenium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://localhost:4444/wd/hub"
      capabilities:
        browserName: chrome
        goog:chromeOptions:
          args: ["--headless=new", "--no-sandbox", "--disable-dev-shm-usage"]
```

[Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci) covers the rest of the CI setup.

## If it isn't working

- **The Playwright browser isn't installed.** Run `optics setup --install playwright` again. `optics doctor` shows a ✅ for `playwright browser` once Chromium is downloaded.
- **"Selenium capabilities not found in config".** Add `browserName: chrome` or `browserName: firefox` under `capabilities`.
- **"Cannot start" with "No Selenium/WebDriver server reachable".** Start the server, and check that `url` points to it.
- **Swipe fails on Selenium.** Selenium has no Swipe. Use Scroll, which moves one screen in any direction.
- **A step acts before the page loads.** Selenium actions do not wait. Put `Assert Presence` on something from the new page before you act on it.
- **"Unknown device".** The `device` name is not a Playwright device. Copy the name exactly, with its capitals and spaces.
- **A connect timeout with a remote browser.** The `protocol` does not match the provider. Try the other value.

## See also

- [Test mobile websites](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/mobile-web)
- [Write your first test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/first-test)
- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define)
- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci)
- [Actions reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions)
- [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config)
