Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/mobile-web

# Test mobile websites and WebViews

> Test web pages in Chrome, Safari and in-app WebViews on a real phone, in the same session as the native app.

Optics tests web pages on Android and iOS phones through the same Appium session that tests native apps. One test can open an app, follow a link into Chrome or Safari, fill a web form, and go back to the app. Your steps never switch contexts.

To test a website in a desktop browser, or in a browser that only emulates a phone, use [Playwright](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web#emulate-a-phone) instead. This page is for real mobile browsers and WebViews.

## How it works

The session stays in the native context. Visible text, resource ids, native XPath and OCR work on web pages too. Chrome and Safari put the text, links and fields of the page into the native UI tree.

Web locators, `css=…` and DOM XPath such as `//button[@type='submit']`, go to the `appium_web` element source. It finds the element in the page in front, scrolls it into view, and gives its position on the screen. The tap or text entry that follows is a native action at that position.

## Before you begin

- An [Android](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android) or [iOS](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios) setup that works: Appium, its driver, and a device or emulator.
- On Android, Chrome on the device.

## Set up

### Start Appium so that it can get chromedriver

Android web lookups need the chromedriver that matches the device's Chrome. Let Appium download it:

```shell
$ appium server --allow-insecure uiautomator2:chromedriver_autodownload
```

Or set `appium:chromedriverExecutableDir` to a folder of chromedriver binaries. iOS needs no extra driver.

### Write config.yaml

Enable `appium_web` next to the other Appium sources. `optics quickstart` and `optics configure` do this for Android and iOS projects.

**Android**

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - appium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://localhost:4723"
      capabilities:
        platformName: Android
        automationName: UiAutomator2
        deviceName: emulator-5554
        browserName: Chrome        # start in Chrome; remove it to start in your app
elements_sources:
  - appium_find_element: {enabled: true}
  - appium_page_source:  {enabled: true}
  - appium_web:          {enabled: true}
  - appium_screenshot:   {enabled: true}
```

With `browserName: Chrome`, the session starts in Chrome and web addresses open in Chrome, whatever the default browser is. To test an app that opens web pages, set `appPackage` and `appActivity` instead.

**iOS**

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - appium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://localhost:4723"
      capabilities:
        platformName: iOS
        automationName: XCUITest
        deviceName: "iPhone 17"
        bundleId: com.apple.mobilesafari   # or your app's bundle id
elements_sources:
  - appium_find_element: {enabled: true}
  - appium_page_source:  {enabled: true}
  - appium_web:          {enabled: true}
  - appium_screenshot:   {enabled: true}
```

Do not set `browserName: Safari`. It turns off the web lookups that `appium_web` uses.

### Let Optics read the page

**Android**

Chrome needs no setup. An app's WebView is readable only when the app calls `WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true)`. Debug builds usually do.

**iOS**

Simulators need no setup. On a real device, turn on **Web Inspector** and **Remote Automation** in **Settings > Apps > Safari > Advanced**.

Safari and in-app Safari sheets are always readable. An app's `WKWebView` is readable when the app sets `isInspectable = true`.

### Run the sample

The `mobile_web` sample searches Wikipedia in Chrome on Android:

```shell
$ optics init --name wiki --template mobile_web
$ optics execute wiki
```

## Open web pages

Launch App and Launch Other App open a URL in the app that handles it. For a web address, that is a browser.

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1
Open shop,Launch App,https://shop.example.com/
Back to the app,Launch App,com.example.shop
```

On iOS, Launch App opens the URL in Safari. To go back to your app, use Launch App with its bundle id.

## Locators for web pages

| Locator | Example | Found by |
|---|---|---|
| Visible text | `Sign in` | The native UI tree, then OCR |
| HTML id | `searchInput` | The native UI tree. Chrome gives HTML ids as resource ids. |
| CSS | `css=input[name='q']`, `#searchInput` | `appium_web` |
| DOM XPath | `//button[@type='submit']` | The native sources first, then `appium_web` |

An XPath that names a native class or attribute, such as `android.widget.Button` or `@resource-id`, goes only to the native sources. Web locators search the top page, not the inside of an `iframe`.

Assert Presence with a web locator checks the page, so an element that is off screen passes. Assert Visibility passes only when the element is in the visible part of the page.

Assert Text reads the text of a web element. Is Element checks the `enabled`, `disabled`, `checked` and `unchecked` states of a web control, and `aria-disabled` and `aria-checked` count too.

## Move between apps and the browser

Every lookup reads the screen as it is now, so a test follows the user from one app to the next:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Read the policy,Press Element,Refund policy
Read the policy,Assert Presence,css=h1,30
Read the policy,Get Text,css=h1,store_as=policy_title
Read the policy,Go Back
Read the policy,Assert Presence,Refund policy,20
```

- **App to browser.** A link in an app opens Chrome or a Chrome Custom Tab. Web locators then find elements in that page. Go Back closes the tab.
- **Browser to app.** A link that an app handles, such as a Play Store link, opens that app. Its native elements are available immediately.
- **Two apps can open the link.** Android asks which app to use. Answer with Detect And Press on the app's name, then on `Just once`.

## Covered elements

When a banner, a dialog or a panel covers the element, Optics does not tap it, because the tap will hit the cover. The step fails with "is covered by another element on the page". Close the cover first. Get Text still reads a covered element.

## Chrome's first-run pop-ups

A new Chrome shows pop-ups over the page, such as a notification prompt or a sign-in offer. You cannot tap the page while one is open. Give Chrome the notification permission before you open a page:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Prepare Chrome,Launch App
Prepare Chrome,Execute Script,"{""script"": ""mobile: changePermissions"", ""args"": {""permissions"": ""android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS"", ""appPackage"": ""com.android.chrome"", ""action"": ""grant""}}"
Prepare Chrome,Launch App,https://www.wikipedia.org/
Prepare Chrome,Detect And Press,negative_button,5
```

Detect And Press closes a pop-up only if it shows, and does not fail if it does not. Other buttons to close: `No thanks`, `Stay signed out` or `signin_fre_dismiss_button`.

## Screen elements

With `appium_web` on, Get Interactive Elements, the MCP `elements` resource and `optics live` list the web page next to the native elements. Each web control has a `loc`: a `css=` or `xpath=` locator that matches only that element and stays the same between runs. Copy it into your elements file.

## Limits

- A web lookup takes one to two seconds on a remote device. Use native locators where they work.
- iOS sign-in sheets (`ASWebAuthenticationSession`) cannot be read. Use text locators or OCR.
- Optics adds capabilities that keep web lookups fast. Values in your `capabilities` replace them. The [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#appium-capabilities) lists them.

## If it isn't working

- **"No web content found in the foreground app".** The app's WebView is not debuggable. Turn on WebView debugging, or use text locators and OCR.
- **"Cannot read the web page shown by …".** The link opened in a browser that Optics cannot read, such as Samsung Internet. Make Chrome the default browser.
- **"Cannot tell which browser tab is on screen".** Several Chrome tabs show the same address. Close the extra tabs.
- **"is in the page but not displayed".** The locator matches a hidden element. Use a locator for the visible one.
- **A Custom Tab ignores the first tap.** Chrome ignores the first tap on a Custom Tab that opens immediately after another one closes. Press the field once before you type.

## See also

- [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android)
- [Test iOS apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios)
- [Test websites](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web)
- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv

# Test TV apps

> Drive Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS apps with remote-control keys and focus.

Optics tests TV apps through **Appium**, the same server it uses for phones. Each TV platform has its own Appium driver, and you pick it with `platformName` in `config.yaml`. On a TV you move around with remote-control keys and check what is on screen with assertions. On Tizen and webOS, the element keywords also work. They move the remote focus for you.

| TV platform | `platformName` | Appium driver | How you move around |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android TV | `Android` | UiAutomator2 | Android key numbers, plus taps and typing |
| Samsung Tizen | `TizenTV` | [appium-tizen-tv-driver](https://github.com/headspinio/appium-tizen-tv-driver) | Remote key names, and element keywords that move focus |
| LG webOS | `LGTV` | [appium-lg-webos-driver](https://github.com/headspinio/appium-lg-webos-driver) | Remote key names, and element keywords that move focus |

The examples use a TV app for Birch, a sample shoe store, with rows of shoes such as "Trail Runner 2" and "Pace Knit".

## Before you begin

You need Optics with the Appium engine and the Appium server:

```shell
$ optics setup --install appium
$ npm install -g appium
```

Each TV also needs its own setup: developer mode on the TV, the vendor's tools, and the TV on the same network as your machine. Those steps belong to each Appium driver, and its project page covers them.

## Android TV

Android TV uses the same setup as an Android phone. Follow [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android), with `platformName: Android` and the TV's serial from `adb devices` as `udid`. Connect to the TV with `adb connect <tv-ip>` when it is not on a cable.

Touch and typing keywords work on Android TV, but most TV apps expect the D-pad. Send it with Press Keycode and Android key numbers:

| Remote button | Number |
|---|---|
| Up / Down / Left / Right | `19` / `20` / `21` / `22` |
| Select (center) | `23` |
| Back | `4` |
| Home | `3` |
| Play/pause | `85` |

Remote key names such as `UP` do not work on Android TV. They only apply to Tizen and webOS.

## Samsung Tizen

Install the Tizen driver into Appium:

```shell
$ appium driver install --source=npm appium-tizen-tv-driver
```

Then configure Optics:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - appium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://localhost:4723"
      capabilities:
        platformName: TizenTV
        appium:automationName: TizenTV
        appium:deviceAddress: 192.168.1.50
        appium:rcToken: "14184553"
        appium:appPackage: com.birch.tv
        appium:app: /path/to/birch.wgt
        appium:chromedriverExecutableDir: /path/to/chromedrivers
elements_sources:
  - appium_find_element: {enabled: true}
```

Optics reads `platformName` and the app id (`appPackage`, with or without the `appium:` prefix). It passes every other capability to the Tizen driver unchanged. The [driver's README](https://github.com/headspinio/appium-tizen-tv-driver) explains each one, including how to get the `rcToken`.

A native screenshot makes a Tizen TV stop answering, so `appium_screenshot` refuses to take one there. To capture the screen, add the `camera_screenshot` element source. See [BLE and camera](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#ble-and-camera) for its settings.

## LG webOS

Install the webOS driver into Appium:

```shell
$ appium driver install --source=npm appium-lg-webos-driver
```

Then configure Optics:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - appium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://localhost:4723"
      capabilities:
        platformName: LGTV
        appium:automationName: webOS
        appium:deviceHost: 192.168.1.50
        appium:appId: com.birch.tv
        appium:rcMode: rc
        appium:useSecureWebsocket: true
        appium:newCommandTimeout: 600
elements_sources:
  - appium_find_element: {enabled: true}
  - appium_screenshot: {enabled: true}
```

`appium_find_element` finds text in the app's DOM. Add an OCR engine (`optics setup --install easyocr`) to read text that the app draws as an image, or [image matching](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) for icons. The [driver's README](https://github.com/headspinio/appium-lg-webos-driver) explains the capabilities.

## Check the setup

Start `appium` in another terminal, then run the doctor:

```shell
$ optics doctor birch-tv
```

The doctor's checks are written for phones. On Tizen and webOS it warns that `deviceName`, `appPackage` or `appActivity` is missing. You can ignore those warnings, and the `adb` rows, as long as `config: driver` and `config: appium element source` show ✅.

Before each run, `optics execute` checks that the Appium server answers at `url`. It does not check the TV itself.

## Move around with remote keys

On Tizen and webOS, Press Keycode takes the name of a remote button:

| Key name | Button |
|---|---|
| `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT` | Arrow keys |
| `ENTER`, `OK`, `SELECT` | OK, the center button |
| `BACK` | Back |
| `HOME` | Home |
| `PLAY`, `PAUSE`, `STOP` | Playback |
| `REWIND`, `FF` | Rewind and fast-forward. `FAST_FORWARD` also works. |

On webOS, these names also work:

| Key name | Button |
|---|---|
| `VOL_UP` or `VOLUME_UP` | Volume up |
| `VOL_DOWN` or `VOLUME_DOWN` | Volume down |
| `MUTE`, `UNMUTE` | Mute and unmute |
| `CHAN_UP`, `CHAN_DOWN` | Channel up and down |

Names are not case-sensitive. On Tizen and webOS, a name that starts with `KEY_`, such as `KEY_MENU`, is sent as is. Any other name fails with **E0104**. The message lists the names that Optics knows.

## Find elements and move focus

A Tizen or webOS app is a web page, so `appium_find_element` finds elements in its DOM. Use these locators:

| Locator | What it matches |
|---|---|
| `Featured` or `text=Featured` | An element whose visible text, `aria-label`, `title` or `alt` is exactly this text |
| `css=.tile.active` | An element that a CSS selector matches |

A TV has no touch screen, so the element keywords press remote keys instead of taps:

| Keyword | What it does on a TV |
|---|---|
| Press Element | Presses the arrow keys until the element has focus, then presses `ENTER`. |
| Enter Text | Types into the element. See [Type on a TV](#type-on-a-tv). |
| Clear Element Text | Presses the backspace key of the on-screen keyboard until the field stops changing. |
| Get Text | Reads the text of the element, or the value of a field. |
| Assert Presence | Waits for the element to appear. Use it in place of Sleep. |

Optics reads the focus from the page after each key press, so you do not count presses. Each focus move costs one key press, and a key press takes 1 to 2 seconds on a TV. When 60 key presses do not bring the focus to the element, the step fails with `E0201`. The same error shows when the element is not on the screen.

## Type on a TV

Enter Text works on a TV in two ways. Optics picks the way from the element:

- **A real `<input>` or `<textarea>`.** Optics types the text into the field directly.
- **A field that the app draws itself.** Optics moves the focus over the on-screen keyboard and presses each key. When the keyboard does not show a character, Optics switches the layer (`123`, `abc`) and looks again.

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Search,Enter Text,Search box,trail runner
Search,Enter Text,Search box,<enter>
```

After the last key, Optics reads the field. If the field does not show the text, the step fails with **E0405**. No fallback value types the text a second time. A different letter case gives only a warning. Some apps choose the case themselves, for example a capital first letter.

Enter Text also takes special keys in angle brackets:

| Text | What it presses |
|---|---|
| `<space>`, `<backspace>`, `<enter>` | The key with that name on the on-screen keyboard |
| `<escape>`, `<up>`, `<down>`, `<left>`, `<right>` | The `BACK` or arrow key of the remote |

Other special keys, such as `<tab>`, fail with E0105 on an app keyboard.

**Tip:**
When the screen has more than one field, press the field first with Press Element. Then Optics types into the field that has focus.

## Keywords that fail on Tizen and webOS

Some keywords do not apply to a TV. They fail with **E0105** ("not supported"):

- Press By Coordinates, Press By Percentage
- Swipe, Swipe By Percentage, Swipe From Element, Swipe Until Element Appears
- Scroll, Scroll From Element, Scroll Until Element Appears
- Select Dropdown Option
- Is Element with the `checked` or `unchecked` state
- Enter Text Direct, Enter Text Using Keyboard and any keyword that enters text without an element
- Go Back. Use `Press Keycode,BACK` instead.

Move the focus with an arrow key, or with Press Element on the element that you need.

These keywords work:

- Launch App, Press Keycode, Close And Terminate App, Sleep, Execute Script and the flow keywords
- Press Element, Detect And Press, Enter Text, Enter Number, Clear Element Text and Get Text
- Assert Presence, Assert Visibility, Validate Element, Validate Screen and Is Element

## Know the limits of screenshots and video

A native screenshot makes a Tizen TV stop answering. For this reason `appium_screenshot` refuses it there with **E0303**. Use `camera_screenshot` to capture the screen, and see [BLE and camera](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#ble-and-camera) for its settings.

DRM-protected video appears black in a screenshot. To check playback, check elements in the app, such as a pause button or a progress bar.

## Example: open a title from a grid

A TV app usually shows rows of tiles. This module moves down one row, right one tile, opens it and starts playback. It checks the screen after each move that changes the page:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Birch TV,Launch App
Open Birch TV,Assert Presence,Featured,30
Open the second shoe in Running,Press Keycode,DOWN
Open the second shoe in Running,Press Keycode,RIGHT
Open the second shoe in Running,Press Keycode,ENTER
Open the second shoe in Running,Assert Presence,Trail Runner 2,10
Watch the video,Press Keycode,ENTER
Watch the video,Sleep,5
Watch the video,Press Keycode,PAUSE
Watch the video,Validate Screen,Paused,5
Go home,Press Keycode,BACK
Go home,Press Keycode,BACK
Go home,Assert Presence,Featured,10
```

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
Watch a shoe video,Open Birch TV
Watch a shoe video,Open the second shoe in Running
Watch a shoe video,Watch the video
Watch a shoe video,Go home
```

A few habits make TV tests reliable:

- **Assert after each page change.** Keys do not wait for the app. Assert Presence waits for the next page, so the following key lands in the right place.
- **Start from a known place.** Begin each test with Launch App and an assertion on the first screen. Do not rely on where an earlier test left the focus.
- **Remember that Validate Screen never fails a step.** Use it for optional checks. Use Assert Presence for checks that must pass.
- **Use the text that the page holds.** A text locator must match the element text, `aria-label`, `title` or `alt` exactly.
- **Let Optics move the focus.** Press Element moves the focus for you. It still works when the layout changes.

## See also

- [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android)
- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images)
- [Press Keycode](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#press-keycode)
- [Verification keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/verification)
- [Error codes](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/errors)

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production

# Test production devices

> Test locked devices and live apps through a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard and a camera.

Optics can test a device with no automation software on it at all. A **BLE dongle** (a small USB Bluetooth adapter) pairs with the device as an ordinary Bluetooth mouse and keyboard. A **camera** pointed at the screen shows Optics what's there. Optics finds things in the camera picture with OCR and image matching, then moves the pointer and taps.

## When to use it

Use this setup when the usual drivers can't reach the device:

- **USB debugging or developer mode isn't allowed**, for example on locked company phones or retail devices.
- **The app blocks screenshots**, as banking and streaming apps often do. The camera sees the screen anyway.
- **You monitor the live app.** Synthetic monitoring runs the same journey on a real, unmodified device and app, the way a customer would.

If you can use Appium or a browser driver, do. They're faster, read the UI tree directly, and support every keyword.

## What you need

- **A USB serial BLE HID dongle.** It plugs into your machine as a serial port, and pairs with the device as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard.
- **A way to see the screen.** Use one of these: a camera or capture card that your machine sees as a webcam, an HTTP(S) URL that returns a picture, or a TCP frame server.
- **An OCR engine**, such as EasyOCR, to read text in the camera picture.
- **Image templates** (optional), cropped pictures of icons that have no text. See [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images).
- **A stand** that holds the camera square over the screen, so the picture doesn't shift between runs.

## Set up

### Install the engines

```shell
$ optics setup --install ble easyocr
```

The `ble` engine adds serial-port support. The camera source and image matching need no extra install.

### Pair the dongle with the device

Plug the dongle into your machine. On the device, open Bluetooth settings and pair with the dongle like any keyboard. A pointer appears on screen once it's connected.

### Find the dongle's serial port

| System | Command | Looks like |
|---|---|---|
| macOS | `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*` | `/dev/cu.usbmodem1101` |
| Linux | `ls /dev/ttyACM*` | `/dev/ttyACM0` |
| Windows | Device Manager, under **Ports (COM & LPT)** | `COM3` |

Instead of a path, you can give the dongle's USB product description, such as `MZ-BLE-VMK-001-v1.2.1`. Optics finds the matching port for you, which helps when the port number changes between reboots.

### Point the camera at the screen

Mount the camera straight on, with the screen upright and filling the picture edge to edge. Optics turns positions in the camera picture straight into pointer moves, so anything around the screen throws the taps off.

If the camera sees the screen at an angle, or sees more than the screen, set `deskew_corners`. Optics then cuts each frame to the screen and makes it straight. See [`camera_screenshot` source](#camera-screenshot-source).

### Write config.yaml

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - ble:
      enabled: true
      capabilities:
        device_id: "Birch test phone"        # a label for the device
        port: /dev/ttyACM0                   # or the dongle's USB product description
        pixel_width: 1080                    # size of the screen in the camera picture
        pixel_height: 2336
        mickeys_width: 1080                  # pointer units to cross the screen
        mickeys_height: 2336
        x_invert: 1                          # -1 if the pointer moves the wrong way
        y_invert: 1
elements_sources:
  - camera_screenshot:
      enabled: true
      capabilities:
        camera_index: 0                      # or url: a screenshot URL, or "192.168.1.20:9000" for a frame server
text_detection:
  - easyocr: {enabled: true}
image_detection:
  - templatematch: {enabled: true}
```

### Calibrate, then run

Follow [Calibrate the pointer](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#calibrate-the-pointer) below, then start the app on the device by hand and run:

```shell
$ optics execute birch-production
```

There's no preflight for this setup, so check the dongle and camera before you start a long run.

## Settings

### `ble` driver

| Name | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `device_id` | Required | A name for the device. |
| `port` | Required | The dongle's serial port (`/dev/ttyACM0`, `/dev/cu.usbmodem1101`, `COM3`), or its USB product description. |
| `pixel_width`, `pixel_height` | `0` | The size of the device screen in camera-picture pixels. Set both. Optics fails to start when they're `0`. |
| `mickeys_width`, `mickeys_height` | `0` | How many pointer units it takes to cross the screen. Set both. Optics fails to start when they're `0`. |
| `x_invert`, `y_invert` | `1` | Set to `-1` to flip the direction the pointer moves on that axis. |

### `camera_screenshot` source

| Name | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `camera_index` | None | The webcam or capture card to use. `0` is the first one your system finds. |
| `url` | None | An `http://` or `https://` URL, or a TCP frame server as `ip:port`. Use instead of `camera_index`. |
| `token` | None | HTTP only. Optics sends it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Optics masks it in logs. |
| `header_size` | `8` | Frame server only. The length of the size header in bytes, `4` or `8`. |
| `byte_order` | `little` | Frame server only. The byte order of the size header, `little` or `big`. |
| `deskew_corners` | None | The four corners of the screen in the camera picture, as `"x,y"`: top left, top right, bottom right, bottom left. Optics cuts each frame to the screen and makes it straight. |
| `out_width`, `out_height` | `1080`, `1920` | The size of the frame after `deskew_corners`. Set the screenshot size of the device. |
| `rotation` | None | `clockwise` or `counterclockwise`. Optics turns the frame a quarter turn after `deskew_corners`. |

Set either `camera_index` or `url`. With neither, Optics reads the environment variables below. If these are not set, Optics stops with "No camera_index or valid URL provided".

For an HTTP URL, Optics sends a `GET` request and decodes the reply as an image. A status other than 200 fails, and the log shows the status with the `code` and `message` of the JSON reply. Optics does not follow redirects, because a redirect will send the token again.

| Variable | Used for |
|---|---|
| `WEBCAM_SCREENSHOT_URL` | The screenshot URL. |
| `WEBCAM_SCREENSHOT_TOKEN` | The bearer token for `WEBCAM_SCREENSHOT_URL`. Optics sends it to no other URL. |
| `WEBCAM_SCREENSHOT_TCP_PORT` | A TCP frame server at `127.0.0.1` on this port. Optics uses it when `WEBCAM_SCREENSHOT_URL` is not set. |

A value in config.yaml wins over a variable. For a `url` in config.yaml, set `token` too. Write `token: ${WEBCAM_SCREENSHOT_TOKEN}` to keep the token out of the file.

Optics checks `deskew_corners` and `rotation` when the session starts. Four points that are not the corners of a convex screen, in order, stop the run. A `rotation` value other than `clockwise` or `counterclockwise` also stops the run.

A frame server receives the line `screenshot`, then replies with the picture's size in a `header_size`-byte unsigned number, followed by the picture as JPEG or PNG.

## Calibrate the pointer

Optics resets the pointer to a corner before each tap, then moves it by the distance it calculated from the camera picture. Calibration makes that distance land in the right place.

1. **Set the pixel size.** Set `pixel_width` and `pixel_height` to the size of the camera picture. Take one with `Capture Screenshot` and check its size.
2. **Start with equal units.** Set `mickeys_width` and `mickeys_height` to the same numbers as the pixels.
3. **Tap a far corner.** Run a one-step module, `Press By Percentage,90,90`, and watch where the pointer lands.
4. **Adjust.** If the pointer stops short of the spot, raise the mickeys for that axis. If it overshoots, lower them. Repeat until the tap lands.
5. **Fix the direction.** If the pointer moves left when it should move right, set `x_invert: -1`. Do the same with `y_invert` for up and down.

Calibrate again whenever you move the camera, change the device, or change its display size or orientation.

## What works and what doesn't

| Works | How |
|---|---|
| Press Element, Detect And Press | With text values (found by OCR) or image values. Optics moves the pointer there and taps. |
| Press By Coordinates, Press By Percentage | Taps a spot in the camera picture. |
| Enter Text | Finds the field by OCR or image, taps it, then types through the Bluetooth keyboard. |
| Enter Text Direct | Types into the field that has focus. |
| Assert Presence, Validate Screen | Read the camera picture with OCR or image matching. |
| Swipe, Swipe By Percentage, Swipe From Element | Press, drag and release with the pointer. |
| Scroll | Up and down only. |

| Doesn't work | Instead |
|---|---|
| Launch App, Launch Other App | Start the app by hand, or tap its icon on the home screen with Press Element. |
| XPath and UI-tree text | There's no UI tree. Use visible text, which OCR reads, or images. |
| Get Text, Get App Version, Execute Script | Not available over Bluetooth. |
| Go Back, and Back, Volume, Power and other phone-only keys | A Bluetooth keyboard has no such keys. Go Back fails with E0105. Tap the app's own back button. |
| Named keys such as `Enter` | `Press Keycode,Enter` and `<enter>` type the letters of the key's name. Tap the on-screen key instead. |
| [Error detection](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection) at the end of a run | It needs the page source, which a camera can't provide. Add Assert Presence checks for error messages you care about. |

`optics live`, `optics serve` and `optics mcp` run Launch App when they start, so that first step fails with this setup. Start the app by hand before you begin.

Here is a sign-in journey written for a production phone. Every value is text that OCR can read on screen:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Birch,Press Element,Birch
Open Birch,Assert Presence,Sign in,20
Sign in,Enter Text,Email,ava@birch.shop
Sign in,Enter Text,Password,@:trailrunner
Sign in,Press Element,Sign in
Sign in,Assert Presence,Trail Runner 2,20
```

The first step taps the Birch icon on the home screen, so the run starts from there.

## Add a camera to an Appium run

Some apps block screenshots only on some screens, such as a payment screen. If Appium can reach the device, keep Appium and add a camera for those screens. On a protected screen, the Appium screenshot is black, and Optics uses the camera frame.

List `camera_screenshot` after `appium_screenshot`:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
elements_sources:
  - appium_find_element: {enabled: true}
  - appium_screenshot: {enabled: true}
  - camera_screenshot:
      enabled: true
      capabilities:
        url: http://127.0.0.1:8080/screenshot
        deskew_corners: ["212,88", "868,95", "861,1262", "205,1255"]
        out_width: 1080
        out_height: 2400
```

Optics maps OCR and image matches on the camera frame into the Appium window, the same as for an Appium screenshot. Appium then taps the correct point on the device.

**Tip:**
Set `deskew_corners` so that the frame shows only the screen. Set `out_width` and `out_height` to the screenshot size of the device, so that the frame has the same shape as the screen. With other drivers, Optics uses the pixels of the frame as they are.

## Known gaps

- **The doctor reports a failure.** `optics doctor` expects an element source whose name starts with `ble_`, and none exists. It shows ❌ for `config: ble element source`. Ignore that row, and don't use `optics doctor --check` on this project in CI.

## If it isn't working

- **"Could not resolve serial port for product description".** No connected port has that description. Check the dongle is plugged in, or use the port path instead.
- **Optics stops at start with a division error.** `pixel_width`, `pixel_height`, `mickeys_width` or `mickeys_height` is `0` or missing. Set all four.
- **"No camera_index or valid URL provided".** Add `camera_index` or `url` under the `camera_screenshot` capabilities.
- **Taps land in the wrong place.** Recalibrate. Check that the screen fills the camera picture and that nothing moved.
- **Text isn't found.** Improve the picture: even light, no glare, the camera in focus. Use an [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest) to search a smaller part of the screen.
- **The pointer doesn't move.** Check the device is still paired with the dongle and that its pointer shows on screen.

## See also

- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images)
- [Search part of the screen](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest)
- [Engines reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines)
- [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config)

# Advanced

> Add data, logic and integrations to your suites once the basics are in place.

Most suites never need the features in this section. A list of modules with good elements and a few checks covers most user flows. Reach for these when a flow depends on data, needs to branch, or when another system needs to drive Optics.

## Logic and data

- [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables): Store values, compute new ones, and use them in later steps.
- [Data-driven tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven): Run one flow once per row of a data file.
- [Conditions and loops](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions): Branch on what's on screen, and repeat modules.
- [Call APIs in a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/api-calls): Fetch or create data over HTTP mid-test, and use the response in later steps.

## Integrate

- [Run keywords over HTTP](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/http-api): Drive a device from your own service with `optics serve`.
- [Generate pytest or Robot code](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/generate): Turn a suite into code you can extend.
- [Let your AI agent build tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent): Connect `optics mcp` to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client.
- [Use Optics from Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python): Call keywords from your own scripts.

**How logic runs in a suite:**
Flow-control keywords run other modules. Steps inside those modules work slightly differently from top-level steps: they use only the first value of each element, and they don't accept `name=value` parameters. Keep modules that run inside loops and conditions simple, and give their elements a reliable first value.

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables

# Variables

> Store values, compute new ones during a run, and use them in later steps.

In Optics, a variable is an element that holds a value instead of a locator. You define some in your elements file, and some keywords create or change them while the test runs. Any step can then use the value with `${name}`.

## Define a variable

Add a row to an elements file, like any element:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
email,ava@birch.shop
search_term,trail runner
discount_code,WELCOME10
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Search,Enter Text,${search_bar},${search_term}
```

## Where ${name} works

| You write | Optics uses |
|---|---|
| `${search_term}` as the whole cell | Each value in turn, the same as [element fallbacks](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define) |
| `Hi ${first}!` or `${first} ${last}` | The first value of each name. An unknown name fails the step. |
| `$${first}` | The text `${first}`, not the value |
| `@:${password}` | The value, typed without `@:` and hidden in logs |

`Evaluate`, `Condition`, the query of `Read Data` and the URL, headers and body of `Invoke API` put in the first value themselves. [Values are text](#values-are-text) shows how they quote it.

`optics live` follows the same rules, so a name inside a longer value works in a recorded step too.

## Keep a value for later

Add `store_as=<name>` to a step to keep the value that its keyword returns. Later steps use the value as `${name}`:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
price_label,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/price']
cart_total,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/total']
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Check Price,Get Text,${price_label},store_as=price
Check Price,Press Element,Add to cart
Check Price,Assert Text,${cart_total},${price}
```

Get Text reads the price and keeps it as `price`. Assert Text fails the step if the cart total shows different text.

- **Any parameter column** can hold the `store_as=` cell, but the column must have a `param_N` header.
- **The keyword must return a value**, as Get Text, Execute Script, Get App Version and Invoke API do. A keyword that returns nothing, such as Press Element, fails the step.
- **Get Text returns no value** when only OCR or an image found the element.
- **A list or a dictionary** is kept as JSON text.
- **Only CSV and YAML suites** read `store_as`. In [Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python) and [Robot Framework](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot), use the return value.

## Create variables during a run

These keywords write a variable. Write its name as `${name}`:

| Keyword | Writes | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `Evaluate` | The result of an expression | `Evaluate,${total},${price} + 5` |
| `Date Evaluate` | A date some days away | `Date Evaluate,${delivery_date},${order_date},+5 days` |
| `Read Data` | A value from a CSV or JSON file, or an environment variable | `Read Data,${admin_email},test_data/users.csv,role == 'admin';select=email` |
| `Invoke API` | Values from an API response | See [Call APIs in a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/api-calls) |
| `Run Loop` | The current item, once per pass | See [Data-driven tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven) |

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3
Check Total,Evaluate,${expected_total},${price} * 2
Check Total,Assert Presence,${expected_total}
```

`Run Loop` takes its count from a variable too: `Run Loop,Add One Item,${n}`.

## How long a value lasts

A value lasts for the whole run. A value set in one test case is available in later test cases and in Suite Teardown. A new value with the same name replaces the old one. Nothing carries over to the next run.

## Dry runs

`optics dry_run` defines each name that `store_as`, `Evaluate`, `Read Data` and `Date Evaluate` write. You do not need placeholder rows for them. Add a placeholder row only for these names:

- An `extract` name from `Invoke API`.
- A `Run Loop` variable that a top-level step uses. The dry run does not check the steps of the looped module.

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
access_token,placeholder
```

## Values are text

Every value is text, even when it looks like a number. That matters in expressions:

- **Evaluate** puts the value into the expression as you wrote it. `${price} + 5` with `price` set to `64` becomes `64 + 5`, which is `69`. To join text, quote it: `'${first_name}' + ' ' + '${last_name}'`.
- **Read Data** puts quotes around a value in its query, unless the value is already between quotes. `name == ${user}` works.
- **Condition** puts each value in quotes as text. `${count} == '3'` works. `${count} > 2` fails, because it compares text with a number. Compare against quoted text, or compute the comparison with Evaluate first. See [Conditions and loops](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions).

Evaluate allows arithmetic (`+ - * / % **`), comparisons, `in`, `and`, `or`, `not` and `x if condition else y`. It does not allow function calls such as `int()`. An expression with other parts, or one that is too large to compute, fails with E0406.

## Hide sensitive values

Optics writes `****` in place of a secret in the console, the log files, `logs.json`, `junit_output.xml`, `failed_steps_elements.json`, the run tree and error output. Optics masks these items:

- A value that `store_as` or `Read Data` sets under a secret name.
- A value in the elements file or a step that starts with `@:`. When the step runs, Optics also masks the value without the prefix in all later output of the run.
- A text value in `config.yaml` under a secret name, such as `api_key`. This includes a value that the config reads from an environment variable with a secret name.
- A password in a URL: `https://user:****@host`.
- A query parameter with a secret name: `?token=****`.

A name is secret when it contains one of these words: `pass`, `password`, `passwd`, `passcode`, `pwd`, `pin`, `otp`, `secret`, `token`, `key`, `apikey`, `auth`, `authorization`, `bearer` or `credential`. `user_password`, `loginOTP` and `myApiToken` match. `passkey` and `pincode` do not.

A value must have 4 or more characters to be masked. This also applies to a value with `@:`.

Optics does not hide a value from the elements file, `Evaluate`, `Run Loop` or an `Invoke API` `extract` by its name. To hide an elements-file value, start it with `@:`: `password,@:correct-horse`. Optics logs `****` and types the value without the prefix.

For real secrets, do not commit them. Read them from the environment at run time:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Sign In,Read Data,${password},ENV:BIRCH_PASSWORD
Sign In,Enter Text,${password_field},${password}
```

Set `BIRCH_PASSWORD` in your shell or CI secrets. `api_details.log` and `api_details.har` are not masked, so a secret in an API call shows there in clear text.

## See also

- [Data-driven tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven)
- [Conditions and loops](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions)
- [Flow control keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven

# Run a flow with different data

> Repeat one module for every value in a list, such as each user, search term or product.

A data-driven test runs the same flow several times with different inputs. In Optics, you write the flow once as a module, keep the inputs in a list, and use `Run Loop` to run the module once per item.

## Loop over a list of values

This example signs in to the Sauce Labs demo store as three different users, signing out after each one. It runs as written with the Playwright setup from [Write your first test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/first-test).

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
username_field,//input[@id='user-name']
password_field,//input[@id='password']
login_button,//input[@id='login-button']
menu_button,//button[@id='react-burger-menu-btn']
logout_link,//a[@id='logout_sidebar_link']
shoppers,standard_user|visual_user|problem_user
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3
Open the store,Launch App,https://www.saucedemo.com
Sign In Each Shopper,Run Loop,Sign In And Out,${username},${shoppers}
Sign In And Out,Enter Text,${username_field},${username}
Sign In And Out,Enter Text,${password_field},secret_sauce
Sign In And Out,Press Element,${login_button}
Sign In And Out,Assert Presence,Products
Sign In And Out,Press Element,${menu_button}
Sign In And Out,Sleep,1
Sign In And Out,Press Element,${logout_link}
Sign In And Out,Assert Presence,${login_button}
```

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
Suite Setup,Open the store
Every shopper can sign in,Sign In Each Shopper
```

`Run Loop,Sign In And Out,${username},${shoppers}` reads: *run the module **Sign In And Out** once for each value in `shoppers`, and set `username` to that value each time.* Inside the module, `${username}` is the current shopper.

A few details make this work:

- **The loop sets `${username}`.** You do not need an elements row for it. See [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables).
- **The values are separated by `|`.** You can also write them straight into the step: `Run Loop,Sign In And Out,${username},standard_user|visual_user`.
- **`Sleep,1`** waits for the menu to slide open. Prefer a check such as `Assert Presence` to wait for a new screen, but use a short sleep for an animation on an element that's already on the page.

The run shows the loop as one step. If any pass fails, the loop stops and the step fails with the reason:

```terminal
└── Every shopper can sign in                            |      7.26s |    PASS
    └── Sign In Each Shopper                             |      7.26s |    PASS
        └── Run Loop (Sign In And Out, ${username}, s... |      7.26s |    PASS
```

## Loop over several lists at once

Give more name and list pairs to set several variables per pass. The lists are read side by side, and the loop stops at the end of the shortest:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3,param_4,param_5
Every Search,Run Loop,Search And Check,${term},trail|pace|ridge,${expected},Trail Runner 2|Pace Knit|Ridge GTX
Search And Check,Press Element,${search_bar}
Search And Check,Enter Text Direct,${term}
Search And Check,Assert Presence,${expected}
```

Each pass sets `term` and `expected` from the same position in their lists: first `trail` and `Trail Runner 2`, then `pace` and `Pace Knit`, and so on.

## Repeat a module a number of times

Give a count instead of lists:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Fill Cart,Run Loop,Add One Item,3
```

Write the count as a number, or as a variable such as `${n}`. Optics reads the value of the variable when the step runs.

## Keep the data in a file

Lists can live in an elements file, as `shoppers` does above, or as a JSON list: `sizes,"[""8"",""9"",""10""]"`. For a single value from a larger data file, such as the email address of the admin user, use `Read Data`:

`test_data/users.csv`:

```csv
username,email,role
ava,ava@birch.shop,admin
ben,ben@birch.shop,shopper
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3
Sign In As Admin,Read Data,${admin_email},test_data/users.csv,role == 'admin';select=email
Sign In As Admin,Enter Text,${email_field},${admin_email}
```

The query picks rows with a filter (`role == 'admin'`) and columns with `select=`. Compare values as quoted text, because every value in the file is read as text. A variable in the query, such as `username == ${user}`, gets its quotes from Optics. `Read Data` is designed to fetch one row; with several matching rows, the variable gets a combined value that's hard to use.

## Rules inside a loop

Steps inside a looped module run a little differently from top-level steps:

- **Only the first value of each element is used.** Fallbacks don't apply, so give looped elements a reliable first value.
- **`name=value` parameters aren't available.** Pass values in order instead.
- **The module's steps don't appear separately** in the run tree or the JUnit report. A failure names the step that failed in its message.
- **After the loop, the variable keeps its last value.**

## See also

- [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables)
- [Conditions and loops](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions)
- [Flow control keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions

# Conditions and loops

> Run different modules depending on what's on screen or in a variable, and handle optional screens such as popups.

Most tests follow one path. Sometimes the app doesn't: a welcome popup appears only on first launch, a returning user skips sign-in, or a feature is behind a flag. Optics handles these with three keywords: `Detect And Press` for optional taps, `Condition` for branches, and `Execute Module` for running one module from another.

## Tap something only if it appears

For a popup that may or may not show, `Detect And Press` waits for the element and taps it if it appears. If it doesn't, the step still passes:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Launch Birch,Launch App
Launch Birch,Detect And Press,Allow notifications,5
Launch Birch,Detect And Press,Not now,5
```

The second value is how many seconds to wait (30 by default). Keep it short: the step always waits the full time when the element never appears.

## Branch with Condition

`Condition` checks one or more conditions in order and runs the module paired with the first one that's true:

```text
Condition, <condition 1>, <module 1>, <condition 2>, <module 2>, …, <otherwise module>
```

The last module, with no condition in front of it, runs when nothing matched. It's optional.

### Branch on what's on screen

A condition can be a **module name**. Optics runs that module: if it passes, the condition is true. Write a small module that checks for something, and use it as the test:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3
Is Signed In,Assert Presence,Picked for you,5
Start Shopping,Condition,Is Signed In,Go To Search,Sign In
```

If the home screen's *Picked for you* appears within 5 seconds, Optics runs `Go To Search`. Otherwise it runs `Sign In`. Put `!` in front to flip a condition: `Condition,!Is Signed In,Sign In`.

**Warning:**
The checking module really runs, so keep it to checks with short timeouts. A failed check waits its full timeout, and an action in it would change the app.

### Branch on a variable

A condition can also be an **expression** that compares variables:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3,param_4,param_5
Choose Flow,Condition,${account_type} == 'business',Business Checkout,${account_type} == 'gift',Gift Checkout,Standard Checkout
```

Optics puts each variable's value in quotes before checking, so always compare with **quoted text**: `${account_type} == 'business'`, `${count} == '3'`.

### Compare numbers

Because values are compared as text, `${count} > 5` fails. Compute the comparison with `Evaluate` first, then check its result:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3
Check Cart,Evaluate,${cart_is_big},${count} > 5
Check Cart,Condition,${cart_is_big} == 'True',Offer Free Shipping
```

`Evaluate` puts values into the expression without quotes, so `${count} > 5` works there and stores `True` or `False`.

## Run one module from another

`Execute Module` runs a module's steps as part of another module:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1
Buy Trail Runners,Execute Module,Sign In
Buy Trail Runners,Execute Module,Search For Shoes
Buy Trail Runners,Press Element,Add to cart
```

A module name written on its own as a step doesn't run that module. Use `Execute Module`.

## Rules for modules run by these keywords

Modules run by `Condition`, `Execute Module` and [`Run Loop`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven) follow simpler rules than top-level steps:

- Each element uses only its **first value**. Fallbacks don't apply.
- **`name=value` parameters aren't available.** Give values in order: `Assert Presence,Picked for you,5`, not `timeout_str=5`.
- Their steps don't appear separately in the run tree. A failure message names the step that failed.

If a branch needs fallbacks, give it its own test case instead and choose which test cases run with [`--include` and `--exclude`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/organise#run-only-some-test-cases).

## See also

- [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables)
- [Data-driven tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven)
- [Flow control keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/api-calls

# Call APIs in a test

> Call an HTTP API in the middle of a test, check the response, and use values from it in later steps.

Some steps are faster or more reliable through an API than through the screen: creating a test account, fetching today's offer code, or checking that an order reached the backend. `Invoke API` calls an endpoint you describe in a YAML file, checks the response, and saves values from it as variables for later steps.

The example on this page runs as written. It uses [DummyJSON](https://dummyjson.com), a free public API for testing.

### Describe the API

Create a YAML file anywhere in the project, with a top-level `api:` key. Group endpoints into **collections**, each with a base URL:

`test_data/api.yaml`:

```yaml
api:
  collections:
    dummyjson:
      name: "DummyJSON"
      base_url: "https://dummyjson.com"
      global_headers:
        content-type: "application/json"
      apis:
        login:
          name: "Sign in"
          endpoint: "/auth/login"
          request:
            method: POST
            body:
              username: "${api_username}"
              password: "${api_password}"
          expected_result:
            expected_status: 200
            jsonpath_assertions:
              - path: $.accessToken
                condition: "len($) > 0"
            extract:
              access_token: $.accessToken
        me:
          name: "Who am I"
          endpoint: "/auth/me"
          request:
            method: GET
            headers:
              Authorization: "Bearer ${access_token}"
          expected_result:
            extract:
              email: $.email
```

- **`request`** sets the method, headers and a JSON body. `${name}` is replaced anywhere in the endpoint, headers and body.
- **`expected_status`** is the HTTP status that the response must have. The step fails when the status is different, before Optics runs any other check or extracts any value.
- **`jsonpath_assertions`** checks the response. `path` picks a value, and `condition` is a small expression where `$` stands for that value. A false condition fails the step.
- **`extract`** saves values from the response as variables, using JSONPath: `$.accessToken`, `$.customer.id`, `$.items[0].name`.

### Add the inputs to your elements file

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
api_username,emilys
api_password,emilyspass
access_token,placeholder
email,placeholder
```

The `placeholder` rows let `optics dry_run` accept variables that only get their value during the run.

### Call the endpoints in a module

Refer to an endpoint as `collection.name`:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1
Sign In Over The API,Invoke API,dummyjson.login
Sign In Over The API,Invoke API,dummyjson.me
```

Add a test case that runs the module:

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
API sign in works,Sign In Over The API
```

The first call signs in and saves `access_token`. The second sends the token and saves the account's `email`. From here, any step can use `${email}`: type it into a field, check it on screen, or compare it in a [condition](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions).

A project with only API and other flow control steps needs no driver. Set every `driver_sources` entry in `config.yaml` to `enabled: false`. If a step uses an action, app or verification keyword, enable a driver.

### Run it

```shell
$ optics execute api-demo
```

```terminal
└── API sign in works                                       |  1.31s |    PASS
    └── Sign In Over The API                                |  1.31s |    PASS
        ├── Invoke API (dummyjson.login)                    |  0.66s |    PASS
        └── Invoke API (dummyjson.me)                       |  0.64s |    PASS
```

Every request and response is logged to `execution_output/api_details.log`, and to `api_details.har`, which you can open in a browser's developer tools.

## Combine API and UI steps

A common pattern is to set up data through the API, then check it in the app:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Order Shows In App,Invoke API,birch.create_order
Order Shows In App,Press Element,Orders
Order Shows In App,Assert Presence,${order_number}
```

Creating the order through the API takes a second. Going through the checkout screens takes a minute and tests something you probably cover elsewhere.

## Good to know

- **Responses must be JSON** when an endpoint has `expected_result`. Other responses fail the step.
- **A different status fails the step.** With `expected_status` set, the failure reads, for example, `API 'Sign in' returned status 200, expected 401.` It has no error code. `json_schema` is accepted in the file but not checked yet. Check a field in the body instead.
- **Every request times out after 30 seconds.** `request.timeout` isn't used yet.
- **Keep credentials out of the file.** Put them in variables and read them from the environment with `Read Data,${api_password},ENV:BIRCH_API_PASSWORD`. See [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables#hide-sensitive-values).
- **API logs are not masked.** `api_details.log` and `api_details.har` show requests and responses in clear text, secrets included. Values from `extract` are not hidden in other logs either.
- **The top-level key must be `api:`.** A file starting with `apis:` is recognised but loads nothing.

## See also

- [Invoke API reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow#invoke-api)
- [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables)
- [Conditions and loops](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/http-api

# Run keywords over HTTP

> Start a local Optics server and drive a device or browser from your own service, one keyword per request.

`optics serve` runs Optics as a small web server on your machine. Another program, such as an internal dashboard, a test orchestrator or a script in another language, can then open a session on a device and run keywords on it with plain HTTP requests. Each request runs one keyword and returns its result.

Use the server when something other than Optics decides what to do next. If you want to run a suite, `optics execute` is simpler. If an AI agent is the caller, use [MCP](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent) instead.

### Start the server

```shell
$ optics serve
```

It listens on `http://127.0.0.1:8000`. Check it's up:

```shell
$ curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/health
{"status":"Optics Framework API is running","version":"1.11.3"}
```

Use `--port` to change the port. Interactive API docs are at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs` while the server runs.

### Start a session

A session is one connection to a device or browser. Send the same settings you'd put in `config.yaml`:

```shell
$ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/start \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{
      "driver_sources": ["playwright"],
      "elements_sources": ["playwright_find_element", "playwright_page_source", "playwright_screenshot"]
    }'
{"session_id":"23db1bdc-07d8-4cca-bfaa-1e9deaf4b794","driver_id":"PLAYWRIGHT_SESSION","status":"created"}
```

Keep the `session_id`. Starting a session also opens the app, as `Launch App` would. For a phone, pass an Appium entry with its URL and capabilities:

```json
{
  "driver_sources": [{"appium": {"url": "http://127.0.0.1:4723", "capabilities": {
    "platformName": "Android", "automationName": "UiAutomator2",
    "deviceName": "emulator-5554", "appPackage": "com.birch.shop", "appActivity": ".MainActivity"}}}],
  "elements_sources": ["appium_find_element", "appium_page_source", "appium_screenshot"]
}
```

### Run keywords

Send one keyword per request, with its values in order:

```shell
$ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/action \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"mode": "keyword", "keyword": "Launch Other App", "params": ["https://www.saucedemo.com"]}'
{"execution_id":"ebbdc919-…","status":"SUCCESS","data":{"result":null}}

$ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/action \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"mode": "keyword", "keyword": "Assert Presence", "params": ["Accepted usernames are"]}'
{"execution_id":"71f5ee34-…","status":"SUCCESS","data":{"result":true}}
```

Keyword names work in any case: `Assert Presence` or `assert_presence`. `params` can also be an object of named values, such as `{"element": "Login", "index": "1"}`. A list inside it gives fallbacks: `{"element": ["//input[@id='login-button']", "Login"]}`.

A keyword that fails returns an error status with the Optics code, for example `404` with `E0201` for an element that is not found. See [Errors](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/http-api#errors).

### Look at the screen

```shell
$ curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/screenshot \
    | python3 -c 'import sys,json,base64; open("screen.png","wb").write(base64.b64decode(json.load(sys.stdin)["data"]["result"]))'
```

`/elements?compact=true` lists the elements on screen. Each one has `loc`, a locator that matches only that element. `/source` returns the UI tree.

### Stop the session

```shell
$ curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/stop
{"status":"terminated"}
```

This closes the app and ends the session.

## Follow a session live

Two endpoints stream updates as [server-sent events](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events):

- `/v1/sessions/{id}/events` sends a message when each keyword starts, passes or fails.
- `/v1/sessions/{id}/workspace/stream` sends a new screenshot and element list whenever the screen changes, which is handy for showing a live view of the device.

```shell
$ curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/events
```

## Keep the server safe

The server has **no authentication**. Anyone who can reach it can control the connected device.

- Keep the default `--host 127.0.0.1`, so only your machine can reach it.
- If another machine must call it, put it behind a proxy that adds authentication, on a trusted network.
- Run one worker (the default). Sessions live in the server's memory, so several workers would lose track of each other's sessions.
- Web pages cannot call the server. To let your own web app call it, list the origin of the app in `OPTICS_CORS_ORIGINS`.
- The server answers only requests whose `Host` is a loopback name, such as `localhost`. Add other names to `OPTICS_ALLOWED_HOSTS`.
- The server does not read its own environment or files for a caller. It refuses `${NAME}` in a driver URL or header, a `storage_state` file path, `user_data_dir` and a browser `profile`. It also refuses `project_path`, `credentials_path`, `file:` URLs, and `Read Data` from a file or `ENV:`. Upload template images with `POST /v1/sessions/{id}/templates`.
- Each session writes its output to its own temporary folder, and the server deletes it when the session stops.

## See also

- [HTTP API reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/http-api), with every endpoint and field
- The [OpenAPI document](https://optics-framework.org/openapi.json), for generating a client
- [Let your AI agent build tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/generate

# Generate pytest or Robot code

> Turn a CSV or YAML suite into a pytest or Robot Framework file you can extend with code.

`optics generate` reads a suite and writes the same test as code: a pytest file or a Robot Framework file. Use it when a suite needs logic the files can't express, or when you're moving a suite into a codebase that already runs everything through pytest or Robot.

The generated file is a starting point. Once you edit it, it no longer follows the suite files, so keep the suite as the source of truth for as long as you can.

## Generate a file

```shell
$ optics generate birch-tests
Generated test file: birch-tests/generated/Tests/test_generated.py
Generated requirements file: birch-tests/generated/requirements.txt
```

For Robot Framework:

```shell
$ optics generate birch-tests --framework robot --output checkout.robot
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--framework` | `pytest` | `pytest` or `robot`. |
| `--output` | `test_generated.py` or `test_generated.robot` | The file name. It's always written to `<project>/generated/Tests/`. |

The project needs a file named exactly `config.yaml`, plus test cases, modules and an elements file.

## What you get

Each module becomes a function (or Robot keyword), each test case becomes a test, and elements become a dictionary:

`generated/Tests/test_generated.py`:

```python
ELEMENTS = {
    'username_field': "//input[@id='user-name']",
    'login_button': "//input[@id='login-button']",
}

def sign_in(optics: Optics) -> None:
    optics.enter_text(ELEMENTS['username_field'], 'standard_user')
    optics.press_element(ELEMENTS['login_button'])
    optics.assert_presence('Products')

def test_shopper_can_add_a_backpack(optics):
    open_the_store(optics)
    sign_in(optics)
```

Run it with pytest from the `generated/Tests` folder:

```shell
$ pip install -r birch-tests/generated/requirements.txt
$ cd birch-tests/generated/Tests
$ pytest test_generated.py
```

## What isn't converted

- **Only the first value of each element** is used. Fallbacks are dropped. Pass a list to keep them: `optics.press_element([ELEMENTS['login_button'], 'Login'])`.
- **Flow-control keywords** (Run Loop, Condition, Read Data, Evaluate, Invoke API and others) and a few more, such as Select Dropdown Option, aren't converted. Steps that use them are left out of the generated code silently. Check the output against your modules.
- **`store_as` cells** are passed to the method as plain text, such as `get_text(..., 'store_as=price')`, which breaks the call. Use the return value instead. See [Use Optics from Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python).
- **`${name}` inside other text** is written as typed: `'Hi ${first}!'`.
- **Every `${name}` comes from the elements file.** A suite that sets values during the run, with Evaluate, Date Evaluate or `store_as`, runs as it is with `optics execute`.
- **Suite Setup and Suite Teardown** become ordinary tests.
- **Image templates** are copied only if they're in an `input_templates/` folder at the project's top level.

## See also

- [Use Optics from Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python)
- [Use Optics in Robot Framework](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot)
- [CLI reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/
