# Test Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS apps with one framework

> Test Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS apps with one tool and remote-control keys.

You can test a TV app the way a viewer uses it: press arrow keys on the remote, open a tile, start playback and check what is on screen. Optics drives Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS through **Appium**, the same server it uses for phones. Your tests are rows in CSV files, so one suite style covers your phone, web and TV apps.

This page walks you through the job and links to the pages that hold the details. [Test TV apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv) is the full reference.

## Check what each TV supports

Each TV platform has its own Appium driver. You pick it with `platformName` in `config.yaml`.

| TV platform | `platformName` | How you move around | How Optics sees the screen |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android TV | `Android` | Android key numbers, plus taps and typing | UI tree and screenshots, like an Android phone |
| Samsung Tizen | `TizenTV` | Remote key names, and element keywords that move focus | The app's DOM, and a camera for screenshots |
| LG webOS | `LGTV` | Remote key names, and element keywords that move focus | The app's DOM, and screenshots |

Tizen and webOS TVs have no touch screen. Press Element and Enter Text still work there. They press remote keys until the focus reaches the element. Touch keywords, such as Swipe and Scroll, fail with **E0105**. [Keywords that fail on Tizen and webOS](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv#keywords-that-fail-on-tizen-and-webos) lists every keyword.

## Set up

### Install Optics and Appium

[Install Optics](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/install), then add the Appium engine and the Appium server:

```shell
$ optics setup --install appium
$ npm install -g appium
```

### Prepare the TV

Turn on developer mode on the TV, install the vendor's tools, and put the TV on the same network as your machine. Each Appium driver's project page covers these steps.

### Add the driver for your TV

- **Android TV** uses the same setup as an Android phone. Follow [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android) and connect with `adb connect <tv-ip>`.
- **Samsung Tizen**: `appium driver install --source=npm appium-tizen-tv-driver`, then copy the [Tizen config](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv#samsung-tizen).
- **LG webOS**: `appium driver install --source=npm appium-lg-webos-driver`, then copy the [webOS config](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv#lg-webos).

### Check the setup

Start `appium` in another terminal, then run `optics doctor` on your project. On Tizen and webOS, the doctor warns about phone settings such as `appActivity`. You can ignore those warnings as long as `config: driver` and `config: appium element source` show ✅. See [Check the setup](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv#check-the-setup).

## Write the test with remote keys and focus

A TV test is a list of key presses with a check after each page change. This module opens the second tile in a row and checks the title:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Birch TV,Launch App
Open Birch TV,Assert Presence,Featured,30
Open the second shoe,Press Keycode,DOWN
Open the second shoe,Press Keycode,RIGHT
Open the second shoe,Press Keycode,ENTER
Open the second shoe,Assert Presence,Trail Runner 2,10
```

On Tizen and webOS, Press Keycode takes key names such as `UP`, `ENTER`, `BACK` and `PLAY`. On Android TV, it takes Android key numbers instead: `19` to `22` for the arrows and `23` for Select. [Move around with remote keys](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv#move-around-with-remote-keys) has both tables.

On Tizen and webOS, you can also name the element and let Optics move the focus. Press Element presses the arrow keys until the element has focus, then presses `ENTER`:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open the second shoe,Press Element,Trail Runner 2
Open the second shoe,Assert Presence,Add to cart,10
```

To type on a Tizen or webOS TV, use Enter Text. Optics types into a real `<input>`, or presses the keys of the on-screen keyboard one by one. If the field does not show the text, the step fails with **E0405**. See [Type on a TV](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv#type-on-a-tv).

## Keep TV tests reliable

- **Assert after each page change.** Keys do not wait for the app. Assert Presence waits for the next page, so the next key lands in the right place.
- **Start from a known place.** Begin each test with Launch App and an assertion on the first screen.
- **Expect each focus move to take time.** Each focus move is one key press, and a key press takes 1 to 2 seconds.
- **Use images for icons.** Add [image matching](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) when a tile or button has no text.

## Run it on every build

Run the suite with `optics execute`, as you would a phone suite. Before each run, Optics checks that the Appium server answers. It does not check the TV itself, so make sure that the TV is on and reachable. [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci) covers the JUnit report your CI system reads.

## See also

- [Test TV apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv), the full TV reference
- [Supported platforms](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/)
- [Press Keycode](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#press-keycode)
- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/protected-apps

# Test apps that block screenshots or USB debugging

> Automate a banking or streaming app on a locked phone, with a Bluetooth dongle for input and a camera for eyes.

Some apps can't be tested the usual way. Banking and streaming apps often block screenshots, so a driver sees a black screen. Locked company phones and retail devices don't allow USB debugging or developer mode, so Appium can't connect at all.

Optics can still test them. It needs no automation software on the device. A **BLE dongle** pairs with the phone as an ordinary Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, and a **camera** pointed at the screen shows Optics what's there. Optics reads text in the camera picture with OCR, finds icons with image matching, then moves the pointer and taps.

This page helps you decide whether you need this setup and points you to each step. [Test production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production) is the full reference.

## Decide if you need it

Use the Bluetooth and camera setup when:

- **The app blocks screenshots.** The camera sees the screen anyway.
- **USB debugging or developer mode isn't allowed** on the device.
- **You monitor the live app.** The same journey runs on a real, unmodified device and app, the way a customer uses it.

If Appium or a browser driver can reach the device, use them instead. They're faster, read the UI tree directly, and support every keyword. See [Supported platforms](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/).

If Appium works and the app blocks screenshots only on some screens, keep Appium and add a camera for those screens. See [Add a camera to an Appium run](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#add-a-camera-to-an-appium-run).

## Get the hardware

- **A USB serial BLE HID dongle**, which plugs into your machine as a serial port.
- **A camera or capture card** that your machine sees as a webcam, or a TCP frame server that sends a picture on request.
- **A stand** that holds the camera square over the screen, so the picture doesn't shift between runs.

You also need an OCR engine, such as EasyOCR, to read text in the camera picture.

## Set up

### Install the engines

```shell
$ optics setup --install ble easyocr
```

### Pair the dongle and frame the screen

Pair the dongle with the device like any Bluetooth keyboard. Then mount the camera straight on, with the screen upright and filling the picture edge to edge. [Set up](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#set-up) shows how to find the dongle's serial port on macOS, Linux and Windows.

### Write config.yaml

Enable the `ble` driver with the dongle's port and the screen size, a `camera_screenshot` element source, and an OCR engine. Copy the [example config](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#write-configyaml) and change the port and sizes.

### Calibrate the pointer

Tap a far corner with `Press By Percentage,90,90` and adjust the pointer units until the tap lands. [Calibrate the pointer](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#calibrate-the-pointer) has the five steps. Calibrate again whenever you move the camera or change the device.

## Write the test with visible text

There's no UI tree on this setup, so XPath doesn't work. Every element is text that OCR can read on screen, or a cropped image of an icon. Start the app by tapping its icon on the home screen, because Launch App doesn't work over Bluetooth:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Birch,Press Element,Birch
Open Birch,Assert Presence,Sign in,20
Sign in,Enter Text,Email,ava@birch.shop
Sign in,Enter Text,Password,@:trailrunner
Sign in,Press Element,Sign in
Sign in,Assert Presence,Trail Runner 2,20
```

Enter Text finds the field by OCR, taps it, then types through the Bluetooth keyboard. The `@:` prefix masks the password in logs. See [Keep data in elements too](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define#keep-data-in-elements-too).

## Know the limits

- **No app launch.** Launch App and Launch Other App don't work. Start the app by hand, or tap its icon.
- **No phone-only keys.** A Bluetooth keyboard has no Back, Volume or Power key. Tap the app's own back button.
- **No end-of-run error detection.** It needs the page source. Add Assert Presence checks for the error messages you care about.
- **Scroll moves up and down only.**

[What works and what doesn't](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#what-works-and-what-doesnt) lists every keyword, and [Known gaps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#known-gaps) covers version-specific issues.

## Make text easier to read

Most failures on this setup come from the camera picture. Light the screen evenly, avoid glare, and keep the camera in focus. When the same word appears twice, search one part of the screen with an [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest).

## See also

- [Test production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production), the full reference
- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images)
- [Engines reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/ai-agent-phone

# Let your AI agent drive a real phone over MCP

> Give Claude Code, Cursor or Codex eyes and hands on a real Android phone or iPhone over MCP.

Your coding agent can read code, but it can't see your app running. `optics mcp` changes that. It is a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server. It shows your agent the phone's screen as a list of rows, and lets it tap, type and check on those rows. The agent can open the app, tap through a flow, reproduce a bug, then write what it did as a test you run again later.

Optics doesn't call any AI service in this mode. The model is whichever one your agent already uses.

This page covers the phone case from start to finish. [Let your AI agent build tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent) covers browsers and every client, and the [MCP server reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp) lists every tool.

## Before you begin

- **An MCP client**, such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Claude Desktop or VS Code.
- **A phone the agent can reach through Appium.** Optics drives phones through an Appium server on your machine.
  - **Android**: turn on USB debugging, connect the cable and accept the prompt. Check that `adb devices` lists the phone. See [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android).
  - **iPhone**: a Mac with Xcode, Developer Mode on the phone, and WebDriverAgent signed with your Apple developer team. See [Test on a real device](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios#test-on-a-real-device).
- **The Appium server running** in a terminal: `appium`.

An emulator or simulator works the same way, if you'd rather start there.

## Set up

### Install the MCP server

The installer always includes the MCP server. Add the Appium engine if you do not have it:

```shell
$ optics setup --install appium
```

With pip, install both extras in the same environment as Optics:

```shell
$ pip install "optics-framework[mcp,appium]"
```

### Add Optics to your agent

**Claude Code**

```shell
$ claude mcp add optics -- optics mcp
```
**Cursor**

Add this to `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project, or `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project:

`.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "optics": { "command": "optics", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```
**Codex**

```shell
$ codex mcp add optics -- optics mcp
```
**Other clients**

Most clients read a JSON file that lists MCP servers, in this shape:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "optics": { "command": "optics", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```

If your agent can't find `optics`, use its full path, for example `~/.optics/bin/optics`.

### Ask for a flow

Tell the agent which phone and app to use, and what to do. Give it the Appium URL and the capabilities, including the phone's serial from `adb devices` as `udid`:

```text
Use the optics tools to start an appium session at http://127.0.0.1:4723
with platformName Android, udid R58M12ABCDE and appPackage com.birch.shop.
Sign in as ava@birch.shop, add Trail Runner 2 to the cart, and check
that the cart shows 1 item. Tell me each step you took.
```

For an iPhone, use `platformName iOS`, the phone's `udid` and the app's `bundleId`.

## What the agent does

A typical session goes like this:

1. **Start a session.** `start_session` connects to Appium with your capabilities, opens the app and returns the first screen as rows, such as `e7 button "Sign in" [tap] #sign_in`.
2. **Act.** The agent calls `tap`, `type_text` and `scroll` on a ref such as `e7`. Optics uses a locator that matches only that element. Each reply shows what changed on the screen. For a system key, the agent calls `press_key` with `back` or an Android key number such as `66`. `press_key` refuses a ref.
3. **Check.** It calls `check` with the text that proves the step worked, such as `present: ["1 item"]`. An action that has `expect_present` or `expect_absent` waits up to 5 seconds for the text.
4. **End the session.** `terminate_session` closes the app.

The agent taps by reference, not by position. The server hides coordinate taps by default, because tests that guess positions break on any other screen size. See [Coordinate taps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp#coordinate-taps).

## Keep the run as a test

What the agent did on the phone can become a suite you run without it. Ask it to save the flow:

```text
Read optics://session/{id}/steps and optics://project-format, and write
the steps you ran as an Optics suite in ./checkout, with a config.yaml
for this phone. Run optics dry_run on it and fix any errors.
```

The steps resource gives the module and element rows of each step that passed. A typed password shows as `<redacted>`. Put the real value in the elements file, or read it from an environment variable. The agent writes the same CSV files a person would: test cases, modules and elements. Review them like a colleague's pull request, then run them:

```shell
$ optics execute checkout
```

The run writes a JUnit report and screenshots to `execution_output/`. See [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results).

## Know the limits

- **No loops or conditions as tools.** `Run Loop`, `Condition` and the other flow-control keywords only work inside suite files. The agent can still write them there.
- **No save tool.** The agent writes the suite files from the steps resource and `optics://project-format`.
- **Sessions are private to the server.** `optics serve` and `optics live` cannot see an MCP session. It ends when the server stops, or after 15 minutes without a call. With two phones open, the agent must pass `session_id` on each call.
- **Apps that block screenshots.** The agent sees what the driver sees. For an app that blocks screenshots, see [Test apps that block screenshots](https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/protected-apps).

## See also

- [Let your AI agent build tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent)
- [MCP server reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp)
- [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android)
- [Test iOS apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios)

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/optics-vs-maestro

# Optics vs Maestro

> Compare two open-source UI test frameworks on platforms, test format, finding elements, TVs, AI agents and where tests run.

Optics and Maestro both let you write end-to-end UI tests as plain files, run them on emulators, devices and browsers, and hand a device to an AI agent over MCP. Both are open source under Apache 2.0. They differ in what they can reach, how they find things on screen, and where tests run.

This page sets out the facts so you can pick the one that fits your apps. Maestro facts come from [Maestro's documentation](https://docs.maestro.dev) and its [GitHub repository](https://github.com/mobile-dev-inc/maestro), checked in October 2026. Maestro changes quickly, so check its docs for anything that matters to your decision.

## At a glance

| | Optics | Maestro |
|---|---|---|
| Licence | Apache 2.0. No paid edition. | Apache 2.0 for the open-source CLI. [Maestro Cloud](https://docs.maestro.dev/maestro-cloud) is a hosted service that needs an account. |
| Android | Emulators and real phones, through Appium | Emulators and physical devices |
| iOS | Simulators and signed real devices, through Appium | Simulators. Its README says physical iOS devices aren't supported yet. |
| Web | Playwright (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, local or remote, with phone emulation) or Selenium (Chrome or Firefox). Real Chrome and Safari on phones through Appium. | Beta, Chromium only |
| TV | Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS | Android TV remote keys in `pressKey`. Tizen and webOS aren't listed as supported platforms. |
| Locked devices | Bluetooth mouse and keyboard plus a camera, no software on the device | Not covered in its docs |
| How it drives the app | Through a driver you run: Appium, Playwright, Selenium or a BLE dongle | A single binary that drives the app through the accessibility layer, with no separate drivers. The CLI needs Java 17 or newer. |
| Test format | CSV or YAML rows of keywords, split into test cases, modules and elements. Also Python and Robot Framework. | YAML flows, with JavaScript for logic |
| Finding elements | Several values per element, then XPath, UI-tree text, OCR and image matching in turn | Selectors on the accessibility layer, such as text and id |
| AI agent support | `optics mcp`, a separate extra | `maestro mcp`, built into the CLI |
| Where tests run | Your machine or CI. No hosted service. | Your machine or CI, or Maestro Cloud |

## Platforms

Optics drives Android and iOS apps through [Appium](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android), websites through [Playwright or Selenium](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web), and TV apps through Appium's TV drivers. iOS tests run on simulators or on a signed real device. See [Supported platforms](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/).

Maestro's [supported platforms](https://docs.maestro.dev/get-started/supported-platform) page lists Android emulators and physical devices, iOS simulators, and web. Its [web support](https://docs.maestro.dev/get-started/supported-platform/web-browser) is in beta and runs on Chromium only. Maestro works with native, React Native and Flutter apps, and its docs cover moving between apps and into system settings.

**If you need to test on a physical iPhone, Optics supports it today.** Maestro's README says that physical iOS devices aren't supported yet.

## TV apps

Optics tests [Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv) through Appium, with remote-control keys. On Tizen and webOS, Press Element and Enter Text move the focus for you, Press Keycode sends keys such as `UP` and `ENTER`, and touch keywords fail with E0105.

Maestro's [`pressKey`](https://docs.maestro.dev/reference/commands-available/presskey) command includes Android TV remote keys, such as `Remote Dpad Up` and `Remote Media Play Pause`. Its supported platforms page doesn't list Tizen or webOS.

## Locked devices and apps that block screenshots

Optics can test a device that has no automation software on it. A [BLE dongle](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production) pairs with it as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, and a camera shows Optics the screen. This works when USB debugging is off or the app blocks screenshots. See [Test apps that block screenshots](https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/protected-apps).

Maestro's docs don't cover this kind of setup.

## Test format

An Optics test is rows in CSV or YAML files. Each row is a keyword and its values, such as `Press Element,${sign_in}`. Steps live in reusable modules, test cases list modules, and elements live in their own file, so a changed button means one edit. Anyone who can use a spreadsheet can read the suite. You can also call the same keywords from [Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python) or [Robot Framework](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot). See [Write a test suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write).

A Maestro test is a [flow](https://docs.maestro.dev/maestro-flows), a YAML file of commands such as `tapOn` and `assertVisible`. Logic and data go in [JavaScript](https://docs.maestro.dev/maestro-flows/javascript/javascript-overview), with `runScript` and `evalScript`.

## Finding elements

Optics gives each element several identities and tries them in order. You can list an XPath, visible text and an image for the same button. Text is looked up in the UI tree first, then read from a screenshot with OCR. Images are found by matching a cropped picture on the screen. When a redesign breaks one value, the next one takes over. See [How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/).

On top of that, optional [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal) asks an AI model to finish a step when every value fails. It's off by default.

Maestro finds elements through the accessibility layer, with [selectors](https://docs.maestro.dev/reference/selectors/core-selectors) such as text and id. Its docs describe experimental AI commands: [`assertWithAI`](https://docs.maestro.dev/reference/commands-available/assertwithai) checks the screen against a sentence, and [`extractTextWithAI`](https://docs.maestro.dev/reference/commands-available/extracttextwithai) reads text from a screenshot into a variable. Its docs don't describe finding an element to tap by OCR or by a template image.

**If your app draws text in images, canvases or video players, Optics can find it.** Its OCR and image fallbacks work when the UI tree is empty.

## Waiting

Maestro [waits automatically](https://docs.maestro.dev/get-started/what-is-maestro) for content and animations, so you rarely add sleeps.

In Optics, assertions such as Assert Presence wait up to their timeout. On Playwright, actions also wait up to 10 seconds for their element. On Appium and Selenium, actions do not wait, so put an assertion before a step that needs a new screen. See [Action keywords don't wait](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/#action-keywords-dont-wait).

## Creating tests and AI agents

Optics has four ways to create a test, and each writes the same files:

- [Write it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write) in a spreadsheet or editor.
- [Record it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) in `optics live`, a terminal session that runs each step on the device and saves the ones that work.
- [Describe it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe) in plain English, and an AI model drives the app.
- [Delegate it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent) to your AI agent through `optics mcp`.

The `optics mcp` server gives the agent ten tools to look, tap, type, scroll and check, plus `run_keyword` for every other keyword. Each action returns what changed on screen. After the run, the agent reads the recorded steps as a ready suite for `optics execute`. See the [MCP server reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp).

Maestro has [Maestro Studio](https://docs.maestro.dev/maestro-studio), a desktop app for building and debugging flows visually. Its [MCP server](https://docs.maestro.dev/get-started/maestro-mcp) ships inside the CLI. It lets the agent inspect the screen, take screenshots, run inline YAML and submit runs to Maestro Cloud, and it includes Maestro Viewer, a web view of the device.

## Running and reporting

Optics runs on your machine or in CI. A run writes a JUnit report and annotated screenshots to `execution_output/`, and [error detection](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection) can fail a run that ends on a crash dialog. One run uses one device. To test several devices at once, start one `optics execute` process per device. See [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci).

The Maestro CLI runs flows locally or in CI. It writes JUnit or HTML reports, and its [`--shards` options](https://docs.maestro.dev/maestro-cli/maestro-cli-commands-and-options) split a run across connected devices. Maestro Cloud runs flows in parallel on hosted devices, and needs a Maestro Cloud account.

## Which one fits

Choose **Optics** when you need:

- Smart TVs on Tizen or webOS, physical iPhones, or locked devices.
- Elements that the UI tree can't see, found with OCR or image matching.
- Suites that non-developers read and edit in a spreadsheet.
- Python or Robot Framework from the same keywords.

Choose **Maestro** when you want:

- A single binary with no Appium server to run.
- Automatic waiting with no extra assertions.
- A desktop app for building tests visually.
- A hosted service that runs suites in parallel for you.

## See also

- [What Optics adds to Appium](https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/optics-and-appium)
- [Get started with Optics](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/)
- [Frequently asked questions](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/faq)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/optics-and-appium

# What Optics adds to Appium

> Optics runs on top of Appium. Keep your Appium server and devices, and add readable suites, fallback locators, OCR and AI agents.

Optics doesn't replace Appium. For Android, iOS and TV apps, Optics drives the device **through** an Appium server. Appium still talks to the device. Optics decides what to press, finds it on screen several ways, and turns the steps into a suite anyone on the team can read.

If you already run Appium, you keep your server, drivers, devices and capabilities. Optics adds a layer on top.

## What stays the same

- **The Appium server.** You run it as before, locally or remotely. Set its address as `url` in `config.yaml`. A device farm works too, as long as you can reach its Appium server.
- **The drivers.** UiAutomator2 for Android and Android TV, XCUITest for iOS, and the Tizen and webOS drivers for TVs.
- **Your capabilities.** Optics passes your capabilities to Appium. It adds a few defaults, such as a 1-second idle wait, and your own values replace them. See [Appium capabilities](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#appium-capabilities).
- **Your inspector.** [Appium Inspector](https://github.com/appium/appium-inspector) still shows each element's id, text and XPath.
- **Driver commands.** The Execute Script keyword runs Appium `mobile:` commands. See [Execute Script](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#execute-script).

## What Optics adds

### Tests anyone can read

An Optics test is rows in CSV or YAML files, not code. Each row is a keyword and its values:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Sign in,Enter Text,${email_field},ava@birch.shop
Sign in,Press Element,${sign_in}
Sign in,Assert Presence,Picked for you,20
```

Steps live in reusable modules, and test cases list the modules they run. Testers can write and review the suite in a spreadsheet. See [Write a test suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write).

### Locators that fall back

An Appium locator either matches or fails. In Optics, an element can have several values, and Optics tries them in order:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
sign_in,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']
sign_in,Sign in
sign_in,sign_in.png
```

When a redesign changes the id, the text value takes over. Name the element once, and every step that uses `${sign_in}` follows. See [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define).

### OCR and image matching

Text drawn inside an image, a canvas or a video player isn't in the UI tree, so Appium can't find it. Optics can. It reads text from a screenshot with OCR, and finds icons by matching a cropped picture. It uses them only after the UI tree fails, because they're slower. See [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images).

Optional [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal) goes one step further. When every value fails, an AI model looks at the screen and tries to finish the step. It's off by default.

### A live recorder

`optics live` opens a terminal session next to the device. You type a step, it runs straight away, and the steps that work are saved as a module. You can also switch to plain-English mode and let an AI model drive. See [Record a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) and [Describe a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe).

### Data-driven tests

`Run Loop` runs one module for each value in a list, such as each user or search term. See [Run a flow with different data](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven).

### An MCP server for AI agents

`optics mcp` lets an AI agent such as Claude Code or Cursor drive the device through Optics keywords, then write the suite. See [Let your AI agent drive a real phone over MCP](https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/ai-agent-phone).

### Web pages without context switches

In Appium, a test that enters a WebView or Chrome must switch contexts and back. Optics stays in the native context. A `css=` or DOM XPath locator finds the element in Chrome, Safari or a WebView, and the tap is native. See [Test mobile websites](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/mobile-web).

### Results and error screens

`optics execute` writes a JUnit report and a screenshot of each step. See [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results). [Error detection](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection) fails a run that ends on a crash dialog or an error message you list.

### Targets beyond Appium

The same keywords run on websites through [Playwright or Selenium](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web). Between phones and browsers, only `config.yaml` changes. On [locked devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production), Optics skips Appium and taps through a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, with a camera watching the screen.

## Keep your code if you want it

If your team writes tests in Python, you don't have to give that up. The `Optics` class exposes every keyword as a method, so you keep the fallbacks, OCR and image matching inside pytest. Robot Framework works the same way. See [Use Optics from Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python) and [Use Optics in Robot Framework](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot).

`optics generate` goes the other way: it turns a CSV suite into a pytest or Robot Framework file. See [Generate pytest or Robot code](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/generate).

## Move existing Appium tests

Optics has no importer for Appium scripts. Rebuild each flow by [recording](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) it in `optics live`, or ask an AI agent to explore the app and write the suite through [MCP](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent). Your config can point at the Appium server and capabilities you already use.

## Get started

- [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android): Set up Appium and adb, then run on a phone or emulator.
- [Test iOS apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios): Run on a simulator or a signed device with XCUITest.
- [Test TV apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv): Drive Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS.
- [Optics vs Maestro](https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/optics-vs-maestro): Compare Optics with a framework that doesn't use Appium.

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/

If you're new to Optics, start with the [quickstart](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/quickstart) and come back here when you need a detail.

- [CLI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli): Every `optics` command, its flags, what it writes and its exit codes.
- [config.yaml](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config): Every setting in a project's config.yaml, with examples for each platform.

# Keywords

> Every keyword you can use in a step, grouped by what it does.

A keyword is one action or check, such as `Press Element` or `Assert Presence`. Each row of a module is one keyword followed by its parameters. This page covers the rules every keyword shares, then lists all of them.

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Sign In,Enter Text,${email_field},ana@birch.example
Sign In,Press Element,${sign_in}
Sign In,Assert Presence,Welcome,20
```

## Keyword names

Write keyword names in Title Case in CSV and YAML files: `Press Element`, `Assert Presence`. In `optics live`, the MCP server and Python, the same keyword is written in snake_case: `press_element`, `assert_presence`.

The runner ignores capitalization and collapses spaces, so `Press Element`, `press element` and `press_element` all reach the same keyword. If you misspell a name, the error suggests the closest match. Run `optics list` to print every keyword name in snake_case.

## Parameters

Parameters are positional. They fill the keyword's parameters in the order shown in each parameter table on these pages.

To set a parameter by name, write `name=value`. This works only when `name` is a real parameter of that keyword. Use it to skip parameters you want to leave at their defaults:

```csv
Browse,Press Element,Trail Runner 2,index=1
```

Here `index=1` sets the fifth parameter of Press Element and leaves `repeat`, `offset_x` and `offset_y` at their defaults.

**Common mistake:**
Leaving a cell empty doesn't skip a parameter. Empty cells are dropped, so the next value slides into the empty slot. `Press By Percentage,50,90,,tap_cta` sets `repeat` to `tap_cta` and fails. Write `Press By Percentage,50,90,event_name=tap_cta` instead.

A value like `css=#cart` stays positional, because `css` is not a parameter name. When a keyword's first parameter is `element`, its first `text=`, `css=` or `xpath=` value is the element, unless you also write `element=`. For example, `Enter Text,text=Name,Ava` types `Ava` into the field `text=Name`. Values that start with `/`, `//` or `(` are never treated as named, and `==`, `!=`, `<=` and `>=` don't count as `=`.

**Note:**
Steps inside a module that runs through [Execute Module, Run Loop or Condition](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow) don't support `name=value`, except `store_as=`. Write every parameter positionally there.

### Every value is a string

Each keyword receives its parameters as text and converts them itself. Timeouts, counts, `index`, `repeat`, lengths and swipe percentages must be whole numbers. A decimal such as `2.5` fails the step. The exceptions are the `aoi_*` values and the `timeout` of Assert Text and Select Dropdown Option. Timeouts are always in seconds.

## Element arguments

Many keywords take an `element`. Optics looks at the text you pass and decides what kind of locator it is. The checks run in this order, and the first match wins:

| If the value… | Optics reads it as |
|---|---|
| starts with `text=` | Text to find on screen |
| starts with `text_only:` | Text to find with OCR (reading the screenshot) only, skipping the app's UI tree |
| ends with `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg` or `.bmp` | An image file name to find on screen |
| starts with `css=` | A CSS selector |
| starts with `xpath=`, `/`, `//` or `(` | An XPath, a path through the app's UI tree |
| starts with `id:` | An id locator, which no element source supports |
| starts with `android.` or `xcui` | A UI class name |
| contains `[` and `]`, starts with `.`, starts with `#` followed by a letter, `_` or `-`, or starts with a tag such as `input`, `button`, `div` or `h1` followed by `[`, `#` or `.` | A CSS selector |
| anything else | Text to find on screen |

Text is matched against the app's UI tree first, then with OCR if you configured text detection. Image file names are matched by file name only, and Optics finds the file anywhere in your project folder. See [Text and images](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) for how matching works.

**Common mistake:**
Plain text that looks like another locator type is read as that type. `(optional)` starts with `(`, so it's read as an XPath. `Price [USD]` and `.com` are read as CSS selectors. Write `text=(optional)`, `text=Price [USD]` or `text=.com` to force text.

Other pitfalls:

- `id:` locators always fail. No element source supports them. Use an XPath such as `//*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/cart"]`.
- The `text=` prefix is understood by the Appium and Playwright element sources. OCR and Selenium search for the whole value, including `text=`, so use it only where you need it.
- The `xpath=` prefix works on Playwright and in web pages on Appium. Use a bare `//…` XPath for native apps and on Selenium.
- On Playwright, the prefixes `id=`, `label=`, `placeholder=`, `role=`, `data-testid=`, `data-test=` and `data-test-id=` also work. See [Locators for web pages](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web#locators-for-web-pages).
- `.tif` and `.tiff` files aren't treated as images. Save templates as `.png`.
- On Samsung Tizen and LG webOS TVs, `text=` and `css=` locators search the app's DOM. `text=` matches the visible text, `aria-label`, `title` or `alt` of an element exactly. See [TV](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv#find-elements-and-move-focus).

Most of the time you pass `${name}` instead and define the locator in your elements file. See [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define).

## Variables

A cell that is exactly `${name}` is replaced with the value of `name` from your elements file, from a keyword that wrote it ([Read Data, Evaluate, Date Evaluate, Run Loop, Invoke API](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow)), or from [`store_as`](#store-as).

When an element has several values, Optics tries each one in order until the element is found. It moves on only when the element isn't found. Any other error fails the step at once. If `name` isn't defined anywhere, the step fails before the keyword runs.

Each `${name}` inside a longer cell is replaced with the first value of `name` when the step runs. A cell can hold several variables, such as `${a}-${b}`. If a `name` is not defined, the step fails with error E0403. Write `$${name}` to keep the text `${name}` as it is.

```csv
Profile,Enter Text,${name_field},Hi ${first} ${last}!
Profile,Enter Text,${note_field},$${first}
```

With `first` set to `Ava` and `last` set to `Lee`, the first step types `Hi Ava Lee!` and the second step types `${first}`. Condition, Read Data and Evaluate use their own rules for `${name}`. See [Flow control keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow).

See [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables) for how values are stored and passed between steps.

## Areas of interest

Keywords that find one element take four optional parameters: `aoi_x`, `aoi_y`, `aoi_width` and `aoi_height`. They limit the search to a rectangle of the screen, in percent from 0 to 100. The defaults `0`, `0`, `100`, `100` mean the whole screen.

```csv
Checkout,Press Element,Pay now,aoi_y=50,aoi_height=50
```

This searches the bottom half of the screen only. Assertion keywords don't take an area of interest. See [Area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest).

## Picking one of several matches

`index` picks which match to use when more than one element matches. It starts at `0`, the first match. `index=1` is the second match.

- Image matches are counted top to bottom, then left to right.
- On Appium, text matches are counted in UI tree order.
- On Playwright, visible matches of every kind of locator are counted in page order.
- On Appium, `index` doesn't apply to XPath in native apps. Write `(//android.widget.Button[@text="Add to cart"])[2]` to pick the second XPath match. XPath counts from 1.
- On Selenium, a non-zero `index` skips the native lookup, so only OCR and image matching can use it.

A text locator on Appium, or any locator on Playwright, can match more than one element. Then the log shows a warning, such as `'Add to cart' matches 6 elements; using the one at index 1.` Add `index=` or a more specific locator to pick another.

## Event names

Most action and app keywords take an optional `event_name`. When you set it, Optics records a timestamped event with that label right before the action. Events show in the live console and are sent to an events endpoint if you configured one. They never change whether a step passes.

## When action keywords wait

On Playwright, Press Element, Enter Text and the other action keywords wait for the element up to `element_timeout_ms`, which is 10 seconds by default. See [Timeouts](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web#timeouts).

On Appium and Selenium, action keywords look at the current screen once. If the element is not there yet, the step fails at once. Put an assertion before an action when the next screen can be slow to load:

```csv
Search,Assert Presence,${search_bar},15
Search,Enter Text,${search_bar},Trail Runner 2
```

Use [Detect And Press](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#detect-and-press) for pop-ups that may or may not appear. See [Verification keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/verification).

## Keywords that never fail a step

These keywords pass even when you might expect a failure. Don't rely on them as checks.

- **Validate Screen** returns false when nothing is found but never fails.
- **Detect And Press** passes and skips the tap when the element doesn't appear.
- **Force Terminate App** on Appium logs any error and passes.
- **Swipe** and **Scroll** on Appium log driver errors and pass.
- **Assert Presence** and **Assert Visibility** pass without checking when every element you give is an `id:` locator or a class name.
- **Initialise Setup** does nothing.

## Store a result

Add `store_as=name` to a step to keep what the keyword returns in the variable `name`. Later steps read it as `${name}`, also in later test cases. A new value replaces the old value.

```csv
Product,Get Text,${price_label},store_as=price
Cart,Assert Text,${cart_total},${price}
```

These keywords return a value:

- Launch App, Get App Version and Get Driver Session Id
- Get Text and Execute Script
- Assert Presence, Assert Visibility and Validate Screen, which return `True` or `False`, and Assert Equality, which returns `True`
- Capture Screenshot, Capture Pagesource, Get Interactive Elements and Get Screen Elements

Lists and objects are kept as JSON.

- `store_as=` with no name fails with error E0403 "store_as needs a name, e.g. store_as=balance."
- A keyword that returns nothing fails with error E0403 "Cannot store 'price': the keyword returned no value." Action keywords, Validate Element, Is Element and Assert Text return nothing.

Over [`optics serve`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli), MCP and [Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python), the value is also returned to you.

| Get Screen Elements | Take a screenshot and list every element | [Get Screen Elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/verification#get-screen-elements) |

### Flow control

| Keyword | What it does | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Execute Module | Run another module | [Execute Module](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow#execute-module) |
| Run Loop | Repeat a module a number of times or once per value | [Run Loop](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow#run-loop) |
| Condition | Run a module only when a condition is true | [Condition](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow#condition) |
| Read Data | Load a value from a CSV or JSON file or an environment variable | [Read Data](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow#read-data) |
| Evaluate | Compute an expression and save the result | [Evaluate](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow#evaluate) |
| Date Evaluate | Add or subtract days from a date and save it | [Date Evaluate](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow#date-evaluate) |
| Invoke API | Call an HTTP API and save values from the response | [Invoke API](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow#invoke-api) |

## Deprecated keywords

Press Checkbox and Press Radio Button still work but log a warning. Use [Press Element](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#press-element) instead. Swipe Seekbar To Right Android fails on Appium. Use [Swipe From Element](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#swipe-from-element) instead.

## Where each keyword works

- **CSV and YAML suites, `optics live` and `optics serve`** have every keyword on this page.
- **The MCP server** gives 10 core tools by default. Its `run_keyword` tool runs most other keywords, but not the flow control keywords. See [MCP server](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp).
- **Python and Robot Framework** have every keyword except Execute Module, Initialise Setup and the three deprecated ones. Some parameters differ. See [Write tests in Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python).
- **`optics generate`** skips flow-control keywords and a few others when it converts a suite to code.

## Python and Robot Framework only

These keywords exist only in the [Python library](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python) and the [Robot Framework library](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot). The CSV and YAML runner reports them as unknown keywords.

| Keyword | What it does |
|---|---|
| Setup | Create a session from a config dictionary or YAML text |
| Setup From File | Create a session from a config file |
| Quit | End the session |
| Add Element | Add a value to a variable, after any values it already has |
| Get Element Value | Return the list of values for a variable |
| Add API | Load API definitions for Invoke API |
| Add Module | Define a module for Run Loop and Condition |
| Add Testcase | Set the session's test cases |
| Add Error Definitions | Add on-screen error definitions |
| Capture And Detect Errors | Check the current screen for defined errors and return any matches |
| Press Element With Index | Press Element with an index |
