### Test cases end as ERROR with `E0106`

The driver session ended during the run. The Appium or Selenium server stopped, or it dropped the session. The test case in progress and each later test case is `ERROR` in the report. Optics does not reconnect.

Find out why the server stopped, start it again, and run the suite. See [`E0106`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/errors#e01-driver-and-session).

### Enter Text or Press Element acts before the page loads

Action keywords act on the screen as it is at that moment. They don't wait for a page or screen to finish loading, so they fail or act on the wrong screen.

Put `Assert Presence` before the action, which waits up to 30 seconds by default: `Search,Assert Presence,${search_bar},15`. Use `Detect And Press` for pop-ups that may or may not appear. See [Action keywords don't wait](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/#action-keywords-dont-wait).

### Condition with numbers fails with `E0403`

Condition compares values as text, so `${count} > 5` can't be evaluated.

Compare with quoted values: `${count} == '7'` or `${status} == 'ready'`. For greater-than or less-than, compute the result with Evaluate first, then test it: see [Compare numbers](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow#compare-numbers).

### `ValueError: invalid literal for int()`

A parameter that must be a whole number got something else. Two causes are common: a timeout or count with a decimal point, such as `2.5`, and an empty cell. Empty cells are dropped, so the values after them shift left into the wrong parameter.

Use whole numbers. To skip a parameter, name the next one instead of leaving a gap: `Press Element,${sign_in},index=1`.

### A test runs as setup or teardown

A test case with "setup" or "teardown" in its name, such as *Setup wizard works*, runs before or after every other test case.

Remove those words from the name. See [Setup and teardown](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files#setup-and-teardown).

### Every step takes about 10 seconds on Appium

Appium waits for the app to be idle before each step. An app with animations or a video is never idle, so each wait runs to its limit. Optics sets this limit to 1 second.

To remove the wait, set it to 0 in the Appium capabilities:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
capabilities:
  appium:settings:
    waitForIdleTimeout: 0
```

See [Appium capabilities](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#appium-capabilities).

### A test step runs nothing

A test case step that names a keyword instead of a module passes without doing anything.

List modules in `test_cases.csv`, and put keywords inside modules in `modules.csv`.

### Validate Screen never fails

Validate Screen returns false when it finds nothing, but it does not fail the step.

To fail on a missing element, use Assert Presence. To fail on wrong text, use `Assert Text,<element>,<expected text>`. See [Keywords that never fail a step](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/#keywords-that-never-fail-a-step).

### Screenshots are missing from a custom output folder

When you set `execution_output_path` yourself, Optics doesn't create the folder. Results and logs create it, but screenshots fail to save without a warning.

Create the folder before the run. See [config.yaml](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#top-level-keys).

### `optics dry_run` fails without a device

A dry run doesn't tap or type, but it still starts the engines in `config.yaml`. Every enabled engine must be installed, a driver must be enabled, and its settings must be valid.

Install the engines with `optics setup --install <name>`, and run `optics doctor <project>` to find what's missing. You don't need a device or a running Appium server for a dry run.

## optics live

### "optics live supports exactly one enabled driver"

`optics live` drives one target at a time, and your `config.yaml` enables more than one driver.

Set `enabled: false` on every driver except the one you want.

### "optics live needs a config.yaml with an enabled driver and elements source"

`optics live` found no config file in the folder. Without a folder argument, it uses the current folder.

Run it from your project folder, or pass the folder: `optics live my-project`. Live has no built-in defaults.

### "No enabled source in config.yaml's elements_sources"

Live needs at least one element source enabled.

Enable the sources for your driver, such as `appium_find_element`, `appium_page_source` and `appium_screenshot`.

### Every step fails with "run `launch_app` first"

The app didn't open when the session started, so no keyword can run (`E0101`).

Check the server and device with `optics doctor <project>`, then type `launch_app` and read its error.

### `[E0901]` Named element is not defined in this project

You typed `${name}`, and no elements file in the project defines it.

Add the name to `test_data/elements.csv`, or type the value directly. Run `/elements` to see the names live found.

### "Unknown keyword: … Keywords use snake_case"

Live didn't recognize the first words you typed as a keyword.

Check the spelling and the suggestion in the message. Press Tab to complete names, or Ctrl+K to browse them.

### `/save` prints "Usage: /save <test_case> <module_name>"

`/save` takes exactly two names, and names can't contain spaces.

Use underscores: `/save Checkout Sign_In`. Rename them in the CSV files afterwards if you like.

### Find the session log

Live writes a full log to `logs/optics_live_<time>.log` in the project folder, and prints its path when you quit. Attach it when you [report a problem](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/#ask-a-question-or-report-a-bug).

## AI features

### "No LLM engine is enabled"

You pressed Ctrl+N in `optics live`, and `config.yaml` has no enabled `llm_models` entry.

Add one, then restart `optics live`:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
llm_models:
  - gemini:
      enabled: true
```

Use `openai` or `anthropic` for those providers. See [Describe a test in plain English](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe#before-you-begin).

### `E0601`: the LLM engine requires an optional dependency

An engine is enabled under `llm_models`, but its extra isn't installed. The message names the engine.

Install it by that name, for example `optics setup --install openai`.

### `E0601`: the LLM engine needs a model or a key

The `openai` and `anthropic` engines have no default model, so set `capabilities.model`. The `openai` engine also stops when it finds no key and no `url`: set `capabilities.api_key`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, or the variable you named in `api_key_env`. See [llm_models](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#llm-models).

### `E0801` or authentication errors from the model

The model provider rejected the request, usually because the key is missing, wrong or out of quota, or the model name is wrong.

Set your engine's key in `capabilities.api_key`, or in the terminal you run Optics from (`GEMINI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or the variable in `api_key_env`). Then check your quota with the provider. See [Environment variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli#environment-variables).

### AI self-heal does nothing

Self-heal needs `ai_self_heal: true`, an enabled `llm_models` entry, the AI engine, a key, and a screenshot source. If any is missing, Optics logs "AI self-heal enabled but no usable LLM" or skips self-heal without a message.

Check each item in [Turn it on](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal#turn-it-on). Self-heal only helps steps that find and act on an element; Assert Presence and other checks never self-heal.

### A plain-English instruction stops before it's done

Each instruction stops after 15 steps, after 3 failed steps in a row, or after 3 taps, swipes or scrolls in a row that are not checked ("Repeated gesture/coordinate actions did not reach the goal"). It also stops when 4 actions in a row do not change the screen ("No progress: the screen did not change after repeated actions.").

Break the goal into smaller instructions, and use the words shown on screen. See [Write goals the model can finish](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe#write-goals-the-model-can-finish).

## Web and Playwright

### The Playwright browser isn't installed

`optics doctor` shows ⚠️ on the `playwright browser` row, or Playwright fails to launch Chromium.

Run `optics setup --install playwright` again. It downloads the Chromium build Playwright needs.

## CI

### Every step passes, but the run fails with `on-screen-error-detection`

When your project has an [error definitions file](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection), Optics checks the final screen for known error messages in `optics execute`. A match adds a failing test case named `on-screen-error-detection` to `junit_output.xml` and to the summary in the terminal. The exit code is `1`.

Open `execution_output/detected_errors_<session>.json` to see which message matched. Fix the app, or the definition if it matched by mistake.

### `optics doctor --check` passes even with a broken config

Without a folder, doctor checks your machine but not any `config.yaml`, so `--check` can't fail on config problems.

Always pass the project: `optics doctor ./my-project --check`.

### The preflight fails in CI

Your CI starts the Appium or Selenium server in a way the preflight check can't reach, or starts it after Optics.

Wait for the server before running Optics. If you know that it is reachable, set `OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1` to skip the check. When the check fails, the report shows each test case as `ERROR` with code `E0102`.

### `junit_output.xml` is cut short

On long runs, Optics may stop before every result is written.

Set `OPTICS_EVENT_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_S` to a higher value, such as `10`. See [Environment variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli#environment-variables).

### CI logs are full of progress output

The live result tree redraws itself, which clutters plain CI logs.

Run `optics execute my-project --no-use-printer`, and set `file_log: true` to keep full logs as build artifacts.

### `--runner pytest` fails

The pytest runner needs the `pytest-cov` package, which Optics doesn't install.

Use the default runner by leaving out `--runner`. To run tests under pytest, generate pytest code with [`optics generate`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/generate) instead.

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/faq

# Frequently asked questions

> Learn what Optics can and can't do, with short answers to the questions people ask most.

Short answers, with links to the pages that explain each one in full. These docs describe Optics 1.11.3.

## About Optics

### Is Optics free and open source?

Yes. Optics is open source under the Apache 2.0 license, and the code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/mozarkai/optics-framework). There's no paid edition, account or license key.

### Does Optics send my data anywhere?

No, not by default. Optics has no telemetry and needs no account. Tests, screenshots and results stay on your machine or CI runner.

Data leaves your machine only through features you turn on:

- **The AI features**, [plain-English mode](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe) and [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal), send screenshots and the screen's UI tree to the provider you configure: Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, or the server in your `url`. A local model keeps them on your machine.
- **Google Cloud Vision** OCR sends screenshots to Google. EasyOCR and Tesseract run locally.
- **Remote OCR and image engines** (`remote_ocr`, `remote_oir`) send screenshots to the URL you configure.
- **Event reporting** sends the events you label with `event_name` to the `eventUrl` in your `event_attributes_json` file, if you set one up.

With the [MCP server](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent), Optics itself calls no AI service. Your agent's client sends what it reads to whichever model it uses.

### What can I test, and where does it run?

Optics tests Android and iOS apps through Appium, websites through Playwright or Selenium, and Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS apps through Appium. It can also drive locked-down [production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production) as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, with a camera watching the screen.

Optics itself runs on macOS, Linux and Windows with Python 3.12 or newer. Testing iOS apps needs a Mac with Xcode. See [Platforms](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/).

### Do I need to know how to code?

No. Tests are rows in CSV or YAML files: a keyword such as `Press Element` and the values it needs. You can [record](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) them by running steps against the live app, or [write](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write) them in a spreadsheet. You'll edit a YAML settings file and use a terminal, but you won't write code. [Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python) and [Robot Framework](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot) are there if you want them.

### What is Optics not good for?

Optics tests what a person does through the interface. Use other tools for unit tests, load testing, API-only contract tests and pixel-by-pixel visual comparison.

## Creating tests

### Should I use CSV or YAML?

Use CSV unless you have a reason not to. CSV opens in any spreadsheet app, and `optics live` saves recordings as CSV. Use YAML when you want a whole suite in one text file that reads well in code review. Both do the same things, and you can mix them in one project. Error definitions are CSV only. See [Write tests in YAML](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/yaml).

### Can people who aren't developers write tests?

Yes. That's what the file format is for. A tester can [record a flow](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) in `optics live` and save it, then edit the CSV files in a spreadsheet. Someone comfortable with a terminal and YAML should set up `config.yaml` once; after that, most work happens in the CSV files.

### Can I import tests from Selenium IDE, Appium or another tool?

No. Optics has no importer. Rebuild the flows by [recording](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) them, or ask an AI agent to explore the app and write the suite through the [MCP server](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent).

Going the other way works: [`optics generate`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/generate) turns a suite into pytest or Robot Framework code. It skips flow-control keywords such as `Run Loop` and `Condition`, so check the output.

### Can AI write my tests?

Yes, two ways. [Describe a flow](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe) in plain English inside `optics live`, and an AI model drives the app and records the steps. Or [connect your AI agent](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent) through MCP and let it explore the app and write the files. Both produce ordinary CSV that you review before you rely on it.

## Running tests

### Can I run tests without a device or browser?

Yes, for a suite that uses only [flow control keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow), such as `Evaluate`, `Condition` and `Run Loop`. Optics needs no driver for it. `optics dry_run` checks any suite without a device, but it still loads the engines in `config.yaml`.

### Can I run tests in parallel?

Not within one run. `optics execute` runs test cases one after another on one device or browser.

To test several devices at once, start a separate `optics execute` process for each one, each with its own project folder and `config.yaml`. Separate folders keep their results apart in each project's `execution_output/`. See [Run the same suite on different devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/organise#run-the-same-suite-on-different-devices).

### How do I run only one test?

Give its name with `--include`. Case does not matter, and `*` and `?` work as wildcards:

```shell
$ optics execute birch-tests --include "Shopper can sign in"
```

Suite Setup and Suite Teardown always run. You can also list names under `include:` and `exclude:` in `config.yaml`. A name that matches no test case stops the run with exit code `3`. See [Run only some test cases](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/organise#run-only-some-test-cases) and the [CLI reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli#pick-test-cases).

### Does Optics retry failed tests?

No. Optics doesn't rerun failed steps or test cases. Within a step, it tries each [fallback value](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define#write-elements) of an element in turn, and assertions such as `Assert Presence` wait up to their timeout. To retry a whole run, rerun the command in your CI.

Before adding retries, look for the cause. Most flaky steps act before the screen is ready; put `Assert Presence` before them. See [Action keywords don't wait](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/#action-keywords-dont-wait).

### Can I run the browser headless?

Yes. With Playwright, set `headless: true` under the driver's `capabilities`. See [Run in CI without a screen](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web#run-in-ci-without-a-screen).

With Selenium, the browser runs wherever your Selenium server runs. A Selenium server in Docker runs the browser inside the container, so no window opens on your machine. See [Web](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web).

### Can I use a remote Appium server or device?

Yes. Set `url` under the `appium` driver to any Appium server you can reach. `optics execute` checks that the server answers before the run starts. See [config.yaml](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#driver-sources).

### What exit code does `optics execute` return?

`0` when every test case passes, and `1` when a test case fails, an error screen is found or the run cannot start. Exit code `2` means that the command line is not valid. Exit code `3` means that `--include` or `--exclude` matches no test case. Optics returns `130` after Ctrl+C and `143` after SIGTERM, and still writes the JUnit report. See [Exit codes](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli#exit-codes).

### Where do the results go?

To `execution_output/` in the project: a `junit_output.xml` report that any CI system can read, screenshots of each step, and logs if you turn them on. See [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results).

### Does Optics hide passwords and keys in its output?

Yes. Optics writes `****` in place of a secret in the console, the logs, `logs.json` and `junit_output.xml`. It masks these items: values that you save under a secret name, values that start with `@:`, secret values in `config.yaml`, passwords in URLs, and secret query parameters. See [Hide sensitive values](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables#hide-sensitive-values).

## AI features

### Which AI models does Optics support?

For plain-English mode and AI self-heal, Optics works with Gemini, Claude and OpenAI models, and with any server that offers an OpenAI-compatible API, such as OpenRouter or a local Ollama. Choose a model that accepts images. See [llm_models](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#llm-models).

The [MCP server](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent) works with any agent that speaks MCP, such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or VS Code, and with whichever model that agent uses.

### Do I need AI to use Optics?

No. Every AI feature is optional and off by default. Recording, writing, running and reporting work without any model or API key.

### What do the AI features cost?

Optics is free. Your model provider bills its usage at its own rates. A local model costs nothing per call.

- **Plain-English mode** makes one model call per step, plus one more to tidy up the steps when the goal is reached. An instruction stops after at most 15 steps.
- **AI self-heal** makes up to six calls for each step it tries to rescue, and none when steps pass normally.
- **MCP** costs whatever your agent's client charges. Optics makes no model calls.

### Will self-heal hide real bugs?

It can. A healed step passes, and the run's summary doesn't say it healed. Turn on `file_log: true` and search the logs for `AI self-heal` after each run, then update the element so the step passes without help. See [Find out what healed](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal#find-out-what-healed).

## Elements

### Why give an element both an XPath and text?

Each fails in different situations, so together they last longer. An XPath is the fastest and most precise way to find an element, but a redesign that changes ids or layout breaks it. Text is readable and survives layout changes, but breaks when the wording changes. List both, and Optics tries them in order until one works. See [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define).

### When should I use images?

Use an image when nothing else identifies the element: an icon with no text or id, something drawn in a game or canvas, or a device you watch through a camera. Image matching is the slowest way to find an element, and a new icon design or theme breaks it, so put it last in the element's values. See [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images).

### Why can't Optics find text that's clearly on screen?

The text is probably drawn inside an image or canvas, so it isn't in the app's UI tree. Enable an [OCR engine](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images#turn-on-ocr) and a screenshot source, and Optics reads the screenshot instead. If the element only appears after a moment, put `Assert Presence` before the step. For more causes, see [Troubleshooting](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/troubleshooting#e0201).

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/glossary

# Glossary

> Learn the terms used across the Optics docs.

Terms are listed alphabetically. Each entry links to the page that explains it in full.

## A

### AOI (area of interest)

An AOI, or area of interest, is a rectangle that limits where Optics looks for an element, given as percentages of the screen from 0 to 100. Use it when the same text or icon appears in several places. See [Search part of the screen](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest).

### Appium

Appium is the open-source automation server Optics uses to drive Android, iOS and TV apps. You run the Appium server yourself, and Optics connects to it at the `url` in `config.yaml`. See [Drivers](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines#drivers).

## B

### BLE driver

The BLE driver makes Optics act as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, for devices that allow no automation software. A camera watches the screen, and Optics finds elements with OCR and image matching. See [Production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production).

### Browser profile

A browser profile is the set of sign-ins, cookies and settings that Chrome or Edge keeps for one person. Set `profile` in the Playwright capabilities, and Optics starts the browser with a temporary copy of it. See [Start signed in with a browser profile](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web#start-signed-in-with-a-browser-profile).

## C

### Capabilities

Capabilities are the settings Optics passes to a driver when it starts a session, such as the device name, the app to open or the browser to use. They go under `capabilities` for each driver in `config.yaml`. See [driver_sources](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#driver-sources).

### config.yaml

`config.yaml` is the settings file in each project. It says which driver to use, how to look at the screen, and how to log and report. See [config.yaml](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config).

### CSV

CSV (comma-separated values) is the plain-text table format most Optics suites use, one row per step. Any spreadsheet app or text editor can open it. See [Choose CSV or YAML](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write#choose-csv-or-yaml).

## D

### Driver

A driver is the engine that controls the target: Appium for phones and TVs, Playwright or Selenium for browsers, or the BLE driver for locked-down devices. You enable one under `driver_sources` in `config.yaml`. See [Drivers](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines#drivers).

### Dry run

A dry run, started with `optics dry_run`, checks a project for unknown keywords, missing modules and undefined variables without tapping or typing anything. Run one before every commit. See [`optics dry_run`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli#optics-dry-run).

## E

### Element

An element is a name for something on screen, such as `sign_in`, plus one or more values that tell Optics how to find it. Steps refer to it as `${sign_in}`. See [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define).

### Element source

An element source is a way for Optics to look at the screen: ask the app for an element, read its UI tree, or take a screenshot. Each driver has its own, listed under `elements_sources` in `config.yaml`. See [Element sources](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines#element-sources).

### Elements file

An elements file is a CSV whose header is `Element_Name,Element_ID`, in any case, listing each element's name and values. The project template keeps it in `test_data/elements.csv`. See [Elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files#elements).

### Engine

An engine is an optional add-on that gives Optics a capability: a driver, an element source, an OCR engine, image matching or an AI model. You install engines with `optics setup` and turn them on in `config.yaml`. See [Engines and extras](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines).

### Error definition

An error definition is a row in a CSV that names a message your app shows when something goes wrong, such as "Something went wrong". At the end of a run, Optics checks the last screen for these messages and reports any it finds. See [Catch error screens](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection).

### Execution output

The execution output is the `execution_output/` folder in a project, where each run writes its JUnit report, screenshots and logs. See [Outputs](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files#outputs).

### Extra

An extra is the pip name for an optional engine, such as `appium`, `easyocr` or `gemini`, installed with `optics setup --install <name>` or `pip install "optics-framework[<name>]"`. Bundles such as `web`, `llm` and `all` install several at once. See [Engines and extras](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines).

## F

### Fallback

A fallback is a second (or third) value for an element that Optics tries when the first one isn't found. For example, an element can have an XPath, then its text, then an image. See [How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/).

## I

### Image detection

Image detection finds an element by matching a small picture of it, called a template, against a screenshot. Turn it on with `templatematch` under `image_detection` in `config.yaml`. See [Turn on image matching](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images#turn-on-image-matching).

### Include and exclude

Include and exclude pick which test cases a run includes or skips, by name. Give them as `--include` and `--exclude` on the command line, or as lists in `config.yaml`. See [Run only some test cases](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/organise#run-only-some-test-cases).

### Index

An index picks one of several matches for the same element, counting from 0, as in `index=1` for the second match. See [Pick one of several matches](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define#pick-one-of-several-matches).

## J

### JUnit report

The JUnit report is `junit_output.xml`, an XML file of every test case's result that CI systems such as GitHub Actions and Jenkins can display. Optics writes it to the execution output after every run. See [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results).

## K

### Keyword

A keyword is one action or check that a step performs, such as `Press Element`, `Enter Text` or `Assert Presence`. Run `optics list` to see them all. See [Keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/).

## L

### LLM

An LLM (large language model) is the AI model behind plain-English mode and self-heal. Optics works with Gemini, Claude and OpenAI, plus OpenAI-compatible servers such as OpenRouter or Ollama, configured under `llm_models` in `config.yaml`. See [llm_models](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#llm-models).

### Locator

A locator is a value that tells Optics how to find an element: an XPath, visible text, a CSS selector or an image file name. Locators live in the elements file. See [Choose the kind of value](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define#choose-the-kind-of-value).

## M

### MCP

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI agents use outside tools. `optics mcp` starts an MCP server that gives an agent Optics keywords as tools. See [Let your AI agent build tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent).

### Module

A module is a named, reusable list of steps, such as *Sign In* or *Add To Cart*. Test cases are made of modules. See [Modules](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/concepts#modules).

## N

### NOT_RUN

`NOT_RUN` is the status of a step or test case that did not start, because an earlier failure or a stop kept it from running. It shows in `junit_output.xml`. See [What each outcome writes](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results#what-each-outcome-writes).

## O

### OCR

OCR (optical character recognition) reads text from a screenshot. Optics uses it to find text the UI tree doesn't contain, such as words drawn inside an image. See [Turn on OCR](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images#turn-on-ocr).

## P

### Page source

The page source is the app's or web page's UI tree written out as text: XML on Android and iOS, HTML on the web. Optics searches it for XPaths and text before it falls back to screenshots. See [How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/).

### Plain-English mode

Plain-English mode is the part of `optics live` where you type a goal in plain English and an AI model works out the steps. Press Ctrl+N to switch to it. See [Describe a test in plain English](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe).

### Playwright

Playwright is a browser automation library that Optics uses as a driver for web testing. It needs no separate server. See [Web](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web).

### Preflight

The preflight is the check `optics execute` runs before a test starts, to make sure the Appium or Selenium server answers and an Android device is connected. Set `OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1` to skip it. See [`optics execute`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli#optics-execute).

### Project

A project is a folder that holds one suite: its `config.yaml`, test cases, modules and elements. Optics finds files anywhere in the folder by their header row. See [Project files](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files).

## S

### Secret masking

Secret masking is the rule that Optics writes `****` in place of a secret in the console, the logs and the reports. A value is secret when its name has a word such as `token`, `password` or `key`. See [Use environment variables and project paths](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#use-environment-variables-and-project-paths).

### Selenium

Selenium is a browser automation tool that Optics can use as a driver for web testing, through a Selenium server or Grid. It supports Chrome and Firefox. See [Web](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web).

### Self-heal

Self-heal is an optional feature in which an AI model looks at the screen and tries to finish a step when Optics can't find its element. Turn it on with `ai_self_heal: true`. See [Recover failing steps with AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal).

### Session

A session is one connection between Optics and a device or browser, from when the driver starts until it closes. Each `optics execute` run, `optics live` session or API session has its own. See [What happens during a run](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/concepts#what-happens-during-a-run).

### Step

A step is one row in a module: a keyword plus the values it needs, such as `Enter Text,${search_bar},Trail Runner 2`. See [Write the steps as modules](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write#write-the-steps-as-modules).

### store_as

`store_as=name` is a cell that keeps the value a keyword returns, such as the text from Get Text. Later steps use it as `${name}`. See [Keep a value for later](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables#keep-a-value-for-later).

### Suite

A suite is all the test cases in one project, run together by `optics execute`. See [how to organize a suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/organise).

### Suite Setup and Suite Teardown

Suite Setup and Suite Teardown are test cases with special names. Suite Setup runs once before every other test case, and Suite Teardown runs once after them, so they're the place to open and close the app. See [Setup and teardown](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files#setup-and-teardown).

## T

### Template (image)

A template is a cropped picture of an element, such as an icon, that image detection looks for on a screenshot. Refer to it by file name in the elements file. See [Capture a good template](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images#capture-a-good-template).

### Test case

A test case is a flow you want to check, made of modules run in order, such as *Shopper can check out*. Each test case passes or fails on its own. See [Test cases](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/concepts#test-cases).

### Text detection

Text detection finds an element by reading the text on a screenshot with an OCR engine, such as EasyOCR or Tesseract. Turn it on under `text_detection` in `config.yaml`. See [Turn on OCR](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images#turn-on-ocr).

## U

### UI tree

The UI tree is the structure of everything an app or web page shows, with each element's type, text and id. Optics reads it through the [page source](#page-source). See [How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/).

## V

### Variable

A variable is a named value written as `${name}` in a step, defined in the elements file or created by a step such as `Evaluate`. Optics replaces it in a whole cell and inside other text. See [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables).

## X

### XPath

An XPath is a path through the app's UI tree that points to one element, such as `//*[@resource-id='login']`. It's the fastest and most precise kind of locator. See [XPath](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define#xpath).

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/privacy

# Privacy

This page covers optics-framework.org and its install scripts. The short version: the site counts how its pages are used, and nothing it counts can identify you.

## This website

optics-framework.org is a static site. It sets no cookies, runs no advertising and loads nothing from third-party servers: the fonts, video and scripts are all served from this domain. Your browser keeps your theme, the docs tabs you pick and the checklist items you tick in its local storage on your device; they are never sent anywhere.

The site is hosted on GitHub Pages behind Cloudflare. Like any web host, GitHub and Cloudflare receive your IP address and request details when you load a page, and may keep them in server logs for security and operations. That processing is covered by the [GitHub General Privacy Statement](https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/privacy-policies/github-general-privacy-statement) and the [Cloudflare Privacy Policy](https://www.cloudflare.com/privacypolicy/).

## What the site counts

To learn which pages help and where people get stuck, the site keeps its own usage counts, stored with Cloudflare and read only by the Optics maintainers. Nothing is shared with or sold to anyone.

For each request it records the page, the time, the response, the kind of client (a browser and its version, a script such as curl, or a named crawler or AI agent), the site that linked to the page and your country. It does not record your IP address.

In the browser, a small script on this domain reports what happens on a page, tagged with a random visit id that lives in your tab's session storage and ends when you close the tab, your device size (mobile, tablet or desktop) and your country. It reports these events:

**Reading:** `view` (a page opened, with the page or site you came from), `campaign` (the `ref` tag of a link you followed), `pref` (your theme, language and reduced-motion setting, once per visit), `section` (a section scrolled into view), `read` (how far down you read and for how long) and `vital` (how fast the page loaded and responded).

**Doing:** `copy` (a command you copied, or the length of other text), `tab` (a tab you picked), `nav` and `out` (a link you followed on this site or to another one), `search` and `result` (what you searched the docs for, how many results it found and which one you opened), `helpful` (your answer to "Was this page helpful?"), `check` (a checklist item you ticked), `details` (a collapsed section you opened), `film` and `scene` (the demo film and animations you played or paused), `theme` and `filter` (the theme toggle and the blog filters), `ui` (the docs menu and search button) and `error` (a script error on the page).

The script sends nothing when your browser asks sites not to track it, through Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track. It never reads what you type outside the docs search box.

## The install scripts

The scripts at `/install` and `/install.ps1` run on your machine. They create a Python environment under `~/.optics` and install the `optics-framework` package from the Python Package Index, so PyPI receives the download request. Fetching a script is counted like any other request; once running, the scripts send nothing about you or your machine anywhere.

## The framework

Optics runs on your own machine or CI and contains no telemetry. Your suites, screenshots and results stay where you run them. If you turn on the optional AI features (natural-language mode in `optics live` or AI self-heal), Optics sends screenshots and page source to the model provider you configure, under that provider's terms.
